Amazingly, all of these weird additives worked perfectly! The callus exploded with cell division. 

Why did they work? Because all those substances secretly contained a brand-new, undiscovered class of hormones that trigger cell division. We now call them 'Cytokinins' (from 'cytokinesis', meaning cell division).

However, Gibberellic acid (a Gibberellin) was NOT part of Skoog's magic recipe. Gibberellins make plants stretch and grow taller, but they are completely useless at making a callus divide in a tissue culture jar. Because the question asks for the 'except' (the one that didn't work / wasn't used), Gibberellic acid is our answer. Science is sometimes just trying everything until something amazing happens!

questions.Question: Given below are some statements about plant growth regulators. A. All GAs are acidic in nature. B. Auxins are antagonists to GAs. C. Zeatin was isolated from coconut milk. D. Ethylene induces flowering in Mango. E. Abscisic acid induces parthenocarpy. Choose the correct set of statements
questions.Hint: Look closely at the names! GAs stand for Gibberellic Acid. Also, Ethylene is famous for ripening, but it's uniquely used by farmers to make mango trees flower synchronously.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's play another game of 'True or False' with our amazing plant hormones! 

Statement A: 'All GAs are acidic in nature.' GA stands for Gibberellin. Scientists have discovered over 100 different types of Gibberellins, and they name them GA1, GA2, GA3, and so on. But do you know what GA actually stands for? 'Gibberellic Acid'! Since they literally have 'acid' in their name, this statement is absolutely TRUE.

Statement B: 'Auxins are antagonists to GAs.' An antagonist is like a superhero's arch-nemesis; they fight against each other. But Auxins and GAs are actually best buddies! They are both growth promoters that work together to make stems longer. The real arch-nemesis (antagonist) to GA is the stress hormone Abscisic Acid (ABA). So, this statement is FALSE.

Statement C: 'Zeatin was isolated from coconut milk.' Zeatin is a naturally occurring Cytokinin (the anti-aging, cell-dividing hormone). It was first discovered in corn kernels (the scientific name for corn is Zea mays, hence 'Zeatin') and it is also found abundantly in coconut milk! This statement is TRUE.

Statement D: 'Ethylene induces flowering in Mango.' Ethylene is a gas mostly known for ripening fruits like bananas and tomatoes. But it has a very special superpower for mango trees: if you spray it, it forces the whole tree to flower at the exact same time, which makes harvesting way easier. This statement is TRUE.

Statement E: 'Abscisic acid induces parthenocarpy.' Parthenocarpy is making seedless fruit. To make a big juicy fruit, you need growth promoters like Auxin or Gibberellin. ABA is a growth inhibitor (the brakes). It would never induce fruit growth! This statement is FALSE.

Since statements A, C, and D are our correct facts, the first option is the winner. Taking it step-by-step makes you a biology master!

questions.Question: Auxin is used by gardeners to prepare weed-free lawns. But no damage is caused to grass as auxin
MCQ_Options: does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants
is rapidly degraded by monocot enzymes
only affects plants with tap roots
causes grass to go dormant instead of dying
questions.Hint: Think about the difference between grass and wide-leaved weeds. Grass is a 'monocot', while most messy weeds are 'dicots'. Auxin acts like a smart-missile that ignores monocots!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you have a beautiful green lawn of grass, but annoying, ugly, broad-leaved weeds keep sprouting up everywhere. If you spray normal poison, you'll kill the weeds, but you'll also kill your precious grass! What you need is a 'smart poison' that only attacks the weeds.

Gardeners found the perfect solution in a synthetic (man-made) Auxin called '2,4-D'. Now, you might be thinking: 'Wait, isn't Auxin a growth promoter? Why would we use a growth hormone to kill a plant?' 

That's the genius of it! When gardeners spray 2,4-D on the lawn, the broad-leaved weeds (which are biologically 'dicots') absorb a massive overdose of this growth hormone. Their cells go totally crazy. They grow so fast and so uncontrollably that their stems twist, their vessels burst, they run out of food, and they literally grow themselves to death! 

But why doesn't the grass die? Grass belongs to a different biological family called 'monocotyledonous plants' (or monocots for short). Monocots have a completely different internal wiring and vessel structure. Their bodies simply do not respond to this synthetic auxin overdose in the same chaotic way. The auxin just sits there without causing the crazy, deadly growth spurt.

Therefore, the correct answer is that this auxin 'does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants'. It's a selective weed killer! It wipes out the dicot weeds by forcing them to grow to death, leaving your monocot grass looking like a perfectly manicured green carpet. Science is pretty clever, isn't it?
questions.Answer: does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants

questions.Question: Formation of interfascicular cambium from fully developed parenchyma cells is an example for
questions.Hint: If a fully trained adult cell decides to 'forget' its specific job and go back to being a baby dividing cell to learn a new job, what is that 'undoing' process called?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about the incredible career path of a plant cell. It's actually a lot like how humans get jobs!

When a plant cell is first born in the root tip or shoot tip (the meristem), it just divides all day. It's like a kid in kindergarten. Eventually, it grows up, graduates, and gets a specific, permanent job—like becoming a 'parenchyma' cell whose job is to store food. This process of graduating and getting a permanent job is called 'Differentiation'.

But plants are amazing survivors. What happens if the plant stem needs to grow much wider to support a heavy tree, or if it gets chopped by an axe? The plant needs new dividing cells to build wood or heal the wound. 

So, it does something magical. It taps those adult parenchyma cells on the shoulder and says, 'Hey, I need you to quit your job, forget everything you know, and go back to being a dividing kindergarten cell.' The adult cell loses its mature features and turns back into a rapidly dividing cell called a 'cambium' (specifically, the interfascicular cambium). 

Because the cell is UNDOING its maturity, we add the prefix 'De-'. The process is called 'Dedifferentiation'. It literally means reversing differentiation! 

(Just to complete the story: once that new cambium divides to make new wood cells, those cells get permanent jobs again. That final step is called 'Re-differentiation'). 

So, a fully developed parenchyma cell turning back into dividing cambium is the perfect textbook example of Dedifferentiation. It's the ultimate biological career change!

questions.Question: Spraying sugarcane crop with which of the following plant growth regulators, increases the length of stem, thus, increasing the yield?
questions.Hint: Think about the hormone famous for causing plants to shoot up in height by expanding the space between their leaves!
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Sugarcane stores its valuable sugar in its stems. To get more sugar, we need longer stems! Imagine the stem of a plant is like a telescope; to make it longer, you need to pull the sections apart. In plants, a special chemical messenger called a hormone acts like the signal to 'pull the telescope open.' Specifically, the hormone responsible for this amazing stem elongation is called Gibberellin. Gibberellins are a class of plant growth regulators that primarily encourage cells to stretch out and divide. When you spray gibberellins on a sugarcane crop in a farm, it tells the stem cells to elongate. This happens mainly in the internodes, which are the spaces on the stem between the leaves. By increasing the length of the internodes, the entire sugarcane stalk grows significantly taller. For sugarcane farmers, this is like pure magic! Longer stems mean a drastically larger volume of space inside the plant to store the sweet sugar juice. In fact, agricultural scientists have calculated that spraying sugarcane with gibberellins can increase the yield by as much as 20 tonnes per acre. It is a wonderful example of how understanding a plant's natural biochemistry and growth chemicals can help humans grow more food, improve agricultural efficiency, and maximize the resources we harvest from nature.

questions.Question: Which hormone promotes internode/petiole elongation in deep water rice?
questions.Hint: This is the only gaseous plant hormone, and it helps rice plants 'gasp for air' when they are submerged underwater!
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Imagine you are a rice plant growing happily in a field, and suddenly heavy monsoon rains come. The field gets flooded with deep water, and you are entirely submerged. If your leaves stay underwater, you cannot get sunlight or carbon dioxide from the air. You cannot perform photosynthesis, and you might eventually drown and die! To survive this crisis, the plant needs a quick rescue mechanism. This is where a very cool, naturally occurring, invisible gas hormone called Ethylene comes into play. Ethylene is highly unique because it is the only plant hormone that exists as a gas. It is produced rapidly by the plant when it finds itself trapped underwater. The ethylene acts as an emergency distress signal. It travels to the upper parts of the stem (specifically the internodes) and the leaf stalks (which botanists call petioles) and commands them to grow upward super-fast. This rapid, accelerated elongation pushes the leaves and flowers high above the surface of the floodwater, functioning exactly like a snorkel for a human swimmer! By reaching the open air, the plant can successfully continue to breathe, transpire, and make food through photosynthesis. While Ethylene is most famously known in biology as the fruit-ripening hormone that turns green bananas yellow, its role as an incredible, life-saving mechanism in deep-water rice survival is one of its most amazing evolutionary tricks!

questions.Question: In tissue culture experiments, leaf mesophyll cells are put in a culture medium to form callus. This phenomenon may be called as
questions.Hint: When mature, specialized cells go backwards to act like unspecialized baby cells again, they lose their specific identity. What is the prefix that means 'to reverse'?
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Let us think about how jobs work in a big city. When a person is young, they have the potential to become absolutely anything—a doctor, an artist, an engineer, or a chef. This is exactly like a young, rapidly dividing plant cell. Once they grow up and become a specialized chef, they have 'differentiated' into that specific job, and they generally stick to that profession. In a plant, leaf mesophyll cells are the mature 'chefs'—they are highly specialized to perform the vital job of photosynthesis, and under normal circumstances, they lose the ability to divide and multiply forever. But plants possess an incredible, almost science-fiction-like superpower! If a plant gets injured, or if clever scientists take these mature leaf cells and place them in a special artificial nutrient bath in a laboratory (a process known as tissue culture), something magical happens. These mature cells can actually quit their chef jobs, forget their highly specialized identity, and revert back into being unspecialized, rapidly dividing 'baby' cells. This resulting mass of completely unspecialized, dividing cells is called a callus. Because the cell was already specialized (which we call 'differentiated') and then completely lost that specialization to divide again, we call this fascinating reversal process 'Dedifferentiation'. The prefix 'de-' literally means reversing or undoing. It is exactly as if a retired professional suddenly went back to kindergarten to start their life all over again! This amazing biological ability is what allows scientists to clone and grow entire new adult plants from just a tiny, single piece of a leaf.

questions.Question: Spraying of which of the following phytohormone on juvenile conifers helps hastening the maturity period, that leads early seed production?
questions.Hint: This is the same hormone that makes stems grow incredibly tall. It pushes plants through their slow 'teenage' years super fast!
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Conifers are a large group of cone-bearing trees, which includes familiar examples like pine, spruce, and fir trees. When these trees are young, or in their 'juvenile' phase, it can take them a phenomenally long time—sometimes several years or even decades—to mature enough to actually produce cones and seeds. This natural delay can be incredibly frustrating for botanists, agricultural scientists, or foresters who desperately want to breed specific trees or harvest their seeds quickly for replanting. Think of the plant's life cycle like a massive, multi-level video game. To get to the final boss and win the game (which for a tree means making seeds to reproduce), you normally have to play through all the long, tedious early levels. But what if there was a biological cheat code to skip those early levels entirely? For conifers, that powerful cheat code is a plant hormone called Gibberellin. When agriculturists spray young, juvenile conifers with gibberellins, it sends a strong chemical signal to their genetics to speed up their life cycle artificially. It essentially forces the young trees to skip their extended childhood and transition rapidly into mature, reproducing adults. As a result of this hormonal boost, they start producing cones and seeds much, much earlier than they naturally would in the wild. Gibberellins act as the ultimate 'growth and fast-forward' messengers in the plant kingdom, proving how manipulating plant biochemistry can drastically accelerate natural timelines!

questions.Question: The ability of plants to follow different pathways in response to environment leading to formation of different kinds of structures is called:
questions.Hint: Think of a material like modeling clay that can be easily molded or shaped into entirely different forms depending on how you press it.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Unlike animals, which can simply pack up and run away or migrate when their environment gets too hot, cold, or tough, plants are anchored to the ground. If a seed sprouts in a muddy swamp, the plant stays in the swamp. If it sprouts in a harsh, dry desert, it stays in the desert. Because they are permanently stuck in one single location, plants had to evolve a brilliant, dynamic survival trick: they possess the inherent capability to change their physical shape, internal structures, and growth pathways based entirely on their surrounding environment! Let us look at a fascinating aquatic plant called the buttercup. The buttercup plant has parts that grow completely submerged underwater and parts that grow upward into the open air. The leaves it produces underwater are highly dissected, meaning they are cut into thin, feathery, ribbon-like strips so strong water currents can pass right through them without ripping the plant apart. Conversely, the leaves it grows above the water surface are entirely different—they are broad, flat, and wide to catch the absolute maximum amount of sunlight for photosynthesis! This incredible ability of plants to alter their developmental pathways and form entirely distinct physical structures in response to their environment (or even different phases of their own life) is scientifically referred to as 'Plasticity'. Just like soft modeling clay (which we describe as being 'plastic') can be easily molded into a round ball or a flat square depending on how your hands press it, a plant can physically mold its structural development to perfectly fit its immediate living conditions. It truly is the plant kingdom's ultimate form of botanical shape-shifting!

questions.Question: Which of the following growth regulators is an adenine derivative ?
questions.Hint: Adenine is a famous nitrogenous base found in DNA. Which plant hormone was famously discovered from old, degraded fish sperm DNA?
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Plant hormones, also known as phytohormones, are naturally occurring chemicals that regulate plant growth, and they come from many completely different chemical families. To deeply understand this specific hormone, let us first look at DNA, which is the fundamental blueprint of all life on Earth. DNA is constructed from four basic building blocks, or 'letters', called nitrogenous bases: Adenine, Thymine, Cytosine, and Guanine. Many decades ago, curious scientists were experimenting in the lab trying to find a specific chemical compound that could force plant cells to divide rapidly in tissue cultures. During their experiments, they accidentally discovered that old, heat-degraded DNA extracted from herring fish sperm caused plant cells to start multiplying like absolute crazy! They carefully isolated this magic, cell-dividing molecule and decided to name it 'Kinetin', which was the very first identified member of a hormone group called Cytokinins. When organic chemists finally looked closely at Kinetin's molecular structure under advanced instruments, they realized something astonishing. Kinetin was actually just a chemically modified version of Adenine, the exact same base found in DNA! Therefore, Cytokinins (which include both the synthetic Kinetin and the naturally occurring Zeatin found in corn) are fundamentally adenine derivatives. Their primary, most important job inside the plant is to promote 'cytokinesis'—which is the scientific term for the physical splitting and division of a cell. Whenever a plant desperately needs to grow new fresh leaves, expand a piece of fruit, or rapidly heal a damaged wound, cytokinins flood the area to tell the local cells, 'Hey, it is time to copy your DNA and immediately split into two!'

questions.Question: The phenomenon by which the undividing parenchyma cells start to divide mitotically during plant tissue culture is called as:
questions.Hint: Parenchyma cells are normally fully mature adults that have lost their ability to divide. When they regain this youthful, dividing ability, they are reversing their specialized state.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: This biological concept is beautifully similar to another incredible plant phenomenon we explored earlier! In the anatomy of a plant, parenchyma cells are the basic, fundamental 'packing' and 'food-making' cells that make up the bulk of leaves and stems. They are fully grown, mature adult cells. Normally, once adult cells in both plants and animals reach this mature stage, they absolutely do not just start dividing again; they have officially retired from the 'growing and multiplying' business and are completely content just performing their daily metabolic jobs. However, plants possess an incredible, almost magical survival and regeneration mechanism. If you carefully extract these retired, non-dividing adult parenchyma cells and place them into a sterile glass test tube filled with the perfect mixture of nutrients and specific plant hormones (a widely used technique known as tissue culture), the cells suddenly 'wake up'. They actively strip away their mature adult identity and systematically revert back to a fast-dividing, highly youthful, unspecialized state, very similar to a human stem cell. The lifelong journey of a baby cell growing up and becoming a specialized adult cell is called 'differentiation'. Consequently, the amazing process of reversing that entire journey to become a blank, dividing cell all over again is called 'Dedifferentiation' (the prefix 'de-' signifies reversing or undoing an action). It is literally like hitting the master reset button on a cell's life cycle! Once these mature parenchyma cells successfully dedifferentiate, they multiply rapidly to form an unorganized mass of dividing cells called a callus, which agricultural scientists can then carefully manipulate to grow a completely new, fully functioning plant from scratch!

questions.Question: 15. Which one of the following plants does not show plasticity?
questions.Hint: Think of 'plasticity' as a plant's ability to change its leaf shape based on its environment or age. Three of these plants are famous for having different-shaped leaves when they are young vs. old, or in water vs. air. One is a simple grass-like crop that grows pretty much the same way no matter what.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let's dive into a really fascinating superpower that some plants have, called 'plasticity'. When you hear the word 'plastic', you probably think of something that can be melted and molded into different shapes, right? Well, in biology, plasticity means exactly that: the ability of an organism to alter its physical form in response to its environment or its stage of life.

Imagine you are a plant. You can't run away from a flood, and you can't walk over to a sunnier spot. To survive, some plants change their actual body structure! A classic example of this is a phenomenon called 'heterophylly' (hetero = different, phylly = leaves). Plants like Cotton, Coriander, Larkspur, and Buttercup are famous for this. If you look at a Buttercup plant growing partly in water and partly in the air, the leaves underwater look like thin, feathery ribbons (so the water currents don't rip them apart), while the leaves in the air are broad and flat to catch maximum sunlight. In other plants like Cotton and Coriander, the leaves of a young, juvenile plant look completely different from the leaves of a mature, adult plant. It's almost like a caterpillar turning into a butterfly, but for leaves!

However, Maize (which gives us corn) belongs to the grass family. It is pretty rigid in its development. A young maize leaf looks like a smaller version of an old maize leaf, and it doesn't dramatically change its shape whether it's in a slightly wetter or drier environment. It sticks to its original genetic blueprint without doing any fancy shape-shifting. Therefore, Maize does not show the kind of developmental or environmental plasticity that we see in Cotton, Coriander, or Buttercup. Understanding this helps biologists and farmers know how different plants will react to changing climates and environments!

questions.Question: 16. The gaseous plant growth regulator is used in plants to :
MCQ_Options: Speed up the ripening of fruits
Increase the length of the stem drastically
Prevent leaves from turning yellow and falling
Keep seeds in a deep sleep (dormancy)
questions.Hint: Have you ever heard the saying 'One bad apple spoils the whole bunch'? That happens because the 'bad' (overripe) apple releases a specific gas that tells all the other fruits around it to ripen immediately.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Isn't it amazing to think that plants communicate using invisible gases? In the world of botany, plants have their own special hormones, just like humans do. We call these 'Plant Growth Regulators' or PGRs. Most of these hormones are liquids moving through the plant's sap, but there is one incredibly unique hormone that is actually a gas! This hormone is called Ethylene.

Ethylene has a very specific and famous job in the plant kingdom: it is the 'aging and ripening' hormone. Think about what happens when you buy a bunch of green, hard bananas from the grocery store. If you leave them on the counter, over a few days, they turn yellow, soft, and sweet. How does the banana know it's time to do this? It starts producing ethylene gas! The gas spreads through the fruit, breaking down complex, hard carbohydrates into sweet, simple sugars, and changing the hard green skin into soft yellow skin.

Because it is a gas, it can even float through the air and affect neighboring fruits! If you put a ripe apple (which breathes out a lot of ethylene) into a paper bag with an unripe, rock-hard avocado, the avocado will ripen much faster. Farmers and supermarkets use this exact biological trick. They pick fruits like tomatoes and bananas while they are still green and hard so they don't get squished during transportation. Once the fruits arrive at their destination, they are pumped with ethylene gas to instantly ripen them so they look perfectly delicious when you walk into the store!

While ethylene does other things like causing old leaves to drop (abscission), its primary, most commercially important use is speeding up the ripening of fruits. The other options describe different hormones: Gibberellins increase stem length, Cytokinins prevent aging (keeping leaves green), and Abscisic acid keeps seeds dormant.
questions.Answer: Speed up the ripening of fruits

questions.Question: 17. The site of perception of light in plants during photoperiodism is
MCQ_Options: The shoot apex (tip of the stem)
questions.Hint: Think of this plant part as the plant's 'solar panels' or 'eyes'. It's the widest, flattest part of the plant, perfectly designed to catch sunlight and measure how long the day is.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered how a plant knows exactly what season it is? How does a cherry tree know it's spring, or a chrysanthemum know it's autumn, telling them it's the perfect time to burst into beautiful flowers? They don't have calendars or watches! Instead, they rely on a brilliant biological clock mechanism called 'Photoperiodism'. 

Let's break down that big word: 'Photo' means light, and 'periodism' refers to a period or length of time. So, photoperiodism is simply a plant's ability to measure the length of day and night. But to measure light, the plant needs a sensor—essentially, a pair of 'eyes'. Where are these eyes located? They are in the leaves!

Here is how the magic happens step-by-step: The leaves contain a special blue-green pigment called Phytochrome. Think of phytochrome as a highly sensitive light-detecting radar. Throughout the day, the wide, flat surface of the leaf absorbs sunlight. The phytochrome pigment carefully monitors exactly how many hours of light and how many hours of total darkness the plant receives. 

Once the leaf detects that the perfect season has arrived (for example, the nights are getting longer in autumn), it creates a mysterious, magical flowering hormone called 'Florigen'. Now, flowers don't grow directly on the leaves; they grow at the tips of the stems (the shoot apex). So, the leaf packs up this Florigen hormone and ships it through the plant's vascular system (the phloem) all the way up to the shoot apex. When the Florigen arrives, it gives the ultimate command: 'Stop growing regular leaves, and start making flowers!'

It's a beautiful relay race. The leaf is the sensor that perceives the light, but it delegates the actual job of making the flower to the stem tip. If you completely strip a plant of all its leaves, it becomes totally blind to the length of the day and will fail to flower! Therefore, the leaves are the crucial site of light perception.

questions.Question: 18. The plant hormone used to destroy weeds in a field
questions.Hint: Weeds are unwanted plants that steal nutrients from crops. Farmers use a very specific synthetic version of a growth hormone that forces certain broad-leaf weeds to grow so fast and so chaotically that they literally exhaust themselves to death.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore a fascinating—and slightly ruthless—battle tactic used in modern agriculture. Imagine you are a farmer. You have planted a massive field of wheat, but soon you notice pesky, unwanted plants (weeds) growing right alongside your precious crops. These weeds are like uninvited dinner guests; they steal the water, sunlight, and nutrients from the soil that your wheat needs to survive. How do you get rid of the weeds without hurting your wheat?

Scientists found an incredibly clever answer using plant hormones, specifically a synthetic hormone called 2,4-D (which stands for 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid). 2,4-D belongs to a family of plant growth hormones called Auxins. Naturally, plants produce very small, careful amounts of auxins to help their cells elongate and grow toward the sun. 

But what happens if a plant gets way too much auxin? It causes absolute chaos. When a farmer sprays 2,4-D over the entire field, something magical happens due to the anatomical differences between plants. Our crop, wheat, is a 'monocot' (it has narrow, grass-like leaves). The weeds we want to kill are mostly 'dicots' (they have broad, wide leaves). 

The broadleaf dicot weeds absorb a massive dose of the 2,4-D through their wide leaves. This huge flood of synthetic hormone sends their growth machinery into hyper-drive. The cells start dividing and expanding uncontrollably, twisting the stems, crushing their own internal water-transport tubes (xylem and phloem), and completely exhausting their energy reserves. Essentially, the weed grows itself to death! 

Meanwhile, the narrow-leaved monocot wheat plants either don't absorb enough of the chemical or have a special ability to quickly break it down safely. As a result, the wheat stands tall and healthy, while the broadleaf weeds wither and die. This selective weed-killing superpower makes 2,4-D one of the most widely used herbicides in the entire world, ensuring we have enough food to feed billions of people!

questions.Question: 19. Which of the following is not an inhibitory substance governing seed dormancy?
questions.Hint: Three of these chemicals act like 'sleeping pills' to keep the seed asleep (dormant) during freezing winters or dry droughts. One of them, however, acts like an 'alarm clock' that wakes the seed up to sprout!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To answer this question, we first need to understand a brilliant survival tactic used by plants called 'Seed Dormancy'. Imagine a seed falls off a tree right before the freezing winter begins. If the seed sprouts immediately, the baby plant will freeze to death in the snow! To prevent this, the seed enters a state of deep sleep, or suspended animation, called dormancy. During dormancy, the seed's metabolism slows down to almost zero, and it waits patiently for the warm, wet days of spring.

But how does the seed know to stay asleep? It is controlled by chemical 'brakes' or inhibitory substances. Inside the seed coat, there are chemicals like Abscisic acid (ABA), Phenolic acids, and Para-ascorbic acid. Think of these chemicals as strong sleeping pills. As long as these chemicals are present in high amounts, the seed is forbidden from waking up and sprouting. They inhibit (stop) growth to protect the seed from harsh environments.

Now, let's talk about the odd one out: Gibberellic acid (GA). Gibberellic acid is the exact opposite of an inhibitor; it is a powerful growth promoter! When spring arrives, the winter snow melts and washes away the inhibitory chemicals like ABA. The seed absorbs the warm water, and suddenly, the levels of Gibberellic acid shoot up. 

Gibberellic acid acts as the ultimate biological alarm clock. It sends a loud chemical signal saying, 'WAKE UP! It is safe to grow!' It triggers the seed to produce special enzymes (like amylase) that break down the stored starch in the seed into sugary food, giving the baby plant the massive burst of energy it needs to burst out of its shell and push through the soil toward the sun. Therefore, Gibberellic acid is NOT an inhibitory substance; it is the key promoter that breaks seed dormancy!

questions.Question: 20. Name the plant growth regulator which upon spraying on sugarcane crop, increases the length of stem, thus increasing the yield of sugarcane crop.
questions.Hint: Sugarcane stores sweet juice in its stem. To get more sugar, you need a longer stem. There is a specific hormone famous for causing dramatic 'internodal elongation'—essentially stretching the plant out like a telescope.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's put on our agricultural scientist hats for a moment! If you are growing a crop, your main goal is to get the highest 'yield'—meaning the maximum amount of usable product from your field. Different crops store their valuable parts in different places. Potatoes store food in underground tubers, apples in their fruit, and spinach in their leaves. 

But what about Sugarcane? Just like the name suggests, sugarcane stores its sweet, sugary sap entirely inside its thick stem. Therefore, if you are a sugarcane farmer, you don't care about the leaves or the roots; you just want the longest, thickest stems possible! The longer the stem, the more sugar juice it can hold, and the more money you make.

So, how do we hack the plant's biology to make the stems grow abnormally long? We spray them with a plant growth regulator called Gibberellin (or Gibberellic Acid / GA). 

To understand how Gibberellin works, look closely at a bamboo stalk or a sugarcane stalk. You will notice solid rings or joints running along the stem. These joints are called 'nodes', and the smooth space between two joints is called the 'internode'. Gibberellin specializes in something called 'internodal elongation'. When you spray Gibberellin on the crop, it signals the cells in the internode region to rapidly divide and stretch out. 

Imagine the sugarcane stem is like a collapsed telescope. When you introduce Gibberellin, it's like pulling the ends of the telescope, making the spaces between the rings stretch out dramatically! By doing this, farmers can increase the length of the sugarcane stems so much that the yield increases by up to 20 tons per acre! It’s a perfect example of using our knowledge of plant hormones to solve real-world food production challenges. Ethylene is for fruit ripening, Cytokinin is for cell division and anti-aging, and Abscisic acid is for stress responses—none of them stretch the stem like Gibberellin does.

questions.Question: 21. Removal of shoot tips is a very useful technique to boost the production of tealeaves. This is because :
MCQ_Options: It removes the main source of auxin, which breaks 'apical dominance' and allows lateral branches to grow.
It increases the production of ethylene, forcing the remaining leaves to ripen faster.
It forces the roots to absorb more water and nutrients from the soil.
It prevents flowers from growing, so all energy goes into the leaves.
questions.Hint: The very tip of a plant is like a bossy manager that produces a hormone telling all the side-branches beneath it, 'Do not grow! Let me grow upward first!' If you cut off the bossy tip, the side-branches finally have the freedom to bush outward.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever seen a gardener trimming the tops of hedges, and over time, those hedges become incredibly thick and bushy? Or have you noticed how tea plantations look like endless carpets of flat, dense, bushy green plants? There is a brilliant biological mechanism behind this called 'Apical Dominance', and understanding it is the key to mastering plant growth!

Let's break it down. At the very top tip of a plant stem is a region called the 'Apical Bud' (apex means top). This apical bud is a tiny factory that constantly pumps out a plant hormone called Auxin. Auxin is a bit of a control freak. It travels downwards through the stem and actively suppresses the growth of the 'lateral buds' or 'axillary buds'—these are the little buds on the sides of the stem that want to grow into new branches. The apical bud essentially tells the rest of the plant, 'I am in charge. Send all the energy to me so I can reach up toward the sun. Nobody else on the sides is allowed to grow until I say so!' This phenomenon is known as Apical Dominance.

But what if you want a plant to be short and super bushy, with lots of branches and leaves? You simply snip off the apical bud! This process is called decapitation (literally 'losing the head'). When you cut off the shoot tip, you are entirely removing the main source of the bossy Auxin. 

Without Auxin constantly shouting 'stop growing' to the lower branches, the lateral buds suddenly wake up. They begin to sprout rapidly, forming tons of new side branches. Each of these new branches produces its own leaves. For a tea farmer, the leaves are the money-maker. By continuously plucking the top shoot tips, the farmer forces the tea plant to branch outwards, creating a dense, wide bush overflowing with fresh, new tea leaves. It’s an elegant, natural way to multiply the harvest by just understanding how plant hormones dictate behavior!
questions.Answer: It removes the main source of auxin, which breaks 'apical dominance' and allows lateral branches to grow.

questions.Question: 22. In order to increase the yield of sugarcane crop, which of the following plant growth regulators should be sprayed?
questions.Hint: Sugarcane stores its sugar in its stem. What hormone is absolutely famous for making plant stems grow longer by stretching the space between leaves?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's think about a sugarcane plant. If you've ever enjoyed a glass of fresh sugarcane juice, you know that the sweet, delicious part of the plant is entirely in its thick stem. Sugarcane plants store their carbohydrates (sugar) as sucrose right inside the vacuoles of their stem cells. 

Now, imagine you are a farmer. Your main goal is to get as much sugar as possible from each plant. Since the sugar is locked up in the stem, the best way to get more sugar is... to get a longer stem! 

This is where our magical plant hormone, 'Gibberellin' (specifically Gibberellic Acid or GA), comes into play. Plant stems are divided into sections called 'nodes' (where the leaves attach) and 'internodes' (the smooth spaces between the leaves). Gibberellins are the master coordinators of something called 'internode elongation'. When you spray gibberellins on a sugarcane crop, it acts like a stretching machine for the plant. The cells in the internode areas absorb more water, loosen their cell walls, and grow incredibly long.

By simply spraying gibberellins over the field, the length of the sugarcane stems increases significantly. In fact, doing this can increase the yield of the sugarcane crop by as much as 20 tonnes per acre! It's practically agricultural magic. 

The other options don't quite fit the bill for this specific goal. Ethylene is more about ripening fruits, Cytokinins are for cell division (making new leaves and branches, not stretching the stem), and Auxins mostly help the tips of roots and shoots grow or bend towards the light. So, for maximum stretch and maximum sugar, Gibberellins are the clear winners!

questions.Question: 23. It takes very long time for pineapple plants to produce flowers. Which combination of hormones can be applied to artificially induce flowering in pineapple plants throughout the year to increase yield?
questions.Hint: Think about the ultimate teamwork! One hormone helps the plant grow its young parts, and the other is famous for ripening and finishing up the process. Together, they force the plant to bloom at the exact same time!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you own a gigantic pineapple farm. You have thousands of pineapple plants. Now, here is the incredibly frustrating thing about pineapples: left to their own devices, they are super lazy and unpredictable! One plant might flower in March, another in July, and another in December. Because they flower at different times, the pineapples ripen at different times. You would have to walk through your entire field every single day just to find the few pineapples that are ready to harvest. That would take way too much time and money!

Farmers and scientists needed a way to shout 'ATTENTION!' to the plants and force them all to flower on the exact same day. To do this, they discovered a brilliant hormonal cocktail: a mix of Auxin and Ethylene.

Here is how the magic works: Auxins (like NAA and 2,4-D) are growth hormones that usually tell a plant to keep growing taller. Ethylene is a gas hormone that usually tells a plant to age, ripen its fruit, or drop its leaves. 

When you spray a specific, tiny amount of Auxin on the pineapples, it actually triggers the plants to produce a burst of their own Ethylene! This sudden, massive wave of Ethylene inside the plant acts like an alarm clock. It tricks the plant's internal systems, shifting it from 'growing leaves' mode into 'making flowers' mode. 

By spraying the whole field with this Auxin and Ethylene combo, every single pineapple plant produces flowers at the exact same time. A few months later, you get a beautiful, uniform field of pineapples all perfectly ripe and ready to harvest on the same day. It's a fantastic example of humans using biology to solve a massive real-world problem!

questions.Question: 24. What is the site of perception of photoperiod necessary for induction of flowering in plants ?
questions.Hint: Where does a plant capture sunlight? Think about the flat, wide, green parts of the plant that act just like giant solar panels!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's uncover a mind-blowing fact about plants: they actually know what time of year it is! Even though they don't have eyes or calendars, plants can tell if it's summer or winter by measuring how long the sun is out. This amazing ability is called 'Photoperiodism'. 

For example, some plants will only grow pretty flowers if the day is very long (summer), while others only flower if the night is long (winter). But here is the big question: how does the plant actually 'see' or measure the sunlight?

If you guessed the flowers or the stem, that's a great guess, but it's actually the LEAVES! Leaves are the ultimate solar panels of the plant world. They are wide, flat, and perfectly positioned to catch maximum sunlight. Inside the leaves, there are special light-detecting proteins called phytochromes. These proteins act like tiny biological stopwatches that count exactly how many hours of light and darkness the plant is experiencing.

When the leaf detects the 'perfect' amount of daylight for its specific species, it says, 'Aha! It is time to make a baby (a flower)!' The leaf then produces a mysterious, magical chemical signal called 'Florigen'. 

Florigen travels all the way from the leaf, down through the plant's plumbing system (the phloem), and goes up to the shoot apex (the very tip of the stem). Once Florigen arrives at the tip, it commands the stem to stop making regular leaves and start building a beautiful flower instead. So, without leaves to act as the 'eyes' or sensors to perceive the photoperiod, a plant would never know when to bloom!

questions.Question: 25. Fruit and leaf drop at early stages can be prevented by the application of
questions.Hint: Think of the 'youth' hormone of the plant. This hormone keeps young parts attached securely, but it actually allows old, yellowing leaves to fall off!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered how a tree knows exactly when to drop its leaves in the fall? Plants have a built-in pair of 'chemical scissors' called an abscission zone. This is a tiny layer of cells right at the base of the leaf stalk or the fruit stem. When the time is right, the cells in this zone weaken and break, causing the leaf or fruit to snap off and fall to the ground. 

Now, imagine you are an apple farmer. You have beautiful young green apples growing on your trees. But suddenly, a strong wind blows, or the tree gets a little stressed, and those baby apples fall off way too early! If they drop early, you have no crop to sell. 

To stop this from happening, farmers spray a hormone called Auxin. Auxin is essentially the 'stay young and stay attached' hormone for early-stage plant parts. As long as a young leaf or a young fruit is actively producing its own Auxin, that hormone flows down the stalk and acts like superglue. It tells the abscission zone (the scissors layer), 'Hey, do not break apart yet! I am still young and growing!' 

By artificially spraying Auxins on the trees, farmers trick the plant into thinking, 'Wow, these fruits are incredibly healthy and young, I better hold onto them tightly.' This stops premature fruit and leaf drop. 

Interestingly, Auxins are super smart! While they prevent young, healthy things from dropping, they actually *promote* the falling of old, mature, dying leaves and fully ripe fruits. So, Auxins act as the perfect traffic directors: they protect the babies but let the old folks go peacefully. Ethylene and Abscisic Acid, on the other hand, are the 'aging' hormones that make things drop early, so we definitely wouldn't spray those!

questions.Question: 26. You are given a tissue with its potential for differentiation in an artificial culture. Which of the following pairs of hormones would you add to the medium to secure shoots as well as roots?
questions.Hint: To build a complete plant from scratch in a lab, you need one hormone to tell the cells to dig down (roots) and a completely different hormone to tell the cells to grow upward into branches (shoots)!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to the fascinating world of Plant Tissue Culture! This is practically sci-fi stuff. In plants, almost any living cell has a superpower called 'totipotency'. This means a single, tiny plant cell has the complete genetic blueprint to grow into a whole new, massive plant. 

If scientists take a tiny chunk of plant tissue (let's say from a carrot) and put it in a petri dish full of nutrients, the cells start dividing like crazy into an unorganized, mushy lump of cells called a 'callus'. But a mushy lump isn't a plant! We need to give this lump instructions to form roots (to drink water) and shoots (stems and leaves to get sunlight). 

To give these instructions, scientists use a magical cocktail of two specific hormones: Auxin and Cytokinin. 

1. Auxin is the 'root-maker'. If you add a lot of Auxin and a little bit of Cytokinin to the petri dish, the cells at the bottom of the lump will get the message and start shooting out little white roots. 

2. Cytokinin is the 'shoot-maker'. If you change the recipe and put in a lot of Cytokinin and a little bit of Auxin, the cells at the top of the lump will start growing beautiful green stems and leaves. 

By carefully balancing both Auxin and Cytokinin in the artificial jelly medium, you tell the tissue to do BOTH. The cells differentiate (specialize) perfectly into roots at the bottom and shoots at the top. The other options are incorrect because Abscisic Acid acts as a stress signal (it halts growth), Ethylene ripens things and causes aging, and Gibberellin mostly just stretches cells out. Only the dynamic duo of Auxin and Cytokinin can architect a completely new plant from a blob of cells!

questions.Question: 27. Phytochrome is a
questions.Hint: Break down the word! 'Phyto' means plant, and 'chrome' means color or pigment. So, this must be a protein bound to a colored molecule that absorbs light!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's be biology detectives and break down this word to find out its secret! The word 'Phytochrome' is made of two parts. 'Phyto-' comes from Greek and means 'plant'. '-chrome' also comes from Greek and means 'color' or 'pigment' (just like how 'Google Chrome' has a very colorful logo!).

But what exactly is it? Phytochromes are the amazing 'eyes' of the plant. They are special photoreceptor molecules inside the plant's leaves that absorb light, telling the plant if it is daytime, nighttime, or even if they are stuck in the shade of another bigger plant.

Proteins on their own are generally clear or white—they can't absorb light very well by themselves. To catch light rays, a protein needs a partner: a pigment! A pigment is a molecule that absorbs specific colors of light (like how chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light, making it look green). 

When a protein bonds together with a light-absorbing colored pigment, we call that whole complex a 'Chromoprotein' (Chromo = color, protein = well, protein!).

Phytochrome is an incredible chromoprotein because it acts like a light switch. It has a blue-light absorbing pigment attached to a protein backbone. When it gets hit by red light (from the sun), it flips its shape into an active form (Pfr). When it gets hit by far-red light (like at sunset or in the shade), it flips back into its inactive form (Pr). This flipping back and forth is how the plant counts the hours of sunlight and decides whether it's time to flower or drop its leaves! 

So, it isn't a Lipoprotein (protein + fat), nor a Glycoprotein (protein + sugar), nor a Flavoprotein (protein + riboflavin derivative). It's a Chromoprotein, a protein with a beautiful light-catching pigment attached!

questions.Question: 28. The Avena curvature is used for bioassay of
questions.Hint: Think about the famous experiment by F.W. Went, where he cut the tips off of young oat seedlings to prove they contained a growth chemical that bends plants toward the light!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this question, we first need to understand two big words: 'Bioassay' and 'Avena'. 

A 'Bioassay' is a really cool science trick. Instead of using a giant, expensive chemical machine to detect if a specific hormone is present in a liquid, we use a living thing! We put the chemical on a living plant or tissue and see how it reacts. If it reacts in a very specific way, we say, 'Aha! The hormone is definitely in there!'

'Avena' is simply the scientific name for the common Oat plant. 

Now, let's go back in time to an amazing scientist named F.W. Went. He was trying to figure out why plants always bend toward the window (toward the light). He took young oat seedlings (Avena coleoptiles) and chopped off their very top tips. Without the tips, the plants completely stopped growing!

Went then took those chopped-off tips and placed them on tiny blocks of jelly (agar). He figured that whatever magical growth chemical was in the tip would leak down into the jelly. Next, he took that jelly block and placed it off to one side on top of the decapitated oat plant. 

What happened next was magic: the side of the plant with the jelly block grew incredibly fast, causing the whole plant to curve and bend in the opposite direction! 

Went discovered that the chemical leaking into the jelly was Indole-3-Acetic Acid (IAA), which is the most common natural Auxin. Auxin causes plant cells to stretch and elongate. Because he proved this using the curving of oat seedlings, it became world-famous as the 'Avena Curvature Test'. 

To this day, if a scientist wants to know if a mysterious liquid contains Auxin (IAA), they just put it on a decapitated oat seedling. If the seedling curves, it's Auxin! It is not used for Ethylene (gas), ABA (stress), or GA3 (which stretches the whole stem straight up, not curving).

questions.Question: 29. Auxin can be bioassayed by
questions.Hint: Think about the famous oat seedling experiment done by F.W. Went, where he measured how much a plant bends to calculate the amount of hormone present!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let us dive into a really fascinating concept called a 'bioassay.' Imagine you have a tiny, microscopic drop of a magical potion, and you want to know exactly how strong it is. The problem is, you don't have a machine sensitive enough to measure it. What do you do? You test it on a living creature to see how it reacts! That is exactly what a 'bioassay' is—using a living biological organism to measure the concentration of a chemical.

Auxin is a powerful plant hormone responsible for growth, but plants produce it in unbelievably tiny amounts. To measure it, scientists use the 'Avena coleoptile curvature test.' Avena is just the scientific name for oats, and a coleoptile is the protective sheath covering the baby shoot of the oat plant. 

Here is how this brilliantly simple test works: A scientist named F.W. Went discovered that if you cut off the tip of an oat coleoptile (which is where auxin is made) and place it on a tiny block of agar (a type of jelly), the auxin flows down into the jelly. Now, if you take that jelly block and place it on only ONE half of a decapitated plant stem, the auxin flows down that specific side. The side receiving the auxin grows longer, causing the plant to bend in the opposite direction! 

The true genius of this experiment is the math behind it: the angle at which the plant bends is directly proportional to the amount of auxin in the jelly block. A small bend means a little auxin; a massive bend means a lot of auxin. So, without needing expensive electronic sensors, scientists can perfectly measure auxin levels just by looking at how much an oat seedling curves!

questions.Question: 30. What causes a green plant exposed to the light, on only one side, to bend towards the source of light as it grows?
MCQ_Options: Light stimulates plant cells on the lighted side to grow faster
Auxin accumulates on the shaded side, stimulating greater cell elongation there
Green plants need light to perform photosynthesis
Light destroys auxin on the shaded side
questions.Hint: Plants bend because one side grows longer than the other. If the plant bends TOWARDS the light, which side of the stem must be growing longer to push it over?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever placed a potted plant next to a window and noticed that, after a few days, it looks like it is stretching its neck to look outside? This superpower is called 'Phototropism' (photo = light, tropism = turning). It looks like magic, but it is actually driven by some incredibly clever cellular mechanics involving our favorite plant hormone: Auxin.

Auxin is produced at the very tip of the plant stem. Its main job is to tell plant cells to elongate (stretch out and get longer). However, auxin has a very quirky personality trait: it is completely 'light-shy.' It hates direct sunlight! 

When light shines on a plant from directly above, auxin travels straight down the stem evenly, so all sides of the stem grow at the exact same rate, and the plant grows straight up. But what happens if the sun is hitting the plant from only the right side? The light-shy auxin panics and migrates away from the light, hiding on the dark, shaded side (the left side) of the stem. 

Because all the auxin is now crowded on the shaded side, the cells on the shaded side receive a massive signal to grow and elongate. Meanwhile, the lighted side is depleted of auxin, so its cells stay relatively short. 

Imagine walking on stilts, but your left stilt is suddenly growing twice as fast as your right stilt. What happens? You would inevitably tip and lean towards the right! This is exactly what happens to the plant. The shaded side stretches out so much that it mechanically pushes the tip of the plant to bend over towards the light. The plant isn't 'trying' to look at the sun; it's just the physical result of uneven cell stretching!
questions.Answer: Auxin accumulates on the shaded side, stimulating greater cell elongation there

questions.Question: 31. Typical growth curve in plants is
questions.Hint: Think about how living things grow: they start off a bit slow, suddenly have a massive, explosive growth spurt, and eventually slow down and stop as they mature.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Whenever we measure how much a living organism grows over time—whether it is a plant, a bacteria colony, or even you—the graph almost always creates the same beautiful shape. It is called a 'Sigmoid' curve, which simply means an 'S-shaped' curve.

Let's break down exactly why plants grow in this S-shape. It happens in three distinct phases:

1. The Lag Phase (The bottom of the 'S'): Imagine you are trying to push a heavy car. At first, it is really hard to get it moving. Similarly, when a seed first sprouts, growth is quite slow. The plant is tiny, has very few cells, and is just setting up its internal machinery to survive.

2. The Log or Exponential Phase (The steep middle of the 'S'): Now the car is rolling downhill, picking up crazy speed! For the plant, it has grown some leaves, it is doing photosynthesis, and its cells are dividing rapidly (1 cell becomes 2, 2 become 4, 4 become 8, 8 become 16, etc.). This causes an explosive, rapid upward shoot in growth. 

3. The Stationary Phase (The flat top of the 'S'): The plant can't grow forever. Eventually, it runs out of nutrients, space, or simply reaches its genetic limit (like how humans stop growing taller in their late teens). The growth rate slows down to almost zero, leveling off into a flat line.

When you put the slow start, the explosive middle, and the flat ending together on a graph of Size versus Time, it draws out a perfect letter 'S'. Therefore, the typical growth curve in plants is universally Sigmoid!

questions.Question: 32. Dr. F. Went noted that if coleoptile tips were removed and placed on agar for one hour, the agar would produce a bending when placed on one side of freshly-cut coleoptile stumps. Of what significance is this experiment?
MCQ_Options: It proved that light is necessary for photosynthesis
It isolated and demonstrated the existence of a chemical growth promoter (auxin)
It showed that agar blocks can grow into new plants
It proved that plants can grow without their tips
questions.Hint: If the physical plant tip is totally removed, but a simple block of jelly (agar) can still make the plant bend, what must have traveled from the tip into the jelly?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is one of the most elegant and famous experiments in the history of biology! To understand its brilliance, you have to understand the mystery scientists were facing. Charles Darwin (yes, the evolution guy!) had already observed that plants bend towards light, and he figured out that the very tip of the plant was somehow 'sensing' the light and telling the rest of the stem to bend.

But the huge question remained: HOW was the tip talking to the stem? Was it an electrical signal like a nerve? Was it a vibration? Was it a chemical?

Enter Dr. Frits Went. He did something extremely clever. He cut off the tips of oat seedlings (coleoptiles) and placed them on tiny blocks of agar. Agar is basically just a firm, porous jelly made from seaweed. He let them sit there for an hour. Then, he threw the plant tips in the trash! He took only the agar jelly blocks and placed them on top of the decapitated plant stems, specifically off to one side.

To his amazement, the plant stems began to bend, exactly as if the tips were still there! 

Why is this so significant? Because an electrical or nervous signal cannot be stored in a block of jelly! The only logical conclusion was that the plant tip was producing a physical substance—a chemical molecule—that oozed down into the jelly. By moving the jelly to a new plant, he proved that this chemical was a 'growth promoter.' He essentially caught the ghost! He had successfully isolated the very first plant hormone, which he later named 'Auxin' (from the Greek word 'auxein', meaning to grow).
questions.Answer: It isolated and demonstrated the existence of a chemical growth promoter (auxin)

questions.Chapter: Anatomy of Flowering Plants / Plant Growth and Development
questions.Question: 33. A few normal seedlings of tomato were kept in a dark room. After a few days they were found to have become white-coloured like albinos. Which of the following terms will you use to describe them?
questions.Hint: Think about what happens to grass if you leave a heavy bucket over it for a week. The plant changes its growth strategy to 'reach' out and search for light!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever moved a brick or a piece of wood in your garden and found a pale, yellow-white, weirdly tall and skinny plant growing underneath it? That plant isn't an alien; it is experiencing a fascinating biological process called 'Etiolation.'

Let's put ourselves in the plant's shoes. A tomato seedling relies on sunlight to make its food via photosynthesis. To catch sunlight, it makes chlorophyll, the pigment that makes plants beautifully green. But chlorophyll is actually very biologically 'expensive' for a plant to manufacture.

Now, imagine you place this seedling in a completely dark room. The plant realizes, 'Hey, there is no light here! It is completely useless for me to waste my precious energy making green chlorophyll because there is no light to absorb!' 

So, the plant stops making chlorophyll entirely, which is why it turns pale, yellow, or white (like an albino). But it doesn't just sit there waiting to die. It goes into survival mode! It takes all of its remaining stored energy and funnels it into extreme stem elongation. The stem grows super long and spindly in a desperate, rapid attempt to reach upward, hoping to break through whatever is blocking the sun (like pushing past leaves or soil).

This specific combination of symptoms—pale/white color (due to lack of chlorophyll), long, weak stems, and tiny unexpanded leaves—is what biologists call being 'Etiolated.' It is a brilliant, desperate survival mechanism designed to help a plant find the light before its energy runs out!

questions.Question: 34. Which one of the following growth regulators is known as 'stress hormone'?
questions.Hint: When you are stressed or in danger, you try to conserve your energy and protect yourself. Which plant hormone acts like an emergency brake, closing the stomata to save water during a massive drought?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine the weather gets terribly tough. There is a massive drought, the soil is dry, and the sun is blazing hot. If the plant keeps growing and acting normally, it will sweat out all its water, wither, and die. It needs a way to panic, hit the emergency brakes, and go into a protective 'lockdown' mode. 

That is exactly the job of a powerful plant hormone called Abscisic Acid, or ABA for short. Because it helps the plant deal with tough, threatening environmental conditions, it is famously known as the 'stress hormone.'

What exactly does ABA do when a plant is stressed out? 
1. It forces the stomata (the microscopic breathing pores on the leaves) to slam shut. This is crucial because it stops water from evaporating out of the leaves, saving the plant from dehydration during a drought.
2. It stops seeds from germinating. If a seed falls onto dry, freezing ground, germinating right away would be suicide for the baby plant. ABA keeps the seed dormant (asleep) until the weather becomes warm and wet enough to survive.
3. It stops general growth. During times of stress, energy needs to go toward survival, not making new leaves.

So, just like adrenaline helps humans react to stressful, dangerous situations, Abscisic Acid (ABA) is the ultimate chemical shield that prepares a plant to survive severe environmental stress!

questions.Question: 35. During seed germination its stored food is mobilized by
questions.Hint: This hormone tells the sleeping seed, 'Wake up, it's spring, time to grow!' and activates special digestive enzymes to break down the seed's starchy food reserves.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Think of a seed as a tiny, sleeping baby plant packed inside a protective lunchbox. The 'lunch' in this box is the endosperm, a starchy tissue that stores food for the baby plant. However, just like you can't swallow a whole loaf of bread without chewing and digesting it first, the baby plant cannot use complex starch directly. It needs that starch broken down into simple, sweet sugars to get the energy to sprout.

So, how does the seed know when it is time to 'digest' its lunch and start growing? 

When the conditions are perfect (lots of water and warmth), the seed absorbs water. This wakes up the baby plant embryo, and the very first thing it does is secrete a powerful hormone called 'Gibberellin' (often called Gibberellic Acid or GA).

Gibberellin acts like an alarm clock and a master switch. It travels to the outer layer of the seed's food storage (called the aleurone layer) and shouts, 'Make enzymes!' The cells respond by producing special digestive enzymes, particularly one called alpha-amylase.

These enzymes flood into the starchy food reserve and chop up the big, complex starch molecules into simple, easy-to-use sugars. These sugars are then 'mobilized'—meaning they are transported directly to the baby plant, providing it with a massive burst of energy. With this energy, the tiny plant bursts out of its seed coat and pushes its way up through the soil to see the sun. Without Gibberellin acting as the trigger, the food would stay locked up, and the seed would never germinate!

questions.Question: 36. The pineapple which under natural condition is difficult to blossom has been made to produce fruits throughout the year by application of
questions.Hint: Think about the synthetic hormones used by farmers to synchronize flowering so they can harvest an entire field of pineapples at once!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are a farmer with a massive field of pineapples. Under natural conditions, pineapples are extremely unpredictable. One plant might decide to produce a flower (which turns into the pineapple fruit) in March, another in July, and another might take years! This random, unsynchronized blooming is a total nightmare for harvesting. You'd have to walk through the field every single day just to find the few pineapples that are ready. 

To solve this, scientists discovered an amazing biological trick using plant hormones. Hormones are chemical messengers that tell a plant what to do and when to do it. By spraying the field with specific synthetic Auxins (like NAA - Naphthalene Acetic Acid, or 2,4-D) or chemicals that release Ethylene gas, farmers can effectively 'hack' the plants' biological clocks. 

When you spray these auxins onto the pineapple plants, it triggers a chain reaction inside their cells. The auxins actually stimulate the plant to produce small bursts of ethylene. Ethylene is usually known as the 'fruit ripening' gas, but in pineapples, it acts as a very specific switch that forces the plant to transition from growing leaves to making a flower. Suddenly, the entire field gets the exact same chemical signal at the exact same time: 'Stop growing leaves and make flowers NOW!' 

As a result, all the pineapples blossom and bear fruit in perfect synchronization. This allows farmers to control exactly when they get their harvest, meaning they can produce pineapples throughout the entire year, regardless of the natural season. It's a perfect example of how understanding plant biochemistry helps us solve real-world agricultural problems!

questions.Question: 37. Through their effects on plant growth regulators, what do the temperature and light control in the plants?
questions.Hint: What is the most critical event in a plant's life cycle that dictates when it is time to reproduce and make seeds?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered how a cherry tree knows it's spring and time to burst into beautiful pink blossoms? Plants don't have calendars, eyes, or brains, but they do have incredibly sophisticated internal sensors that monitor two crucial environmental factors: Light and Temperature. 

The length of daylight (and more importantly, the length of the dark night) is monitored by special light-sensitive pigments in the leaves called phytochromes. This phenomenon is called 'Photoperiodism'. Meanwhile, the plant also tracks prolonged periods of cold temperatures, a process known as 'Vernalization'. 

Why does the plant care about light and cold? Because producing flowers takes a massive amount of energy, and the flowers are delicate. If a plant makes flowers right before a freezing winter, those flowers will die, no seeds will be made, and the plant's genetic line ends. That's a biological disaster! 

So, light and temperature act as the ultimate 'safeguards'. When the days get the right length (indicating spring or summer is here) and the plant has successfully survived the winter freeze (vernalization), these environmental cues alter the levels of plant growth regulators (hormones). They trigger the leaves to produce a hypothetical flowering hormone called 'florigen'. Florigen travels up the stem to the growing tips and completely changes their instructions. Instead of saying 'build more leaves', it says 'build flowers!' 

Therefore, by controlling hormone levels, temperature and light perfectly time the most important event in a plant's life: Flowering. This ensures the plant only reproduces when the environment is safe and welcoming for its future seeds.

questions.Question: 38. Which one of the following generally acts as an antagonist to gibberellins?
questions.Hint: Gibberellins act like the 'gas pedal' for a plant, waking up seeds and making stems grow fast. Which hormone acts like the 'brakes' to keep seeds asleep during tough times?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
In biology, an 'antagonist' is like an arch-nemesis. If one molecule tries to do something, its antagonist will fight to do the exact opposite. Within the world of plant hormones, we have a classic battle between two powerful chemicals: Gibberellins (GA) and Abscisic Acid (ABA). 

Let's look at a tiny seed buried in the soil. Inside that seed is a sleeping baby plant (an embryo) and a packed lunch (starchy food reserves). When spring arrives, water enters the seed and triggers the release of Gibberellins. GA acts as the ultimate 'wake-up call'. It commands enzymes to break down the starch into sugars, giving the embryo the energy it needs to burst out of the seed coat and grow towards the sun. Gibberellins promote growth, stem elongation, and seed germination. 

But what if it's the middle of a freezing, dry winter? If the seed wakes up now, the baby plant will instantly freeze to death. This is where Abscisic Acid (ABA) comes to the rescue. ABA is known as the 'stress hormone'. It acts as a strict, protective parent. ABA actively blocks the effects of Gibberellins. It prevents those starch-digesting enzymes from working, forcing the seed to remain in a deep sleep, a state we call 'dormancy'. 

So, while Gibberellin is hitting the gas pedal trying to make the plant grow and germinate, Abscisic Acid is slamming on the brakes to protect the plant from dangerous environmental conditions. Because they have completely opposite effects on seed germination and growth, Abscisic Acid is considered the primary antagonist to Gibberellins. It's a beautiful, chemical tug-of-war that keeps plants alive through harsh seasons!

questions.Question: 39. Vernalization stimulates flowering in
questions.Hint: Look for a biennial plant. This is a common orange root vegetable that spends its first year storing food underground, survives the winter, and uses that stored energy to flower in its second year.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this question, we first need to understand a fascinating plant superpower called 'Vernalization'. Vernalization is a process where a plant absolutely refuses to flower unless it has first experienced a prolonged period of chilling, winter-like temperatures. 

Why would a plant demand to be frozen before making a flower? It's a genius survival strategy! Imagine a plant that starts growing in the late summer. If it immediately grew flowers in autumn, the incoming winter frost would kill the delicate flowers before they could ever make seeds. To prevent this tragic mistake, the plant has a built-in lock on its flowering mechanism. Only the sustained cold of winter can 'unlock' it. Once spring arrives and temperatures warm up, the plant knows winter is over and it is finally safe to bloom. 

This behavior is famously seen in 'biennial' plants—plants that take two years to complete their life cycle. The Carrot is a classic example of a biennial plant that requires vernalization. 

During its first year of life, a carrot plant just grows bushy green leaves and pours all its energy into making a thick, nutritious taproot underground (this is the orange part we love to eat!). It doesn't even try to make a flower. Then, winter comes. The leaves die back, but the thick root survives underground, enduring the cold. This long freeze is the vernalization period. Deep inside the cells of the root, the cold alters the plant's gene expression. When spring arrives in year two, the carrot uses all the food stored in that thick root to rapidly shoot up a tall stem and produce beautiful, umbrella-like clusters of white flowers. Without that cold winter shock, the carrot would just keep growing leaves and never flower!

questions.Question: 40. Phototropic curvature is the result of uneven distribution of
questions.Hint: Think of the growth hormone produced at the tip of the stem that 'runs away' from sunlight to the shaded side, causing that side to grow longer and bend the plant.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
If you put a potted plant next to a window, you'll notice something magical after a few days: the stem will bend and reach out directly toward the sunlight. This directional growth in response to light is called 'Phototropism' ('Photo' = light, 'tropism' = turning). But how does a plant, which has no muscles or skeleton, physically bend itself? 

The secret lies in a brilliant plant hormone called Auxin, and a phenomenon known as the 'Acid Growth Hypothesis'. Auxin is constantly being manufactured right at the very tip of the plant stem (the shoot apex). Auxin has one main job: it tells plant cells to stretch and grow longer. However, Auxin has a quirky personality—it absolutely hates direct sunlight! 

When sunlight hits the plant from directly above, Auxin travels straight down the stem evenly, and the plant grows straight up. But, if sunlight is shining from one side (like from a window), the Auxin panics and actively migrates over to the dark, shaded side of the stem. 

This creates an 'uneven distribution' of the hormone. Now, there is a massive amount of Auxin on the dark side of the stem, and very little on the sunny side. The cells on the dark side respond to this high dose of Auxin by pumping acid into their cell walls, making the walls soft and stretchy. Water rushes into these cells, causing them to elongate incredibly fast. 

Because the cells on the shaded side are suddenly growing much longer than the cells on the sunny side, the physical structure of the stem is forced to curve. It’s like having a car where the wheels on the left side are spinning faster than the wheels on the right—the car is naturally going to turn! Therefore, the phototropic curvature (the bending) is a direct, mechanical result of Auxin piling up on the shaded side of the plant.

questions.Question: 41. Photoperiodism was first characterised in
questions.Hint: This famous historical discovery was made by scientists Garner and Allard in the 1920s using a mutant 'Mammoth' variety of a plant famously farmed to make cigars and cigarettes.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
The discovery of 'Photoperiodism'—the ability of plants to measure the length of day and night—is one of the coolest detective stories in botany. It all started in the 1920s with two scientists named W.W. Garner and H.A. Allard, who were working for the US Department of Agriculture. 

They were observing a very strange mutant variety of a tobacco plant called the 'Maryland Mammoth'. Most normal tobacco plants would grow to a certain height and then dutifully produce flowers in the middle of summer. But the Maryland Mammoth was weird. It just kept growing, and growing, and growing—sometimes reaching 10 to 15 feet tall!—producing massive, beautiful leaves, but absolutely zero flowers during the summer months. 

However, Garner and Allard noticed something fascinating. If they took these giant Mammoth plants into a greenhouse and kept them alive into the late autumn and winter, the plants would suddenly burst into flowers! 

Why did they wait until winter to bloom? The scientists set up experiments, placing the plants in dark closets for different amounts of time. They discovered that the plants weren't reacting to temperature or age. They were reacting to the length of the darkness! The Maryland Mammoth tobacco was what we now call a 'Short-Day Plant' (or more accurately, a 'Long-Night Plant'). It possessed a strict internal alarm clock and would absolutely refuse to flower until it experienced an uninterrupted period of darkness lasting longer than a certain critical number of hours. Summer nights were too short, so it just kept growing leaves. Winter nights were long enough, so the darkness triggered the flowering hormones! 

This groundbreaking realization with the Maryland Mammoth tobacco was the very first time humans understood and characterized Photoperiodism, proving that plants can literally 'sense' the time of year by measuring shadows.

questions.Question: 42. Coiling of garden pea tendrils around any support is an example of
questions.Hint: In scientific terms, 'Thigmo' means touch, and 'tropism' means directional growth. How does a vine know to wrap itself around a fence?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
If you've ever looked closely at a climbing plant like a garden pea or a grapevine, you might have seen tiny, curly green threads reaching out and wrapping tightly around a fence or a wooden stake. These structures are called 'tendrils'. But how on earth does a brainless plant know that a fence is there, and how does it know how to tie a knot around it? 

The answer is an incredible biological phenomenon called 'Thigmotropism'. Let's break that big word down. In Greek, 'Thigmo' means 'touch', and 'tropism' means 'turning or growing in a specific direction'. So, Thigmotropism literally means directional growth in response to being touched. 

Here is how the magic trick works at a cellular level: As a pea plant grows, its tendrils slowly sweep around in the air in circles, searching for something to grab onto. When the side of a tendril brushes against a solid object, like a wooden pole, special sensor proteins on the plant's skin detect the physical friction. 

This sense of touch triggers a rapid change in the plant's growth hormones (specifically Auxin). The plant quickly shifts its auxin away from the side touching the pole, sending it to the opposite side of the tendril (the side facing the open air). Just like we learned with phototropism, auxin makes cells grow longer. So, the cells on the outside of the tendril start growing and stretching much faster than the cells on the inside touching the pole. 

Because the outside of the tendril is getting longer while the inside stays short, the tendril physically curves inward, curling tightly around the support structure. It acts like a biological lasso, anchoring the weak-stemmed pea plant so it can climb high up toward the sunlight. It's a masterpiece of botanical engineering driven entirely by the sense of touch!

questions.Question: One of the commonly used plant growth hormone in tea plantations is
questions.Hint: If you want to grow a massive tea plantation quickly, you don't use seeds. You cut stems from existing plants and plant them in the soil. Which hormone tells a cut stem to grow new roots?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are the manager of a massive, beautiful green tea plantation. Your goal is to grow thousands of identical, healthy tea plants so you can harvest their leaves.
