To understand this, we need to picture the anatomy of your chest. Your lungs are like two soft, highly elastic sponges housed inside a sturdy cage of ribs. Because they are elastic, your lungs naturally want to shrink and pull inward at all times. Meanwhile, your rib cage naturally wants to spring outward. 

So, why don't the lungs shrink away from the ribs into tiny balls? Between the outside of the lungs and the inside of the chest wall is a tiny, fluid-filled gap called the pleural cavity. Imagine taking two smooth, flat plates of glass, putting a few drops of water between them, and pressing them together. You can easily slide them side to side, but if you try to pull them directly apart, they are stuck together like glue! This is due to surface tension creating a suction effect.

This exact same suction exists in the pleural cavity. Because the lungs are constantly pulling inward and the chest is pulling outward, they create a tiny vacuum in that fluid-filled gap. In scientific terms, we say the pressure in the pleural cavity is 'negative' (meaning it is lower than the outside atmospheric pressure). 

This negative intrapleural pressure acts like a permanent suction cup, pulling outward on the walls of the lungs and keeping them stretched open against the inside of the chest wall. If this vacuum is ever broken—for example, if someone gets a deep puncture wound in their chest—air rushes into the space, the suction is lost, and the lung collapses like a deflated tire. But as long as you are healthy, that beautiful negative pressure holds your lungs open day and night, ensuring some air always remains inside!
questions.Answer: There is a negative intrapleural pressure pulling at the lung walls

questions.Question: 26. Reduction in pH of blood will
MCQ_Options: Decrease the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen
Increase the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen
Reduce the blood supply to the brain
questions.Hint: A drop in pH means more acid. When muscles work hard, they make acid. What do working muscles desperately need the blood to 'drop off' to them?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore one of the most brilliant, automatic delivery systems in the human body! Inside your red blood cells is a special protein called Hemoglobin. Think of Hemoglobin as a microscopic Uber driver whose entire job is to pick up oxygen passengers at the lungs and drop them off at tissues that need them.

But how does the Uber driver know exactly WHICH tissues need oxygen the most? The secret lies in the pH of your blood. The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a liquid is. A lower pH means something is more acidic. 

When you run, jump, or exercise, your muscle cells work incredibly hard. As they burn energy, they produce waste products, specifically carbon dioxide and lactic acid. These waste products enter the blood passing through the muscle and cause the pH of that blood to drop (become more acidic). 

When our Hemoglobin 'Uber driver' drives through this acidic, low-pH neighborhood, it acts as a massive chemical alarm bell. The acid actually interacts with the Hemoglobin and changes its physical shape slightly. This shape change makes the Hemoglobin loosen its tight grip on the oxygen passengers. 

In biological terms, we say the lower pH 'decreases the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen' (affinity means attraction or grip). Because its grip is loosened, the Hemoglobin readily drops off its precious oxygen exactly where it is needed most—at the hard-working muscle! 

This brilliant phenomenon is called the Bohr Effect. It ensures that oxygen is beautifully distributed to the active tissues that are screaming for it. If the pH didn't drop, the hemoglobin might just hold onto the oxygen stubbornly and drive right past the muscle, leaving you instantly exhausted! So, a reduction in pH beautifully decreases hemoglobin's grip, forcing it to share its oxygen with your body.
questions.Answer: Decrease the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen

questions.Question: 27. Name the chronic respiratory disorder caused mainly by cigarette smoking.
questions.Hint: Think of a condition where the tiny air sacs in the lungs lose their elasticity and merge into large, floppy spaces, making it very hard to breathe out.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Sometimes, the choices people make can deeply damage the incredible biological machines we live inside. Let's talk about the tragic effects of cigarette smoking.

Deep inside your lungs, at the very end of your breathing tubes, are millions of microscopic, balloon-like air sacs called alveoli. These little balloons have incredibly thin, delicate, and stretchy walls. When you breathe in, they expand, and when you breathe out, their natural stretchiness (elasticity) helps them shrink back to size, pushing the used, stale air out of your body effortlessly.

Now, cigarette smoke is packed with thousands of toxic, burning chemicals. When a person smokes for many years, these harsh chemicals constantly bathe those delicate alveolar balloons. Your immune system tries to fight off the toxins by releasing powerful defender chemicals, but in the crossfire of this battle, these chemicals actually start digesting and destroying the walls of the alveoli themselves! 

The result is a chronic (long-term) disease called Emphysema. In a healthy person, there are millions of tiny, firm balloons providing lots of surface area to absorb oxygen. In someone with Emphysema, the walls between these little balloons break down, merging them into large, floppy, damaged sacs that have completely lost their bouncy elasticity. 

Imagine trying to deflate a crinkly plastic grocery bag instead of a rubber balloon; it just doesn't snap back. Because the lungs lose their stretch, the person cannot effectively push old air out. The stale air gets permanently trapped in their lungs, making them feel constantly out of breath, as if they are suffocating even while resting. Emphysema is mostly irreversible, which is one of the most powerful biological reasons to treat your lungs with love and never start smoking!

questions.Question: 28. Asthma may be attributed to
MCQ_Options: Accumulation of fluid in the lungs
Allergic inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles
questions.Hint: Think about a sudden allergic reaction that makes the lung's branching tubes swell up and squeeze tight, causing wheezing.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about Asthma, a condition you might have heard of, or perhaps you or a friend even have it! 

When we breathe, air travels down the windpipe (trachea) and branches into smaller and smaller tubes called bronchi and bronchioles. You can think of these tubes like the branches of an upside-down tree inside your chest. In a person with asthma, the inner lining of these tubular branches is incredibly sensitive. 

Asthma is essentially a sudden allergic reaction happening right inside the lung tubes. When a person with asthma breathes in certain triggers—like cold air, pet dander, pollen, or dust—their hyper-sensitive immune system completely overreacts, thinking the body is under attack. 

This overreaction does two major things to the bronchi and bronchioles. First, it causes severe inflammation, meaning the inner walls of the tubes swell up and get thick, just like a twisted ankle swells up. The immune system also makes the tubes produce a ton of thick, sticky mucus. Second, there are tiny bands of muscle wrapped around the outside of these tubes. During an asthma attack, these muscles violently spasm and squeeze the tubes shut. 

Imagine trying to drink a super thick milkshake through a tiny, narrow straw while someone is pinching the straw tightly with their fingers. It requires a tremendous amount of effort just to get a sip! This swelling, extra mucus, and muscle squeezing drastically narrow the airways, resulting in a whistling sound when breathing (called wheezing), coughing, and a terrifying feeling of a tight chest. 

So, asthma is primarily attributed to the allergic inflammation and narrowing of the bronchi and bronchioles. Fortunately, modern medicine gives us rescue inhalers, which contain magical medicine that relaxes those squeezing muscles and reduces the swelling, opening the tubes right back up so the person can breathe easily again!
questions.Answer: Allergic inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles

questions.Question: 29. Name the pulmonary disease in which alveolar surface area involved in gas exchange is drastically reduced due to damage in the alveolar walls.
questions.Hint: Think about a disease often caused by cigarette smoking that destroys the tiny, delicate 'balloons' in your lungs, merging them into bigger, floppy balloons that don't work as well.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Imagine your lungs are packed with millions of tiny, incredibly stretchy balloons called alveoli. These little balloons give your lungs a massive amount of surface area$\u2014$in fact, if you flattened them all out, they would cover an entire tennis court! This huge area is absolutely crucial because it provides the space for plenty of oxygen to enter your bloodstream and for carbon dioxide waste to leave. Now, let's talk about a disease called Emphysema, which is most commonly caused by smoking cigarettes. When someone smokes, the toxic chemicals in the smoke trigger inflammation that slowly eats away and breaks down the delicate, paper-thin walls of these tiny balloons. Instead of millions of small balloons, the walls rupture and merge, and you end up with fewer, much larger, and very floppy balloons. Why is this so bad? Think about a sponge. A sponge has thousands of tiny holes, giving it a huge surface area to soak up water. If you cut out the insides to make one giant hole, it won't soak up water nearly as well. With less surface area in the lungs, less oxygen gets into the blood. The person feels constantly exhausted and out of breath, like they are trying to breathe through a tiny straw. The lung tissue also loses its elastic stretchiness, so it's incredibly hard to push the old, stale air back out. Emphysema is a stark, powerful reminder of exactly why our lungs need to stay healthy and smoke-free!

questions.Question: 30. When you hold your breath, which of the following gas changes in blood would first lead to the urge to breathe?
questions.Hint: Your brain's automatic breathing center actually doesn't care as much about running out of fresh oxygen as it does about a certain 'trash' gas piling up inside your body.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Have you ever tried holding your breath underwater or seeing who can hold it the longest in your living room? After a few seconds, you start to feel this overwhelming, burning panic in your chest screaming at you to BREATHE! Most people logically assume this happens because your body is running out of oxygen. But guess what? That is completely wrong! The real trigger is a buildup of a waste gas called Carbon Dioxide (\$CO_2 \$). When your cells burn sugar to make energy, they produce \$CO_2 \$ as trash. This trash is dumped into your blood to be carried to your lungs. When you hold your breath, you stop exhaling, so the \$CO_2 \$ has absolutely nowhere to go. It starts building up in your blood very quickly. When \$CO_2 \$ mixes with the water in your blood, it creates a mild acid called carbonic acid. This makes your blood slightly more acidic. Deep inside the base of your brain, in a primitive control center called the medulla oblongata, you have special chemical detectors called chemoreceptors. These little sensors are incredibly sensitive to acid and \$CO_2 \$ levels. As soon as the \$CO_2 \$ spikes, these detectors sound a massive biological alarm! They fire frantic electrical signals down nerves to your diaphragm and chest muscles, forcing you to take a breath so you can blow off that toxic \$CO_2 \$. So, the intense urge to breathe is actually your body desperately trying to take out the trash, not searching for fresh air!

questions.Question: 31. Approximately seventy percent of carbondioxide absorbed by the blood will be transported to the lungs
MCQ_Options: As free carbonic acid in the red blood cells
questions.Hint: Carbon dioxide is a tricky molecule. To travel safely in massive amounts without making the blood incredibly acidic, it takes on an 'undercover disguise' as an ion before heading to the lungs.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Let's think about your bloodstream as a super busy, bustling highway system carrying cargo all around the body. One of the main pieces of cargo that needs to be hauled away is Carbon Dioxide (\$CO_2 \$), the waste product that your hardworking cells create. Your blood has to transport this \$CO_2 \$ all the way back to the lungs so you can exhale it. But \$CO_2 \$ doesn't just travel in one simple way$\u2014$it splits up into three different 'vehicles' to make the journey. About 7% is lazy; it just dissolves directly into the watery part of the blood (the plasma), exactly like how sugar dissolves in a cup of hot tea. Another 20-25% physically boards the delivery trucks (the Red Blood Cells) and binds straight onto the hemoglobin protein, becoming something called carbaminohemoglobin. But what about the massive majority? Around 70% of the \$CO_2 \$ undergoes a fascinating chemical magic trick! It enters the red blood cells, where a lightning-fast superhero enzyme named Carbonic Anhydrase forcefully smashes the \$CO_2 \$ together with water (\$H_2O \$) to create Carbonic Acid. This acid instantly splits apart into Hydrogen ions and Bicarbonate ions (\$HCO_3^- \$). These bicarbonate ions then step out of the red blood cell and float safely in the blood plasma all the way up to the lungs. Once they reach the lungs, the magic trick runs in reverse: bicarbonate turns back into \$CO_2 \$ gas, bubbles out into your lungs, and you breathe it away! This clever bicarbonate disguise allows your blood to carry huge amounts of waste without turning dangerously acidic.

questions.Question: 32. The figure shows a diagrammatic view of human respiratory system with labels A, B, C and D. Select the option which gives correct identification and main function and / or characteristic.
MCQ_Options: Alveoli - Thin-walled vascular bag-like structures for exchange of gases
Trachea - Supported by complete circular cartilaginous rings
Pleural membrane - Surrounds ribs on both sides to provide cushion against rubbing
Lower end of lungs - Diaphragm actively pulls it up during inspiration
questions.Hint: The most important part of the entire lung's anatomy is the absolute end of the line$\u2014$the microscopic zone where the actual trade of oxygen and carbon dioxide happens. Look for the tiny, hollow air sacs.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Even though we don't have the exact picture right in front of us, biology exams love to label the exact same main parts of the respiratory tract over and over: the trachea (windpipe), the bronchi, the lungs, and the alveoli. Let's act like biological detectives and look at the most famous label in these diagrams: the Alveoli. Think of your respiratory system like a giant, upside-down tree inside your chest. The thick trunk is your trachea, the big branches are the bronchi, the tiny twigs are the bronchioles, and the leaves at the very ends of those twigs are the alveoli. The alveoli are tiny, incredibly thin-walled, balloon-like structures. Why does their wall need to be so incredibly thin? Imagine you are trying to pass a secret paper note (representing oxygen) to your friend through a thick, heavy brick wall. It's impossible! But what if the wall was made of a single layer of tissue paper? Easy! Because the walls of the alveoli are only one single cell thick and are completely hugged by tiny, delicate blood vessels (capillaries), oxygen can easily slip right across the 'tissue paper' wall into the blood, and carbon dioxide can easily slip out. Therefore, describing Alveoli as 'Thin-walled vascular bag-like structures for exchange of gases' is the absolute perfect biological description. (As a fun side note to avoid traps: Trachea rings are actually incomplete, shaped like a 'C' so the food tube right behind it can expand, and the diaphragm pulls *down*, not up, when you breathe in!)
questions.Answer: Alveoli - Thin-walled vascular bag-like structures for exchange of gases

questions.Question: 33. Which one of the following is the correct statement for respiration in humans?
MCQ_Options: Inspiration occurs when the pressure within the lungs is less than the atmospheric pressure
Expiration occurs when the pressure within the lungs is less than the atmospheric pressure
The diaphragm relaxes and arches upward to initiate inspiration
Contraction of internal intercostal muscles violently pulls the ribs outward
questions.Hint: Think of your lungs exactly like a medical syringe. When you pull the plunger back to make the space inside bigger, it creates a vacuum (lower pressure inside) that automatically sucks fluid or air in.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Let's dive into the amazing physics of how you breathe! In physics, gases always follow a very strict rule: they want to move from an area of High Pressure to an area of Low Pressure. They hate being crowded together and will always rush to where there is more empty space. Your body uses this exact rule brilliantly to breathe without you even having to think about it. To take a breath in (this is called Inspiration), your brain sends a signal to your main breathing muscle, the diaphragm (a parachute-shaped sheet of muscle sitting right under your lungs). When told to contract, the diaphragm pulls itself flat and moves down. At the same time, muscles between your ribs pull your ribcage up and out. This sudden movement makes the space (volume) inside your chest cavity much bigger. Because the space inside your chest is suddenly larger, the air molecules inside have more room, which means the air pressure inside your lungs instantly drops. Now, the pressure inside your lungs is slightly *lower* than the atmospheric pressure outside your nose. Because air loves moving from high pressure to low pressure, atmospheric air physically forces its way into your nose and rushes down to inflate your lungs! You don't actively 'suck' air in; you just create a low-pressure vacuum, and the weight of the Earth's atmosphere pushes the air in for you. So, inspiration only happens because lung pressure falls below atmospheric pressure!
questions.Answer: Inspiration occurs when the pressure within the lungs is less than the atmospheric pressure

questions.Question: 34. People who have migrated from the planes to an area adjoining Rohtang Pass about six months back
MCQ_Options: Have more RBCs and their hemoglobin has a lower binding affinity to oxygen
Have fewer RBCs and their hemoglobin has a higher binding affinity to oxygen
Are physically unable to play strenuous games like football
Suffer constantly from severe altitude sickness with symptoms like nausea and fatigue
questions.Hint: Up high in the mountains, the air is 'thin' (meaning there is way less oxygen available). How does the body permanently upgrade its transport system over a few months to grab whatever little oxygen is floating around?
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Imagine you have lived your whole life on the flat plains near the ocean (at sea level), and suddenly you decide to move to the freezing, towering high mountains of Rohtang Pass. When you first step out of the car up there, you will probably feel dizzy, exhausted, and sick to your stomach. This is called 'Altitude Sickness.' Why does it happen? Because high up in the mountains, the atmospheric pressure is much lower, meaning the oxygen molecules in the air are spread really far apart. You literally get less oxygen entering your blood with every single breath! But the human body is an absolute masterpiece of adaptation. If you fight through the sickness and stay up there for six months, your body will 'acclimatize' (which is a fancy word for getting completely used to the new environment). How does it do this? First, your kidneys detect that your blood is starving for oxygen. They panic and release a special hormone called erythropoietin (EPO). EPO travels to your bone marrow and commands it to crank up a massive production of Red Blood Cells (RBCs). So, people living at high altitudes have significantly more RBCs than people at sea level! It's like sending out 50 delivery trucks instead of 10, because each truck can only carry a tiny amount of cargo. Second, to make sure these delivery trucks (hemoglobin) actually drop off the precious, scarce oxygen to your starving muscles instead of holding onto it selfishly, the hemoglobin's 'binding affinity' for oxygen physically decreases. This means the hemoglobin becomes more generous, eagerly giving the oxygen away to your tissues. It's a brilliant, life-saving biological hack!
questions.Answer: Have more RBCs and their hemoglobin has a lower binding affinity to oxygen

questions.Question: 35. The figure given below shows a small part of human lung where exchange of gases takes place. Select the option which represents labelled part (A, B, C or D) correctly identified along with its function.
MCQ_Options: Alveolar cavity - main site of exchange of respiratory gases
Red blood cell - transport of carbon dioxide mainly
Capillary wall - composed of thick stratified squamous epithelium
Basement substance - secretes mucus to trap dust
questions.Hint: The alveolar cavity is the completely hollow, empty space inside the microscopic 'lung balloon' where fresh, oxygen-rich air waits to cross the barrier into your bloodstream.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Think of a single tiny alveolus as a microscopic, round balloon deep inside your lung. This balloon is tightly wrapped in a net of tiny, flowing blood vessels called capillaries. The question refers to a classic biology diagram showing the junction between the air balloon and the blood vessel. What magical thing happens here? This is the ultimate trading post in the human body! The hollow, empty space right in the center of the balloon is called the Alveolar cavity. Every single time you take a deep breath in, this cavity fills up with fresh, oxygen-rich air from the outside world. This alveolar cavity is the absolute *main site of exchange of respiratory gases*. The oxygen from the fresh air inside the cavity diffuses (sneaks straight across) the ultra-thin walls of the balloon, passes through a tiny glued-together space called the basement membrane, and enters the red blood cells inside the capillary. At the exact same microsecond, the toxic carbon dioxide waste from the red blood cells jumps across the barrier in the exact opposite direction, leaving the blood and entering the alveolar cavity so you can forcefully breathe it out into the room. If a biology diagram points to the big empty space inside the lung balloon, it's pointing to the Alveolar cavity, the bustling hub where life-giving gas exchange actually takes place. (As a quick tip: the capillary wall is made of a single thin layer called 'simple squamous', not thick stratified, and red blood cells mainly transport oxygen, not CO2!)
questions.Answer: Alveolar cavity - main site of exchange of respiratory gases

questions.Question: 36. A large proportion of oxygen remains unused in the human blood even after its uptake by the body tissues. This O2
MCQ_Options: Acts as a reserve during muscular exercise.
Raises the pCO2 of blood to 75 mm Hg.
Is enough to keep oxyhaemoglobin saturation at 96%.
Is permanently bound to haemoglobin and never released.
questions.Hint: Think about what happens to your body when you suddenly start running and your muscles demand a massive amount of extra oxygen immediately.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine your blood is a massive fleet of delivery trucks (Red Blood Cells), and the precious cargo is oxygen molecules. When your blood passes through the tiny air sacs in your lungs, these trucks get fully loaded to the brim with oxygen. Under normal resting conditions—like when you are just sitting on the couch reading a book—as this blood travels around your body, your tissues only 'unload' about 25% of that oxygen to stay alive. That means when the blood returns to your heart and goes back to the lungs, the trucks are still 75% full! Why on earth would the human body be so incredibly inefficient? Why not just drop off all the oxygen at once? 

Well, it is actually a genius, life-saving survival mechanism! This leftover 75% oxygen is known in biology as the 'venous reserve'. Imagine you are casually walking home from school, and suddenly a fierce stray dog starts chasing you. Your leg muscles instantly need a massive, immediate amount of energy to sprint away, which means they need tons of extra oxygen right that exact second. If your blood only carried exactly what you needed while resting, you would literally collapse from exhaustion the moment you tried to run. Because you have this massive 75% backup reserve already circulating in your bloodstream, your active muscles can immediately start pulling extra oxygen from the blood without having to wait for your lungs to catch up and breathe faster. It acts as an emergency backup battery or chemical reserve that your body can tap into instantly during heavy muscular exercise, sports, or stressful fight-or-flight situations!
questions.Answer: Acts as a reserve during muscular exercise.

questions.Question: 37. Which one of the following is a possibility for most of us in regard to breathing, by making a conscious effort?
MCQ_Options: One can consciously breathe in and breathe out by moving the diaphragm alone, without moving the ribs at all.
The lungs can be made fully empty by forcefully exhaling all air from them.
One can breathe out air totally without any oxygen in it.
One can consciously stop breathing forever to cause self-asphyxiation.
questions.Hint: Think about the two main muscles involved in pulling air into your lungs—the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles between your ribs. Can you control them independently?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's break down how we actually pull air into our lungs. Your lungs are basically like soft, squishy balloons; they cannot inflate themselves. To get air inside them, you have to make the space inside your chest cavity bigger. When the chest cavity expands, it creates a vacuum (negative pressure) that sucks air in. Your body uses two main tools to expand the chest: the diaphragm (a strong parachute-shaped muscle underneath your lungs) and the intercostal muscles (tiny muscles between your ribs). 

When you breathe normally, both of these work together. The diaphragm pulls downward towards your stomach, and the rib muscles pull the ribs upward and outward. But here is the really cool part: because these are voluntary skeletal muscles, you have conscious control over them! If you focus, you can actually choose to keep your ribcage completely still and just push your belly out and in. Pushing your belly out pulls the diaphragm down, expanding your lungs to draw air in without moving your ribs at all. This is called 'diaphragmatic breathing' or 'belly breathing', and singers use it all the time! 

Let us look at why the other options are wrong. You can never force all the air out of your lungs; there is always a 'residual volume' left over so your lungs do not collapse and stick together like a wet deflated balloon. You also cannot consciously hold your breath forever; your brain's survival center (the medulla) will eventually force you to pass out and start breathing automatically. Finally, exhaled air still contains a lot of oxygen (about 16%), which is exactly why mouth-to-mouth CPR works to save lives!
questions.Answer: One can consciously breathe in and breathe out by moving the diaphragm alone, without moving the ribs at all.

questions.Question: 38. Bulk of carbon dioxide (CO2) released from body tissues into the blood is present as
MCQ_Options: Bicarbonate in blood plasma and RBCs.
Free CO2 dissolved in blood plasma.
questions.Hint: Carbon dioxide doesn't just float as a gas in your blood; most of it undergoes a chemical change with water to become a special, highly soluble ion.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
When your body cells burn sugar to make energy, they produce carbon dioxide (CO2) as a waste product. This CO2 needs to be transported through the blood back to your lungs so you can breathe it out. But CO2 is a tricky gas—if too much of it dissolves straight into your blood plasma as a free gas, it turns into acid and makes your blood dangerously acidic, which could damage your organs! 

To solve this massive problem, your body has three different ways of shipping CO2 safely. First, a tiny amount (only about 7%) just dissolves into the watery blood plasma. Second, about 20-25% hitches a ride by attaching directly to the haemoglobin protein inside your red blood cells. But what about the remaining 70%? This massive bulk needs a special trick. 

Inside your red blood cells, there is a super-fast superhero enzyme called 'Carbonic Anhydrase'. When CO2 enters the red blood cell, this enzyme grabs it and smashes it together with water to create a completely new chemical called a Bicarbonate ion (HCO3-). Think of it like taking a huge, bulky piece of trash and running it through a high-tech trash compactor. The new bicarbonate ion is incredibly safe, does not make the blood overly acidic, and dissolves effortlessly into the blood fluid. It travels all the way up to the lungs in this safe, 'compacted' bicarbonate form. Once it reaches the lungs, the enzyme works in reverse, magically turning the bicarbonate back into CO2 gas so you can exhale it into the air. Therefore, the vast majority of your body's CO2 travels as bicarbonate!
questions.Answer: Bicarbonate in blood plasma and RBCs.

questions.Question: 39. Listed below are four respiratory capacities (i − iv) and four jumbled respiratory volumes of a normal human adult. Which one of the following is the correct matching of two capacities and volumes?
MCQ_Options: Vital Capacity = 4600 mL, Inspiratory Capacity = 3500 mL
Residual Volume = 2500 mL, Vital Capacity = 3500 mL
Inspiratory Reserve Volume = 1000 mL, Expiratory Reserve Volume = 3000 mL
Total Lung Capacity = 3500 mL, Functional Residual Capacity = 1500 mL
questions.Hint: Vital Capacity is the absolute maximum amount of air you can exhale after taking the deepest possible breath. Think about adding your normal breath plus your maximum forced extra breathing.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this question, you need to understand how doctors measure the capacity of human lungs. Imagine your lungs are a bank account. 

1. 'Tidal Volume' (TV) is your everyday pocket money. It is the normal, relaxed amount of air you breathe in and out without even thinking about it, which is about 500 mL. 
2. 'Inspiratory Reserve Volume' (IRV) is like your emergency savings. It is the maximum extra air you can forcibly suck into your lungs after a normal breath in. This is huge, usually about 2500 to 3000 mL! 
3. 'Expiratory Reserve Volume' (ERV) is the loose change you scrape out of your pockets. It is the extra air you can forcibly push out after a normal exhale, about 1000 to 1100 mL. 
4. 'Residual Volume' (RV) is the minimum balance your bank absolutely requires to keep the account open. It is the air left trapped inside your lungs even after you push out as much air as humanly possible. This is roughly 1100 to 1200 mL, and it keeps the lungs from collapsing flat. 

Now, 'Capacities' are just mathematical combinations of these volumes! 'Inspiratory Capacity' (IC) is the total maximum amount you can breathe in. That is your normal breath plus your emergency savings (TV + IRV = 500 + 3000 = 3500 mL). 'Vital Capacity' (VC) is the absolute maximum amount of air you can move in and out of your lungs in a single giant, forceful breath. It includes your deepest inhale and your deepest exhale combined (TV + IRV + ERV = 500 + 3000 + 1100 = 4600 mL). So, looking at our biological math, the perfectly correct matching is Vital Capacity at 4600 mL and Inspiratory Capacity at 3500 mL!
questions.Answer: Vital Capacity = 4600 mL, Inspiratory Capacity = 3500 mL

questions.Question: 40. What is true about RBCs in humans?
MCQ_Options: They transport about 20-25 per cent of carbon dioxide.
They carry about 99.9 per cent of carbon dioxide.
They do not carry oxygen at all, only blood plasma carries oxygen.
They possess a large, multi-lobed nucleus in their mature stage.
questions.Hint: Red Blood Cells are totally famous for carrying Oxygen, but do they completely ignore Carbon Dioxide? Think about a compound called 'Carbamino-haemoglobin'.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Red Blood Cells (RBCs), scientifically called erythrocytes, are the ultimate delivery vans of the human body. When these cells mature in your bone marrow, they do something absolutely crazy: they actually spit out their own nucleus and most of their internal organs (organelles)! Why would a cell destroy its own brain? Because it wants to make as much empty room as possible inside itself to pack in millions of red proteins called haemoglobin. Haemoglobin is the magical, iron-rich molecule that acts like a claw to grab onto gases. 

Now, we mostly hear about RBCs carrying oxygen, and that is very true—they carry about 97% of all the oxygen in your blood from your lungs to your toes. But they also help clean up the cellular waste gas, carbon dioxide (CO2), on the return trip. However, they don't carry all of it. As we learned, most CO2 (about 70%) travels disguised as bicarbonate ions in the watery blood fluid (plasma). But a solid 20 to 25 percent of the CO2 physically binds directly to the haemoglobin claws inside the RBCs. When CO2 attaches to haemoglobin, it forms a compound with a very long, fancy name: carbamino-haemoglobin. 

So, let us evaluate the options: Human RBCs do not have a nucleus when mature (they threw it out!), they definitely carry massive amounts of oxygen (97%), and they certainly do not carry 99.9% of CO2. The perfectly true statement is that they transport about 20 to 25 percent of the carbon dioxide produced by our bodies. It is a brilliant division of labor that keeps our internal chemistry running smoothly!
questions.Answer: They transport about 20-25 per cent of carbon dioxide.

questions.Question: 41. The haemoglobin of a human foetus
MCQ_Options: Has a higher affinity for oxygen than that of an adult.
Has a lower affinity for oxygen than that of an adult.
Has exactly the same affinity for oxygen as that of an adult.
Has only two protein subunits instead of four.
questions.Hint: A baby developing inside the womb doesn't breathe air; it has to literally 'steal' oxygen from its mother's blood across the placenta. What kind of molecular magnetism would it need to win that tug-of-war?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Think about how you are breathing right now: you effortlessly pull fresh air into your lungs, and oxygen easily passes right into your blood. But a baby growing inside a mother's womb (a foetus) has a unique problem. It cannot breathe air because its lungs are filled with, and floating in, amniotic fluid! Instead, the foetus has to get all of the oxygen it needs to grow entirely from the mother's blood. 

The mother's blood and the baby's blood come very close to each other inside a fascinating organ called the placenta, but their blood never actually physically mixes. The oxygen has to magically jump from the mother's red blood cells over a barrier and into the baby's red blood cells. Here is the biological dilemma: if the baby's haemoglobin was exactly the same strength as the mother's haemoglobin, they would be equally matched, and the baby wouldn't be able to pull much oxygen away from the mother. 

To brilliantly solve this, nature gave the foetus a specialized kind of haemoglobin called Fetal Haemoglobin (HbF). Fetal haemoglobin is structurally a little different and acts like a super-magnet for oxygen! In biology terms, we say it has a much 'higher affinity' (a stronger chemical attraction) for oxygen. Imagine a microscopic game of tug-of-war where the oxygen molecule is the rope. The baby's haemoglobin is a giant champion bodybuilder, easily overpowering the mother's regular haemoglobin and pulling the oxygen across the placenta into the baby's bloodstream. This ensures the baby always gets enough oxygen! Shortly after birth, when the baby starts breathing air directly, their body slowly replaces this super-magnet fetal haemoglobin with regular adult haemoglobin.
questions.Answer: Has a higher affinity for oxygen than that of an adult.

questions.Question: 42. The majority of carbon dioxide produced by our body cells is transported to the lungs as
MCQ_Options: Dissolved simply in the blood plasma.
Carbonates bound to white blood cells.
questions.Hint: This is a recurring, super important concept! Remember the 'flat-pack' chemical form that CO2 takes so it can safely and efficiently travel through the blood without turning it into an acid.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Even though we touched on how carbon dioxide (CO2) is transported earlier, this exact concept is so incredibly important in human physiology that it shows up on tests over and over again! Let us dive into a new way to visualize the chemistry of it so it sticks in your brain forever. 

Every single time you move a muscle, digest food, or even just think, your microscopic cells are burning fuel (glucose) to make energy. The exhaust fume left over from this biological engine is CO2. If this CO2 gas built up in your tissues, it would be toxic and lethal. So, it gets dumped into your bloodstream to travel to the lungs for disposal. 

Imagine CO2 is bulky, flat-pack Ikea furniture in large cardboard boxes. You cannot fit many of these huge boxes into your small compact car (which represents the liquid blood plasma). If you just tried to forcefully cram CO2 gas into the plasma, you could only fit about 7% of it. Another 20-25% gets strapped to the roof rack of the car (this represents the CO2 binding directly to the haemoglobin inside red blood cells). But you still have a whopping 70% of the furniture left sitting on the sidewalk! 

To transport this massive majority, a brilliant worker enzyme inside the red blood cell called 'Carbonic Anhydrase' takes the bulky CO2 and chemically reacts it with water, changing its shape entirely into a tiny, easy-to-carry 'bicarbonate ion' (HCO3-). This is like taking the furniture out of the huge box and magically folding it down into a tiny pocket-sized cube. Now, 70% of the CO2 can easily and safely float in the blood plasma without turning the blood dangerously acidic! When it finally reaches the lungs, the magic cube unfolds back into CO2 gas, and you breathe it out into the world.

questions.Question: 43. Which one of the following statements is incorrect?
MCQ_Options: Oxygen is mostly transported bound to haemoglobin in the red blood cells.
Carbon dioxide is transported primarily as a dissolved gas in the blood plasma.
The diaphragm contracts and flattens out during inspiration (breathing in).
Alveoli are the primary sites where actual gas exchange takes place in the lungs.
questions.Hint: Think about how carbon dioxide travels. Does it prefer to float freely in the liquid of the blood, or does it undergo a chemical change to travel safely?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! The original text left this question a bit blank, so I've created a classic test question for you based on the surrounding topics of respiration. Let's talk about how your blood acts as a massive transport highway. Imagine your bloodstream is a river, and the red blood cells are little cargo boats. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are the cargo. Oxygen is kind of shy; it doesn't like dissolving in water (which makes up most of your blood plasma). Because of this, 97% of the oxygen hops onto the 'cargo boats' (red blood cells) and binds to a special protein called haemoglobin. So, the first option is totally true! 

Now, let's look at carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is a bit of a troublemaker. When your cells produce CO2 as waste, it needs to get to the lungs to be exhaled. While a tiny bit (about 7%) just dissolves in the plasma, and some (around 20-23%) catches a ride on haemoglobin, the vast majority of it—a whopping 70%—does a magic trick! It reacts with water in your blood to form something called 'bicarbonate ions'. It travels back to the lungs safely disguised as bicarbonate. Therefore, saying carbon dioxide is transported *primarily* as a dissolved gas is completely false. It's transported primarily as bicarbonate! 

The other options are true: your diaphragm (a parachute-shaped muscle under your lungs) definitely pulls down and contracts so you can suck air in. And the alveoli are indeed those tiny little air sacs in your lungs where oxygen enters the blood and CO2 leaves. So, the incorrect statement is the second one!
questions.Answer: Carbon dioxide is transported primarily as a dissolved gas in the blood plasma.

questions.Question: 44. People living at sea level have around 5 million RBC per cubic millimeter of their blood whereas those living at an altitude to 5400 metres have around 8 million. This is because at high altitude
MCQ_Options: Atmospheric O2 level is less and hence more RBCs are needed to absorb the required amount of O2 to survive.
There is more UV radiation, which directly stimulates the bone marrow to produce RBCs.
People eat more iron-rich food at high altitudes, leading to a surplus of red blood cells.
The cold temperature slows down blood flow, requiring more cells to keep the body warm.
questions.Hint: At the top of a giant mountain, the air is 'thinner'. If there is less oxygen available in every breath, how would your body try to capture as much of it as possible?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are trying to catch rain in buckets. Down at sea level, it's raining heavily (lots of oxygen pressure). You only need a few buckets (Red Blood Cells, or RBCs) to gather enough water (oxygen) for your body to survive. But what happens when you climb up to a super high altitude, like 5,400 meters? Up there in the mountains, the atmospheric pressure drops significantly. It's like the heavy rain turns into a very light drizzle. The air is 'thinner', meaning the partial pressure of oxygen is much, much lower. If you keep using the same small number of buckets, you won't catch enough water, and your body will start feeling exhausted, dizzy, and sick—a condition known as hypoxia.

But the human body is incredibly smart! When you stay at a high altitude for a while, your kidneys sense that your blood isn't carrying enough oxygen. In response, they hit the panic button and release a special hormone called Erythropoietin (EPO). EPO travels straight to your bone marrow and yells, 'Hey! We need more buckets out here!' Your bone marrow kicks into overdrive and manufactures millions of extra red blood cells. By increasing your RBC count from 5 million to 8 million, your body effectively puts out way more 'buckets'. Now, even though it's only 'drizzling' oxygen, having so many extra cells means you can still capture enough of it to keep your organs happy and functioning normally. This amazing adjustment process is called acclimatization. That's why high-altitude athletes often have incredible stamina when they come back down to sea level!
questions.Answer: Atmospheric O2 level is less and hence more RBCs are needed to absorb the required amount of O2 to survive.

questions.Question: 45. Blood analysis of a patient reveals an unusually high quantity of carboxyhaemoglobin content. Which of the following conclusions is most likely to be correct? The patient has been inhaling polluted air containing unusually high content of
questions.Hint: Look closely at the word 'carboxyhaemoglobin'. While carbon dioxide forms 'carbamino' haemoglobin, another very dangerous, invisible gas forms 'carboxy' haemoglobin. What gas comes from car exhausts and smoke?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's crack the code of the word 'carboxyhaemoglobin'. Your red blood cells are packed with a special protein called haemoglobin. Think of haemoglobin as a taxi cab circulating through your bloodstream. Usually, oxygen hops into the cab at the lungs, takes a ride, and gets dropped off at your muscles and brain. Sometimes, carbon dioxide hops into the cab for the return trip to the lungs (when it does this, it forms something called *carbaminohaemoglobin*—notice the 'amino' part). 

But here is where things get dangerous. Carbon monoxide (CO) is a toxic, invisible, and odorless gas that is produced when things burn incompletely—like in car engines, faulty heaters, or fires. Carbon monoxide is like a gigantic, incredibly stubborn bully. It loves haemoglobin. In fact, carbon monoxide's affinity (attraction) for haemoglobin is over 200 times stronger than oxygen's! 

When a person breathes in polluted air filled with carbon monoxide, this bully gas rushes into the lungs and violently shoves oxygen out of the way to get into the haemoglobin 'taxis'. Once carbon monoxide is in the seat, it locks the doors and refuses to leave. The complex it forms is called **carboxyhaemoglobin**. Because the carbon monoxide won't let go, oxygen can't get into the blood. Even if the person is breathing rapidly, their brain and organs start starving for oxygen. This is what causes carbon monoxide poisoning, making people feel incredibly sleepy and confused before eventually losing consciousness. So, if a doctor sees 'carboxyhaemoglobin' on a blood test, they know immediately: the patient has been breathing in carbon monoxide.

questions.Question: 46. When CO2 concentration in blood increases breathing becomes
MCQ_Options: Unaffected, because oxygen is the only gas that controls breathing
questions.Hint: Think about what happens when you hold your breath. Your body starts to panic not because you lack oxygen, but because a waste gas is building up. What do you immediately do once you stop holding your breath?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever tried to see how long you can hold your breath underwater? After a minute or so, your lungs start to burn, your chest heaves, and your brain screams at you to gasp for air. It's a common myth that your body is panicking because it's running out of oxygen. In reality, your body is panicking because carbon dioxide (CO2) is building up! 

Your body is constantly doing cellular respiration to make energy, and CO2 is the exhaust gas—the waste product. When you don't breathe out, CO2 gets trapped in your blood. Here is where chemistry comes in: when CO2 mixes with the water in your blood plasma, it forms carbonic acid. Yes, acid! If your blood gets too acidic, your enzymes and cells can't function properly. 

Deep inside your body, near your heart and in your brainstem, you have special 'smoke detectors' called chemoreceptors. These sensors don't really care about oxygen levels; their main job is to monitor CO2 and acid. The second they detect that CO2 levels are rising and the blood is becoming acidic, they sound a massive alarm. They send high-speed nerve signals to the respiratory center in your brain (the medulla oblongata). The brain immediately overrides your control and sends powerful signals to your diaphragm and rib muscles, ordering them to work harder. The result? Your breathing instantly becomes **faster and deeper** (hyperventilation). Why? Because your body is desperately trying to 'blow off' that extra CO2 into the atmosphere to get your blood pH back to a safe, normal level. This brilliant reflex keeps you alive!

questions.Question: 47. An average person not doing hard work requires energy per day about
questions.Hint: Even if you are just lying in bed all day binge-watching TV, your heart is beating, your brain is thinking, and your kidneys are filtering. How many calories do you think an average adult needs just to keep the 'engine' running moderately?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Think of your body like a highly advanced smartphone. Even when the screen is off and you aren't actively playing heavy video games, the battery is still slowly draining. Why? Because the phone is still running background apps, staying connected to Wi-Fi, and receiving messages. 

Your body works exactly the same way! Energy in biology is measured in calories (specifically, kilocalories or kcal). When we talk about an 'average person not doing hard work', we are talking about someone with a sedentary (sitting-heavy) lifestyle or engaging in very light daily tasks. Even if you don't run a marathon, your body's 'background apps' need tons of energy. Your heart has to beat 100,000 times a day. Your lungs have to take 20,000 breaths. Your liver is a chemical factory working 24/7. And your brain? Your brain is an energy hog, using up about 20% of all your daily calories just to keep you thinking and dreaming! 

The energy required just to keep you alive at rest is called your Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR). For a normal adult, the BMR alone usually requires around 1,500 to 1,800 kcal. When you add in the energy needed to walk around the house, digest food, and do basic light activities, the total daily requirement bumps up to about 2000 to 2800 kcal per day depending on age, size, and gender. If you were a lumberjack chopping wood or a professional athlete doing 'hard work', you might need 4,000 or even 5,000 kcal! But for average, everyday life, 2000 to 2800 kcal is the perfect sweet spot to keep your human battery fully charged without storing excess fat.

questions.Question: 48. Haemoglobin is a type of
questions.Hint: Look at the name itself. 'Globin' is a very common suffix used for biological molecules made of amino acids. And its main job is to give blood its red color while carrying oxygen.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's play biological detectives and dissect the word 'Haemoglobin' to understand exactly what it is. 

First, let's look at the second half: 'globin'. In biology, whenever you see the word 'globin', you are looking at a protein. Proteins are like the complex 3D Lego structures of your body, built out of tiny blocks called amino acids. Globin is a large, intricately folded protein. 

Now, let's look at the first half: 'Haem' (or Heme). The heme is a special, non-protein molecule that sits right in the middle of the globin protein. Right at the very center of this heme molecule is an atom of Iron (Fe). This iron is magical because it acts like a magnet for oxygen. When oxygen binds to the iron, it turns bright red. This is why when you get a cut, your blood looks crimson red!

So, when we put it together, Haemoglobin is a massive protein with an iron center whose entire purpose is to capture oxygen in the lungs and carry it to every cell in your body. Because it carries respiratory gases (oxygen and carbon dioxide) and gives blood its color, biologists officially classify it as a **respiratory pigment**. It's definitely not a carbohydrate (like sugar), a lipid (like fat), or a vitamin. It is a vital, hardworking respiratory protein that literally keeps you breathing and alive every single second!

questions.Question: 49. The respiratory centres, which control inspiration and expiration, are located in
questions.Hint: Breathing is an involuntary action, meaning you don't have to think about it to do it (thank goodness, or we'd forget while sleeping!). Which part of the lower brainstem acts as the 'autopilot' for fundamental survival rhythms like breathing and heart rate?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Think about how amazing your body is: you can go to sleep, completely lose consciousness, and yet your body keeps breathing perfectly all night long. You don't have to consciously command your lungs to say, 'Inhale... exhale... inhale... exhale.' That would be exhausting! 

The reason you don't have to think about it is because you have a built-in biological autopilot system. This autopilot is located at the very base of your brain, right where the brain connects to your spinal cord. This vital region is called the brainstem, and the superstar of the brainstem is a structure called the **Medulla oblongata**.

The Medulla oblongata is basically the primal survival center of your brain. It doesn't handle complex math problems or artistic creativity; it handles the absolute essentials of staying alive. Deep inside the medulla is a cluster of neurons called the 'Respiratory Rhythm Center'. This center acts like a drummer in a band, constantly tapping out a steady beat. It fires nerve signals down to your diaphragm and rib muscles, telling them exactly when to contract (breathe in) and when to relax (breathe out). If you go for a run and need more oxygen, the medulla quickly speeds up the drumbeat. The other options do different things: the cerebellum coordinates your physical balance, the hypothalamus controls things like body temperature and thirst, and the spinal cord is just the highway that carries the signals. But the true maestro conducting the symphony of your breath is the mighty Medulla oblongata!

questions.Question: 50. The exchange of gases in the alveoli of the lungs takes place by
questions.Hint: Think about how the smell of baking cookies naturally travels from the kitchen across the house; it doesn't need a motor or extra energy to spread out!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let's imagine your lungs are like a massive tree turned upside down, and at the very ends of the branches are tiny, microscopic balloons called 'alveoli'. When you take a deep breath in, these balloons fill up with fresh air, which is packed full of oxygen. Right wrapped around these tiny balloons are incredibly thin blood vessels called capillaries, carrying blood that has just traveled all around your body. This blood is tired, low on oxygen, and full of carbon dioxide (the waste gas your body wants to get rid of).$

So$, how do we get the good oxygen into the blood and the bad carbon dioxide out? Do we need to build tiny molecular pumps and spend energy? Nope! Nature uses a brilliant, free, and completely natural process called 'Simple Diffusion'. $

Simple$ diffusion is just the rule of the universe that molecules love to spread out. If there is a high concentration of something in one place, and a low concentration next door, the molecules will naturally drift over to the less crowded area until things are perfectly balanced. $

Inside$ the alveoli, there is a super high concentration of oxygen. In the blood right next to it, oxygen is very low. Because of simple diffusion, the oxygen naturally sneaks right through the thin walls of the balloon and into the blood. At the exact same time, the blood has a super high concentration of carbon dioxide, while the fresh air in the alveoli has almost none. So, the carbon dioxide diffuses the other way, leaving the blood and entering the balloon, ready for you to breathe it out. It happens purely driven by concentration differences, without your body spending a single drop of energy! Isn't that perfectly efficient?

questions.Question: 51. The CO2 content by volume, in the atmospheric air is about
questions.Hint: Even though we talk about it a lot when discussing climate change, this gas actually makes up a tiny, tiny fraction of a single percent of the air we breathe!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about the invisible ocean of air we walk around in every single day! If you were to take a magic jar, scoop up some normal atmospheric air, and separate it into its individual ingredients, you might be really surprised by the recipe. $

A$ lot of people think the air we breathe is mostly oxygen, but that's actually a myth! About 78% of the air around us is a gas called Nitrogen. Nitrogen is super stable and essentially just 'filler' gas for us; we breathe it in, and we breathe it right back out without using it. Oxygen makes up about 21% of the air, which is the perfect amount to keep our bodies running without being dangerously flammable. $

Now$, what about Carbon Dioxide (CO2)? Because we hear about CO2 so much on the news regarding pollution and global warming, it is super easy to assume there's a huge amount of it in the sky. But incredibly, by volume, CO2 makes up only about 0.03% to 0.04% of atmospheric air! $

Think$ of it like adding a pinch of extremely potent salt to a giant pot of soup. Even though it's just a tiny fraction of a percent (0.03%), it plays a massive role in our planet's temperature by trapping heat (the greenhouse effect), and it is the crucial ingredient plants need to perform photosynthesis and make food for the whole world. So, when you look at that 0.03%, remember that in biology and ecology, even incredibly tiny numbers can have a gigantic impact!

questions.Question: 52. In lungs, the air is separated from the venous blood through
MCQ_Options: Squamous epithelium of alveoli and endothelium of blood capillaries
questions.Hint: Imagine needing a wall so thin that gases can phase right through it. You'd want to build it using the flattest, thinnest 'pancake' cells possible from both the lung and the blood vessel.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
If you want gases (like Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide) to swap places in the lungs quickly, you have a big structural challenge. If the wall between the air and the blood is too thick, the gases will take forever to cross, and you'll run out of breath! So, your body constructs the ultimate ultra-thin barrier, known as the 'respiratory membrane' or 'diffusion boundary.'$

Let$'s look at the architecture of this amazing microscopic wall. It is essentially made of two ultra-thin layers of cells glued together.$

1$. **The wall of the Alveolus (Air Sac):** The air balloon in your lung is lined with incredibly flat, scale-like cells. In biology, we call flat, tile-like cells 'squamous'. And because it lines a surface, it's called an 'epithelium'. So, layer one is the 'squamous epithelium of alveoli'. Imagine this as a layer of extremely thin, wet tissue paper.$

2$. **The wall of the Capillary (Blood Vessel):** The tiny blood vessel hugging the alveolus is also made of extremely flat cells. When these flat cells line a blood vessel, we give them a special name: 'endothelium'. So, layer two is the 'endothelium of blood capillaries'.$

Between$ these two single-cell layers is a tiny bit of glue called the 'basement substance' that sticks them together. Together, this entire barrier is less than a millimeter thick! It is so staggeringly thin that oxygen and carbon dioxide molecules can just effortlessly drift right through them. So, the air and your blood are separated only by the squamous epithelium of the alveoli and the endothelium of the blood capillaries!
questions.Answer: Squamous epithelium of alveoli and endothelium of blood capillaries

questions.Question: 53. Which vertebrate organ receives only oxygenated blood?
questions.Hint: Look for the organ that acts like an immune system base and blood-filter. The lungs and liver get 'dirty' or deoxygenated blood to process, but this organ gets a pure, fresh supply straight from the main artery!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a fantastic puzzle about how the body plumbs its blood supply! You might think, 'Doesn't every organ need oxygenated blood?' Well, yes, but many organs are multi-taskers and have dual blood supplies, meaning they receive a mix of oxygenated (fresh) and deoxygenated (used) blood.$

Let$'s break down the suspects:$
$- **Lungs:** The lungs' main job is to put oxygen INTO the blood. So, the heart actively pumps dark, deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery so it can get fresh oxygen. (They also get a tiny bit of oxygenated blood to stay alive, but they definitely receive a massive amount of deoxygenated blood).$
$- **Liver:** The liver is the body's chemical factory. It receives oxygenated blood to keep its cells alive, but it ALSO receives a massive river of deoxygenated, nutrient-rich blood straight from the intestines (via the hepatic portal vein) to filter out toxins and store food.$
$- **Gills:** In fish, gills do exactly what lungs do for us—they receive deoxygenated blood to fill it up with oxygen.$

But$ what about the **Spleen**? The spleen is a purple, fist-sized organ tucked under your ribcage. It acts as a strict quality-control filter for your blood, destroying old, worn-out red blood cells and serving as a barracks for white blood cells fighting infections. To do this, it only needs one main pipeline in. It receives purely fresh, oxygen-rich blood directly from the aorta via a large pipe called the 'splenic artery'. It doesn't have any incoming veins carrying used blood from other organs. It takes the pure arterial blood, filters it, and sends it out. Therefore, out of these classic options, the Spleen is the organ receiving ONLY oxygenated blood!

questions.Question: 54. How the transport of O2 and CO2 by blood happens?
questions.Hint: Think of your blood like a bustling river. Gas transport relies on both the liquid water of the river itself AND the billions of little red 'cargo boats' floating in it.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
If your body were a giant city, your bloodstream would be the intricate highway system delivering oxygen (the cargo needed for energy) to all the cell 'houses' and taking away carbon dioxide (the garbage). But how do these gases actually travel in the blood?$

They$ use two main methods: the 'Cargo Boats' and the 'River Water'.$

1$. **The Cargo Boats (Red Blood Cells - RBCs):** Your Red Blood Cells are literally packed with a magical iron-rich protein called Hemoglobin. Hemoglobin acts like a magnet for oxygen. When blood passes through the lungs, about 97% of the oxygen jumps onto these RBC cargo boats. Hemoglobin also helps transport carbon dioxide! On the trip back to the lungs, about 20-25% of the body's CO2 waste jumps onto the RBCs.$

2$. **The River Water (Blood Plasma):** Blood isn't just cells; it's mostly a yellowish liquid called plasma (which is over 90% water). While oxygen doesn't dissolve very well in water (only about 3% travels dissolved in plasma), carbon dioxide loves to mix with water! About 7% of CO2 travels simply dissolved directly in the plasma. More impressively, the remaining 70% of CO2 is chemically converted into something called 'bicarbonate ions' and travels right inside the liquid plasma.$

So$, without the Red Blood Cells, we wouldn't be able to carry anywhere near enough oxygen to survive. And without the watery Blood Plasma, we'd have a huge traffic jam trying to get rid of our carbon dioxide. Transporting these crucial gases requires incredible teamwork between the RBCs and the blood plasma!

questions.Question: 55. When 1500ml air is in the lungs, it is called
questions.Hint: Even if you squeeze your chest and blow out as hard as humanly possible, you can never completely empty your lungs. A specific volume of air always 'resides' in there!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever tried blowing up a wet plastic bag, and then squeezing all the air out of it? If you squeeze it completely flat, the wet inner sides stick to each other, making it incredibly hard to pull apart and blow up again! $

Your$ lungs work on a very similar principle. If you were to blow out absolutely every single drop of air inside them, the tiny delicate air sacs (alveoli) would collapse and stick together like that wet plastic bag. To prevent this dangerous collapse, nature designed your lungs so that no matter how hard you exhale—even if you squeeze your stomach and push out all the air you can—a certain amount of air is trapped inside permanently to keep the balloons slightly inflated.$

This$ leftover, life-saving air is called the **Residual Volume (RV)**. It 'resides' or stays behind in your lungs permanently. $

Now$, different textbooks sometimes give slightly different numbers for biological measurements. On average, standard textbooks (like NCERT for medical exams) put the Residual Volume between 1100 ml and 1200 ml. However, depending on a person's size, age, and the specific medical literature, Residual Volume is frequently cited in the range of up to 1500 ml. Since this volume represents the un-exhalable air left in the lungs, 'Residual Volume' is the biological concept this question is aiming for. It's the ultimate biological safety cushion for your respiratory system!

questions.Question: 56. Lungs are enclosed in
questions.Hint: Your lungs are constantly expanding and shrinking against your ribs. To stop them from getting scratched, they are wrapped in a special double-layered sleeping bag starting with the letter 'P'.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Take a deep breath in. Your lungs just inflated like two giant sponges, expanding inside your chest and pressing up right against the hard bones of your ribcage. Now breathe out. They shrink back down. You do this about 20,000 times a day! $

Now$, imagine rubbing a soft sponge against a hard bone 20,000 times a day. Very quickly, the sponge would get completely shredded and destroyed by the friction. So why don't your lungs get damaged? $

It$'s because nature gave your lungs their very own ultra-slippery sleeping bag called the **Pleural Membrane** (or Pleura). $

It$ works like this: it's actually a double-layered sac. One layer sticks tightly to the outside of the lung itself, and the other layer sticks to the inside of your ribcage. Between these two layers is a tiny, microscopic space filled with a slippery liquid called 'pleural fluid.' This fluid acts exactly like engine oil in a car. When you breathe, the two layers gracefully slide and glide past each other on this fluid without creating any friction or heat at all. $

Let$'s quickly look at the other options so you know them too: The 'Pericardium' wraps the heart (cardiac). The 'Peritoneum' wraps your stomach and intestines. And the 'Meninges' wrap your brain and spinal cord. But for the lungs, their protective, friction-free home is the Pleural membrane!

questions.Question: 57. At high altitude, the RBCs in the human blood will
questions.Hint: Think about the air on a high mountain. The air is thinner, meaning there is less oxygen available with each breath. How would your body's 'oxygen delivery system' adapt to make sure your cells still get enough oxygen?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine your body's oxygen delivery system is like a pizza delivery company. Your Red Blood Cells (RBCs) are the delivery drivers, and the oxygen molecules are the pizzas. At sea level, there's a massive supply of pizzas (high oxygen pressure), so a normal number of drivers can easily pick up enough pizzas and deliver them to your hungry cells. However, when you travel to a high altitude—like climbing Mount Everest or visiting a high mountain town—the atmospheric pressure drops. The air becomes 'thinner'. This means there are fewer 'pizzas' available at the lungs for pickup. 

Because each RBC can't pick up as much oxygen as it normally would, your tissues start crying out for more energy. This state of low oxygen is called 'hypoxia'. Your body is incredibly smart, though! Your kidneys act like the managers of this delivery company. They 'sniff' the blood and notice the oxygen levels are dropping. In panic, they release a special hormone called Erythropoietin (EPO). EPO travels straight to your bone marrow (the factory where blood cells are made) and shouts, 'We need more delivery drivers immediately!' 

As a result, your bone marrow ramps up production, heavily increasing the total number of Red Blood Cells in your blood. This condition is called 'polycythemia'. By having millions of extra RBCs, your blood can now capture the scarce oxygen molecules more effectively, ensuring your brain and muscles get the fuel they need. This amazing process is a key part of 'acclimatization'—your body's way of adjusting to a new environment. This is exactly why athletes often train at high altitudes; it naturally boosts their RBC count, giving them super-charged stamina when they return to sea level!

questions.Question: 58. Although much CO2 is carried in blood, yet blood does not become acidic, because
MCQ_Options: Blood buffers play an important role
It is absorbed by the leucocytes (WBCs)
It combines with water to form H2CO3 which is neutralized by Na2CO3
It is continuously diffused through the tissues and is not retained
questions.Hint: When carbon dioxide dissolves in water, it forms an acid. But your blood has special chemical 'sponges' that soak up extra acid to keep the pH perfectly balanced.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this, we first need to look at what happens when carbon dioxide (CO2) meets water. When your cells burn food for energy, they produce CO2 as waste. This CO2 gets dumped into your blood, which is mostly made of water. In chemistry, when CO2 mixes with water (H2O), it forms Carbonic Acid (H2CO3). This acid quickly splits into Hydrogen ions (H+) and Bicarbonate ions (HCO3-). 

Now, here is the danger: Hydrogen ions (H+) are the very definition of acidity. If too many H+ ions float around in your blood, your blood's pH would drop, turning it highly acidic. This would be fatal, because the proteins and enzymes in your body would literally melt or lose their shape in an acidic environment! So, why doesn't this happen? 

Enter the heroes of our story: Blood Buffers. A 'buffer' is a chemical system that acts exactly like a sponge. If you spill a little water (acid) on a table, you use a sponge to soak it up so it doesn't ruin the wood. In your blood, proteins—especially Hemoglobin inside the Red Blood Cells—act as these sponges. When the Carbonic Acid breaks apart and releases those dangerous H+ ions, Hemoglobin quickly grabs onto them and holds them tight. By locking away the H+ ions, Hemoglobin prevents them from floating free and making the blood acidic. 

Additionally, the bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) themselves act as an amazing buffer system in the blood plasma, soaking up extra acid or releasing it when necessary to keep the blood pH strictly at around 7.4. Thanks to these microscopic chemical sponges, you can carry massive amounts of CO2 waste from your toes all the way to your lungs without your blood ever turning into a dangerous acid bath!
questions.Answer: Blood buffers play an important role

questions.Question: 59. The carbon dioxide is transported via blood to lungs mostly
questions.Hint: Carbon dioxide travels in the blood in three different ways. While some simply dissolves or rides on red blood cells, the vast majority wears a 'chemical disguise' created by a super-fast enzyme.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore the great escape of Carbon Dioxide! Every single cell in your body produces CO2 as a waste product of cellular respiration—kind of like the exhaust fumes from a car engine. This CO2 needs to travel through the bloodstream to reach the lungs so you can exhale it. But how does it travel? It actually splits into three different travel groups.

Group 1 takes the lazy route: About 7% of the CO2 just dissolves directly into the watery part of the blood (the plasma), exactly like the fizzy gas dissolved in a bottle of soda. 

Group 2 hitches a ride: About 20% to 25% of the CO2 physically binds to the Hemoglobin molecules inside your Red Blood Cells. When it attaches to Hemoglobin, it forms a compound with a very long name: 'Carbaminohemoglobin'. 

Group 3 is the massive majority—about 70% of the CO2! Because there is so much CO2, it can't all just dissolve or hitch a ride. It needs a chemical disguise. This 70% enters the Red Blood Cell, where it meets a superhero enzyme called 'Carbonic Anhydrase'. This enzyme works at lightning speed to smash the CO2 and Water (H2O) together, creating Carbonic Acid (H2CO3). The acid quickly breaks apart into a Hydrogen ion (H+) and a Bicarbonate ion (HCO3-). 

Once disguised as this Bicarbonate ion, it is kicked out of the Red Blood Cell and into the blood plasma, where it safely floats all the way up to the lungs. Once it reaches the lungs, the whole process runs in reverse! The Bicarbonate turns back into CO2, and you breathe it out. So, while CO2 uses a few methods to travel, its favorite and most common mode of transport is in the disguised form of Bicarbonate ions!

questions.Question: 60. The ventilation movements of the lungs in mammals are governed by
questions.Hint: Your lungs are just floppy bags of tissue; they don't have their own muscles to pull air in. They rely entirely on a large dome-shaped muscle below them and the tiny muscles between your ribs to do the heavy lifting.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Take a deep breath in. Now let it out. What exactly just happened inside your chest? A lot of people think the lungs themselves 'flex' or 'suck' the air in, but that is actually a myth! Lungs are practically like two wet, elastic balloons. They do not have skeletal muscles of their own to force themselves open. To get air to flow in and out (a process called ventilation), your body has to rely on the physics of pressure and volume, governed by a team of muscles outside the lungs.

Here is how the magic happens. Your chest cavity is an airtight box. The bottom floor of this box is a thick, dome-shaped sheet of muscle called the 'Diaphragm'. The walls of the box are your ribs, and between your ribs are tiny muscles called 'Intercostal muscles'. 

When your brain tells you to inhale, the Diaphragm flexes and pulls downward, flattening out. At the exact same time, the external Intercostal muscles flex and lift your rib cage up and outward (like lifting the handle of a bucket). Because the floor dropped and the walls expanded, the inside of your chest cavity suddenly gets much bigger! According to Boyle's Law in physics, when the volume of a closed space increases, the pressure inside it drops. 

So, the air pressure inside your lungs becomes lower than the air pressure in the room around you. Nature hates empty spaces, so the higher-pressure air from the outside rushes through your nose and down your throat to fill up your expanding lungs. When it's time to breathe out, those muscles simply relax. The Diaphragm pops back up into a dome, the ribs drop down, the chest cavity shrinks, the pressure shoots up, and the air is squished right back out. Your lungs are just along for the ride, controlled entirely by the mighty Diaphragm and Intercostal muscles!

questions.Question: 61. The respiratory centre which regulates respiration is located in
questions.Hint: Breathing is an automatic survival function, so its control center sits in the most primitive part of your brainstem, right at the base of your skull where it connects to the spinal cord.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Think about all the things you did today. You probably walked around, talked, played a game, or ate food. While you were distracted doing all those things, who was reminding your lungs to breathe 15 times every single minute? If you had to consciously remember to breathe, you wouldn't be able to sleep, because the moment you fell asleep, you'd forget to breathe!

Thankfully, breathing is controlled by an 'autopilot' system in your brain. The brain is divided into several parts. The 'Cerebrum' is the big wrinkly part on top where you do your math homework and think conscious thoughts. The 'Cerebellum' at the back helps you balance. But deep down at the very base of the brain, connecting straight to your spinal cord, is the brainstem. A crucial part of this brainstem is called the 'Medulla Oblongata'.

The Medulla Oblongata is the primal, survival headquarters of your body. It contains a specialized cluster of neurons called the Respiratory Rhythm Center. You can think of it as a metronome or a drummer setting the beat for a band. It constantly sends electrical signals down your spinal nerves to your diaphragm and rib muscles, shouting 'Flex! Relax! Flex! Relax!' 

What is incredibly cool is that the Medulla acts like a thermostat. But instead of measuring temperature, it constantly measures the levels of Carbon Dioxide (CO2) in your blood. If you start running, your muscles make more CO2. The Medulla instantly senses this acidic rise and speeds up the 'drumbeat', making you pant and breathe faster to clear the waste gas. So, the Medulla Oblongata is the master control center keeping you alive breath by breath, completely behind the scenes!

questions.Question: 62. Carbon dioxide is transported from tissues to respiratory surface by only
questions.Hint: Carbon dioxide doesn't just use one type of vehicle to get to the lungs. It uses both the liquid 'river' of the blood and the red 'boats' floating within it.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To get carbon dioxide (CO2) out of our busy tissues and back to our lungs (the respiratory surface), the body uses a brilliant, multi-layered transport system. The word 'only' in the question can be tricky, but we are looking for the two primary components of blood that make this transport possible: the Blood Plasma and the Red Blood Cells (RBCs).

Let's break down the blood. Blood is roughly 55% a yellowish, watery liquid called Plasma, and 45% solid cells (mostly Red Blood Cells). 

When tissues dump their CO2 trash into the bloodstream, the plasma acts like a flowing river. About 7% of the CO2 just dissolves directly into this river of plasma and flows to the lungs. 

But the river can't hold all the trash! So, the Red Blood Cells act like special cargo boats. The remaining 93% of the CO2 enters the RBCs. Inside the RBC, two things happen. First, about 20-25% of the CO2 binds directly to the Hemoglobin protein inside the boat. Second, the massive remaining chunk (about 70%) gets converted by an enzyme in the RBC into a Bicarbonate ion. Once it turns into Bicarbonate, the RBC actually tosses it back out into the river (the plasma) for the rest of the journey. 

So, as you can see, both the Blood Plasma (the liquid river) and the Red Blood Cells (the cargo boats) are absolutely essential and work together as a synchronized team to transport CO2. White Blood Cells (WBCs) fight infections and have absolutely nothing to do with transporting gases. Therefore, CO2 is transported from the tissues to the lungs by both Blood Plasma and RBCs!

questions.Question: 63. The alveolar epithelium in the lung is
questions.Hint: The alveoli are the tiny air sacs where oxygen crosses into the blood. For gas to pass through as fast as possible, these cells need to be incredibly thin and flat, like paving stones, and shouldn't have any tiny hairs blocking the way.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's zoom way, way down into the deepest, microscopic parts of your lungs. When you breathe air in, it travels down your windpipe, through branching tubes, and finally ends up in millions of tiny, microscopic balloon-like sacs called 'Alveoli'. These alveoli are wrapped in tiny blood vessels. This is the exact magical spot where Oxygen leaves the air and enters your blood, and Carbon Dioxide leaves your blood to enter the air.

Because this gas exchange happens through 'diffusion' (molecules simply floating from high concentration to low concentration), the barrier between the air and the blood needs to be ridiculously thin. If the barrier were thick, it would be like trying to pass a secret note through a thick brick wall—it would take way too long!
