Your pupil physically shrinks to let less light in, the overloaded Rods take a break, and your daytime Cones wake up and take over the job of seeing. Once the Cones are fully in charge, your vision becomes perfectly clear and normal again!

questions.Question: Which of the following statements is the characteristics of human cornea?
MCQ_Options: It is avascular and absorbs oxygen directly from the air
It is highly vascularized to maintain cell health
It is the innermost layer of the eye containing rods and cones
It secretes the vitreous humor to keep the eye round
questions.Hint: If the clear front window of your eye had red blood vessels running through it, you wouldn't be able to see clearly!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about the cornea! If you look at your eye closely in a mirror, the cornea is the completely clear, dome-shaped window covering the very front of it (right over the colored part, which is the iris). It acts like a camera lens and is absolutely crucial for focusing incoming light so you can see properly.

Now, think about the rest of your body. Almost every single tissue—your skin, your muscles, your organs—needs red blood vessels to deliver oxygen and nutrients, right? But imagine if you had tiny red blood vessels crisscrossing over the clear front window of your eye. Your vision would be incredibly blurry and tinted red! To solve this problem, the cornea has a fascinating biological characteristic: it is completely 'avascular', meaning it has absolutely NO blood vessels.

But wait, if it has no blood vessels, how do the living cells in the cornea survive? Where do they get their oxygen? The answer is mind-blowing: the cornea literally breathes the outside air! It dissolves oxygen directly from the air into your tears, which then nourish the front surface of the eye. The inside part of the cornea gets its food from a clear, watery fluid inside the eye called the aqueous humor. 

Because the cornea has no blood supply, it's also highly hidden from the body's immune system. This is why corneal transplants are one of the most successful transplant surgeries in the world—without blood vessels, the immune system's attack cells rarely notice the new tissue, so the body almost never rejects it!
questions.Answer: It is avascular and absorbs oxygen directly from the air

questions.Concept: Generation and Conduction of Nerve Impulse
questions.Question: Depolarization of axolema during nerve conduction takes place because of
questions.Hint: During the resting state, the inside of the neuron is negative. To fire an electrical signal, positive ions from the outside must rush IN. Which salty ion is waiting outside?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's unravel the amazing mystery of how nerves send electrical signals! Imagine a single nerve cell (a neuron) as a 'salty banana'. Why? Because when a nerve is just resting and doing nothing, it has a lot of Potassium (which bananas are full of) on the INSIDE, and it swims in a lot of Sodium (salt) on the OUTSIDE. 

Because of how these chemicals are naturally arranged, the inside of the resting neuron is slightly negatively charged compared to the outside. This resting state is called being 'polarized'. It's like a stretched rubber band, loaded with potential energy, just waiting to snap!

When your brain wants to send a quick message (like telling your arm muscles to move), an electrical signal starts traveling down the nerve fiber (the axolemma, which is simply the membrane of the nerve's long tail). To actually fire this signal, special trapdoors in the membrane suddenly fly open. Because there is so much Sodium (Na+) waiting impatiently on the outside, it instantly RUSHES INTO the cell. 

Since Sodium ions carry a positive electrical charge, this massive 'influx' (rushing in) of Sodium suddenly makes the inside of the cell highly positive. Going from a negative resting state to a positive firing state is called 'Depolarization'. This sudden flip in electricity is the actual 'spark' or action potential that travels rapidly down the nerve wire. So, depolarization happens purely because Sodium gates open and Na+ floods inside!

questions.Question: Which cranial nerve has the highest number of branches?
questions.Hint: This nerve's name literally means 'wanderer' because it wanders all the way from the brain down into the chest and abdomen to control your heart and digestive system.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Your brain has 12 special pairs of cables that come directly out of it, bypassing the spinal cord entirely. These are known as the 'cranial nerves'. Most of these nerves stay strictly in your head and neck area—they let you smell a pizza, see a movie, chew your food, and smile. But there is one absolute superstar among them that refuses to stay put in the head. It's Cranial Nerve X (the 10th one), famously known as the 'Vagus Nerve'.

The word 'Vagus' comes from Latin and literally means 'wanderer' (it shares the exact same root word as vagabond). This is the absolute perfect name for it! After leaving the brainstem, the Vagus nerve goes on a massive road trip. It wanders down your neck, travels deep through your chest, and goes all the way down into your abdomen. 

Because it travels so incredibly far through the body, it has to send out branches everywhere it goes. It has branches connecting to your throat (so you can speak and swallow), branches attached to your heart (to help slow down your heart rate), branches to your lungs (to regulate your breathing), and countless branches wrapping all around your stomach and intestines (to control your digestion). No other cranial nerve covers this much territory or controls so many different internal organs. Therefore, because of its epic, wandering journey and the sheer number of organs it talks to, the Vagus nerve is the cranial nerve with the highest number of branches!

questions.Question: Sympathetic nervous system induces
MCQ_Options: Increased heart rate and pupil dilation (Fight or Flight)
Constriction of pupils and deep sleep
questions.Hint: Think of the word 'Sympathy'. When you are stressed or in danger, this system feels 'sympathy' for you and gives you superpowers to fight or run away!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are walking through the jungle, minding your own business, when suddenly a massive, hungry tiger jumps out of the bushes! What happens to your body? Your heart instantly starts pounding out of your chest, you start breathing heavily, your eyes widen, and you feel a massive surge of adrenaline and energy. This intense reaction is your body's classic 'Fight or Flight' response, and it is entirely triggered and controlled by your Sympathetic Nervous System!

Your autonomic nervous system (which controls things automatically without you thinking about them) works exactly like the gas pedal and the brake pedal in a sports car. The Sympathetic Nervous System is the 'Gas Pedal'. When your brain senses danger, stress, or excitement, this system instantly induces a cascade of survival reactions to keep you alive. 

It tells your heart to beat much faster so it can pump more oxygen-rich blood to your leg muscles. It dilates (widens) your pupils so your eyes can gather more light to clearly see the danger and spot escape routes. It opens up your lung airways so you can gulp huge amounts of oxygen. 

At the exact same time, it temporarily shuts down non-essential bodily systems—like digestion! If you are actively running for your life from a tiger, your body doesn't care about digesting the turkey sandwich you ate for lunch; it needs to divert all that energy to your muscles to help you survive. So, whenever you see the word 'Sympathetic' in biology, just think of the 'Fight or Flight' superhero mode that aggressively gears your body up for intense action!
questions.Answer: Increased heart rate and pupil dilation (Fight or Flight)

questions.Question: 57. The junction between the axon of one neuron and the dendrite of the next is called
questions.Hint: Think of the tiny 'gap' where two nerve cells meet to pass a message, almost like handing off a baton in a relay race.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine playing a massive game of telephone or running a relay race. One runner finishes their part of the track and is ready to pass the baton to the next runner. In your brain and throughout your entire body, your nerve cells (which are called neurons) are these runners, and the electrical messages they carry are the baton. However, there is a fascinating twist: neurons don't actually physically touch each other! There is a tiny, microscopic physical gap between the end of one neuron (called the axon terminal) and the receiving end of the next neuron (called the dendrite). This special meeting point or junction where the communication happens is called a 'synapse'.

Because the electrical spark cannot jump across this empty space, the first neuron has to use a chemical trick. It releases tiny chemical messengers called 'neurotransmitters' into this gap. These chemicals float across the synapse like little boats crossing a river and lock into special docking stations (receptors) on the dendrite of the second neuron. Once enough boats dock, they trigger a brand-new electrical spark in the second neuron, allowing the message to continue its journey to your brain or muscles! Without synapses, our nerve signals would just hit a dead end, and we wouldn't be able to think, feel, or move. Looking at the other options: 'Nodes of Ranvier' are just uninsulated gaps on a single neuron's axon to help the signal jump faster, a 'Neuromuscular junction' is specifically where a nerve meets a muscle fiber (not another neuron), and the 'Myelin sheath' is the fatty insulation wrapping the nerve. Therefore, the junction between two distinct neurons is simply and beautifully called a synapse.

questions.Question: 58. Which of the following is regarded as a unit of nervous tissue?
questions.Hint: What is the individual 'wire' or microscopic building block cell that makes up your brain, spinal cord, and all your nerves?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Think of your nervous system as a gigantic, ultra-fast, and incredibly complex computer network that controls absolutely everything you do. It allows you to breathe, solve difficult math problems, feel the warmth of the sun, and play your favorite sports. Every big structure in our body is made of tiny, living building blocks or 'units'. Just like a single brick is the fundamental building unit of a massive brick wall, the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system is a highly specialized cell called a 'neuron' (or nerve cell).

Neurons are arguably the most amazing cells in the human body. They are shaped a bit like ancient trees with long roots and branching canopies. They are uniquely designed to receive, process, and transmit electrical and chemical signals across vast distances in your body, almost instantly. A single neuron in your leg can be over a meter long! When millions of these neurons link up, they form your brain, your spinal cord, and all your nerves. Let's look at the other options to see why they belong to completely different systems in your body: A 'nephron' is the tiny filtering unit of the kidney, which belongs to the urinary system and cleans your blood. An 'alveolus' is the microscopic, balloon-like air sac in the lungs where oxygen enters your blood, part of the respiratory system. A 'sarcomere' is the basic contracting unit of a muscle fiber, part of the muscular system. So, the undisputed star player and fundamental unit of the nervous tissue is definitely the neuron!

questions.Question: 59. The Nissl's granules of nerves cell are made up of
questions.Hint: Nerve cells work hard and need to manufacture lots of proteins to create chemical messengers. Which cell organelles act as the cell's 'protein factory'?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's imagine the main body of a neuron (called the cell body, or soma) as a highly bustling, heavily industrialized factory. In order for a neuron to do its job and communicate with other cells, it constantly needs to manufacture special proteins. These proteins are used to build the neuron's structure, repair damage, and most importantly, create the chemical messengers known as neurotransmitters that are fired across synapses.

If you take a neuron, stain it with special dyes, and look at it under a powerful microscope, you'll see tiny, dark, grainy structures scattered all throughout its main body and branching dendrites. Scientists named these 'Nissl's granules' (or Nissl bodies) after Franz Nissl, the brilliant scientist who first discovered them. But what are they actually made of, and what are they doing? Well, in cell biology, they are essentially massive clumps of Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER) studded with thousands of ribosomes! In our factory analogy, ribosomes are the actual 'protein manufacturing machines,' and the Rough ER is the intricate assembly line where these proteins get folded, modified, and properly sorted. Because neurons work incredibly hard and constantly fire signals, they need an enormous supply of proteins, which is why they are packed full of these Nissl granules. Let's look at the alternatives: Mitochondria are the powerhouses making ATP energy, Golgi bodies act like the post office packaging the proteins, and lysosomes are the cellular trash disposals breaking down waste. But the grainy Nissl bodies themselves are specifically clumps of Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum and Ribosomes, acting as the heavy-duty protein manufacturing centers of the nerve cell.

questions.Question: 60. In the chemistry of vision in mammals, the photosensitive substance is called
questions.Hint: This chemical is found inside the 'rod' cells of your retina. It relies heavily on Vitamin A to function properly and helps you see in the dark.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered how our eyes actually manage to 'see' light and translate it into a picture in our brain? It all comes down to an incredibly fast and magical chemical reaction! Inside the retina—which is the biological movie screen lining the back wall of your eye—there are special light-detecting cells called rods and cones. Cones help us see sharp details and bright colors during the day. Rods, on the other hand, are the cells that help us see shapes and movement in dim light or at night.

Inside these rod cells is a remarkable purplish-red protein pigment called 'rhodopsin' (sometimes referred to as visual purple). Think of rhodopsin as a highly sensitive piece of photographic camera film. When even a single particle of light (a photon) enters your eye and hits the rhodopsin molecule, the molecule physically absorbs the energy and literally changes its shape in a fraction of a millisecond! This sudden shape-change acts like flipping a molecular light switch. It triggers a chain reaction that fires an electrical signal down your optic nerve and straight into your brain, which your brain instantly translates into the image of the world around you.

Interestingly, rhodopsin is made from two parts: a protein called 'opsin' and a light-absorbing molecule called 'retinal,' which is derived directly from Vitamin A. This is the exact scientific reason why people say eating carrots (which are rich in Vitamin A) is good for your night vision! Without Vitamin A, your body can't make rhodopsin, leading to night blindness. As for the other options: Melanin is the pigment that gives our skin and hair its color, keratin is the tough protein that makes up our hair and nails, and hemoglobin is the iron-rich protein that carries oxygen in our red blood cells. Therefore, rhodopsin is the ultimate photosensitive (light-sensitive) superstar of mammalian vision.

questions.Question: 61. The vagus nerve is the cranial nerve numbering
questions.Hint: Think of the Roman numeral 'X'. This incredible nerve 'wanders' all the way from your brain down into your chest and belly!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Did you know that not all of your nerves have to travel down your spinal cord to reach your body? Your brain actually has 12 special pairs of 'VIP' nerve cables that exit directly out of the brainstem, bypassing the spinal cord entirely. These are called the Cranial Nerves, and doctors and scientists number them using Roman numerals from I to XII (1 to 12).

Most of these cranial nerves stay strictly within the head and neck area. For example, they control your eye movements, let you taste your food, help you hear music, and allow you to smile. But there is one rebellious, incredibly important nerve that wanders far out of the head and goes all the way down into your chest and belly, reaching vital organs like the heart, lungs, stomach, and intestines. Because it wanders so incredibly far, early anatomists named it the 'Vagus' nerve. The word 'vagus' comes directly from the Latin word for 'wanderer' or 'straying' (it is the exact same root word that gives us the English word 'vagabond'!).

The Vagus nerve is designated as Cranial Nerve number X (the Roman numeral for 10). It is the absolute superstar of your parasympathetic nervous system, which is the 'rest and digest' mode of your body. When you are relaxed, the Vagus nerve is the telephone line that tells your heart rate to slow down, tells your lungs to breathe at a steady pace, and commands your stomach and intestines to churn and digest your food. Looking at the other options: The 5th (V) is the Trigeminal nerve (feeling in your face), the 7th (VII) is the Facial nerve (making expressions), and the 12th (XII) is the Hypoglossal nerve (moving your tongue). So, the famous wandering Vagus is definitively Cranial Nerve X.

questions.Question: 62. By which nervous system and of what type, the blood is supplied into visceral organs?
questions.Hint: Think about the organs hidden inside your belly (the viscera). Do you have to consciously think to control their blood supply, or does your body do it 'automatically' in the background?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Your amazing body has two primary ways of controlling its various parts, and it divides the work perfectly. First, there is the 'Somatic' nervous system. This is your voluntary control system. When you consciously decide to raise your hand in class, kick a soccer ball, or chew a piece of gum, your brain sends signals through the somatic nervous system to your skeletal muscles.

However, what about the organs safely tucked inside your chest and belly? These internal organs—like your heart, stomach, intestines, liver, and blood vessels—are collectively called your 'visceral organs'. Imagine how exhausting it would be if you had to consciously think about controlling them! 'Okay, stomach, release some acid now to digest that pizza! Okay, liver blood vessels, dilate to let more blood through!' Thankfully, you don't have to think about this at all. Your body does this on complete autopilot.

The blood supply to these visceral organs is strictly controlled by the 'Autonomic Nervous System' (ANS). The word autonomic sounds a lot like 'automatic,' which is the perfect way to remember it! The ANS runs entirely in the background without your conscious effort. It is further divided into two opposing teams. The Sympathetic nervous system is your 'fight or flight' response; if you get scared, it instantly squeezes the blood vessels to your stomach and redirects the blood to your leg muscles so you can run. The Parasympathetic nervous system is your 'rest and digest' response; when you are safe on the couch, it opens up the blood vessels to your visceral organs so they get plenty of blood to absorb nutrients and heal. Therefore, the automatic, non-conscious control of blood to your internal organs is the masterpiece of the Autonomic Nervous System.

questions.Question: 63. Ivan Pavlov performed experiments on
questions.Hint: Think about a very famous furry pet that naturally drools when it sees or smells a tasty bone.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
In the world of biology and psychology, Ivan Pavlov is one of the most famous scientists in history. He was a brilliant Russian physiologist who was originally studying the digestive system. During his studies, he discovered something profoundly amazing about how the brain learns, leading to a concept now known worldwide as 'classical conditioning'.

Pavlov noticed a very simple, biological reflex: when a dog sees or smells delicious meat, it automatically starts to salivate (drool). The dog doesn't have to learn how to do this; it is an automatic, unlearned reflex built into the dog's nervous system to prepare its mouth for eating. Being a curious scientist, Pavlov decided to run a clever experiment. Every single time he was about to give his laboratory dogs their food, he would loudly ring a bell.

At the very beginning, the sound of the bell meant absolutely nothing to the dogs. It was just a random noise. But after repeating this exact sequence many times—Ring the bell, give the food, the dog drools—the dog's brain did something incredible. It built a powerful, brand-new neural pathway connecting the sound of the bell to the arrival of food. Eventually, Pavlov could just ring the bell without giving the dogs any food at all, and the dogs would start drooling heavily anyway! The dogs had 'learned' to perfectly associate the sound with dinner. This kind of learned, automatic biological response is called a 'conditioned reflex'. Thanks to this groundbreaking discovery, Pavlov won the Nobel Prize, and his famous experiments on dogs changed the way we understand animal behavior and the nervous system forever. (For context on the distractors: Rats were made famous by B.F. Skinner in operant conditioning, pea plants by the father of genetics Gregor Mendel, and fruit flies by Thomas Hunt Morgan).

questions.Question: 64. Light rays entering the eye is controlled by
questions.Hint: Think about the beautiful, colored part of your eye. It acts just like a camera aperture to shrink or widen the black hole in the center based on how bright the room is!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Have you ever stood in front of a mirror, turned off the lights for a few seconds, and then quickly turned them back on? If you look closely at your eyes when you do this, you will see the little black circle in the middle of your eye shrink incredibly fast! 

Think of your eye like a very fancy biological camera. For a camera to take a perfect picture, it needs exactly the right amount of light. Too much light, and the picture is completely white. Too little light, and the picture is pitch black. A camera has a mechanical opening called an aperture that can get wider or narrower to control light.

In your eye, the little black hole in the center$\u2014$the **pupil**$\u2014$acts exactly like that camera aperture! But here is the trick: the pupil cannot change its own size because it is not an actual object; it is literally just an empty hole that lets light into the eye. The real hero here is the colored part of your eye called the **iris**.

The iris is actually a ring of tiny, super-smooth muscles. When you step out into bright sunlight, the iris muscles flex and close inward, making the pupil very small. This blocks extra light and protects the highly sensitive inside of your eye from getting overwhelmed. When you go into a dark room, the iris muscles pull back, making the pupil huge so it can capture every tiny bit of light available, helping you see in the dark.

So, while the light passes *through* the pupil, the amount of light entering the eye is actively **controlled by the iris**! It acts as the ultimate gatekeeper for your vision.

questions.Question: 65. Retina is most sensitive at
questions.Hint: Think about the specific spot on the back of your eye that gives you the sharpest, highest-definition vision when you look directly at something like a book or a TV screen.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever noticed that when you really want to see something clearly$\u2014$like reading the fine print on a video game manual or threading a tiny needle$\u2014$you have to look directly at it? You cannot read tiny words if they are just in the corner of your vision. Why is that? It is all because of a tiny, superhero-level spot on the back of your eye called the **fovea centralis**!

To truly understand this, let us look at how the eye works. The inside back wall of your eye is covered in a wallpaper-like layer called the **retina**. The retina is packed with millions of special light-detecting cells called photoreceptors. There are two main types: **rods** (which help us see in dim light but only in black and white, mostly used for peripheral vision) and **cones** (which are amazing at seeing brilliant colors and sharp details, but they need bright light to work).

Now, your body did not just spread these cones out evenly. Instead, it packed a massive number of cone cells into one tiny, microscopic pit right in the very center of your retina. This densely packed VIP area is the **fovea centralis** (located within a yellowish area called the macula lutea). 

Because it has so many cones tightly crammed together with no blood vessels in the way to block the light, it provides the sharpest, most detailed, highest-resolution vision in your entire body! When you focus directly on a face or a word, your eye muscles shift your eyeball so that the incoming light hits the fovea centralis perfectly. Therefore, while the rest of the retina is great for noticing movement in the dark, the fovea centralis is where your retina is absolute most sensitive to sharp details and visual clarity.

questions.Question: Cardiac activities of the heart are regulated by: A. Nodal tissue B. A special neural centre in the medulla oblongata C. Adrenal medullary hormones D. Adrenal cortical hormones
MCQ_Options: Nodal tissue, Medulla oblongata, and Adrenal medullary hormones
Only Nodal tissue and Medulla oblongata
Only Adrenal cortical hormones and Nodal tissue
Medulla oblongata and Adrenal cortical hormones
questions.Hint: Think about the heart's natural pacemaker, the brain's control center for involuntary actions, and the 'fight or flight' emergency hormones.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand how our heart beats, let us imagine the heart as a high-tech sports car. 

First, we have the 'Nodal tissue' (like the SA node). This is the car's built-in engine computer. The human heart is 'myogenic', meaning it creates its own electrical impulses to beat. Even if you took the heart entirely out of the body and put it in a special fluid, it would keep beating for a while! The nodal tissue sets this default rhythm, acting as the ultimate auto-pilot.

But what if you start running? Your body needs the heart to beat faster. This is where the 'Medulla oblongata' comes in. This is a primitive part of your brainstem that acts as the gas and brake pedals. It has a special neural center connected to the heart via the autonomic nervous system. The sympathetic nerves act as the gas pedal (speeding up the heart), and the parasympathetic nerves (like the vagus nerve) act as the brake pedal (slowing it down to a resting state).

Finally, what if a tiger suddenly jumps out at you? You need an instant, massive surge of power. This is where the 'Adrenal medullary hormones' (adrenaline/epinephrine) step in. The adrenal medulla (the inner part of the adrenal glands sitting on your kidneys) dumps adrenaline straight into your bloodstream. This acts like a nitrous oxide (nitro) boost in a racing game, supercharging the heart to beat incredibly fast and hard so you can run away.

Option D, the adrenal cortical hormones (like cortisol or aldosterone), are involved in long-term stress, salt balance, and metabolism, but they do not directly regulate the second-to-second beating activity of the heart. Therefore, the heart is regulated by A, B, and C!
questions.Answer: Nodal tissue, Medulla oblongata, and Adrenal medullary hormones

questions.Question: Why can't insulin be given orally to diabetic patients?
MCQ_Options: Because insulin is a protein and would be digested by stomach acids and enzymes before reaching the blood.
Because oral insulin directly damages the lining of the stomach and intestines.
Because the liver will immediately store it as glycogen before it acts.
Because oral insulin causes an immediate and fatal drop in blood sugar levels.
questions.Hint: Think about what insulin is made of (amino acids) and what your stomach does to foods like meat and eggs.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered why people with diabetes have to use needles or insulin pumps instead of just swallowing an insulin pill? It all comes down to the microscopic structure of the insulin molecule and how our digestive system works.

Hormones come in different chemical 'flavors.' Some, like testosterone or estrogen, are steroids (made from cholesterol). Because they are made of fats, they can easily survive the stomach and absorb into the bloodstream. But insulin is entirely different. Insulin is a 'peptide hormone.' This means it is essentially a tiny protein made up of a specific chain of amino acids, folded into a very specific 3D shape.

Now, imagine eating a piece of chicken. Chicken is packed with protein. When it hits your stomach, a highly acidic fluid (Hydrochloric acid) unfolds the protein, and powerful digestive enzymes (like pepsin) act like tiny biological scissors, chopping the protein chain into individual amino acids so your body can absorb them. 

If you were to swallow an insulin pill, your digestive system would not recognize it as a life-saving medicine. It would simply look at it and say, 'Yum, protein!' The stomach acid and enzymes would completely shred the insulin molecule into tiny, useless pieces long before it ever had the chance to reach your bloodstream and lower your blood sugar. Its 3D shape, which is required to act like a 'key' to open the doors of your cells to let sugar in, would be completely destroyed.

To bypass this destructive digestive process, insulin must be injected directly into the fat layer under the skin, where it can be safely and slowly absorbed into the blood intact.
questions.Answer: Because insulin is a protein and would be digested by stomach acids and enzymes before reaching the blood.

questions.Question:
Match List-I with List-II. 
List-I 
A. Heart 
B. Kidney 
C. Gastro-intestinal tract 
D. Adrenal Cortex 
List-II 
I. Erythropoietin 
II. Aldosterone 
III. Atrial natriuretic factor 
IV. Secretin
questions.Hint: The heart releases a factor to lower blood pressure, the kidneys make a hormone to boost red blood cells, the gut manages digestion, and the adrenal cortex deals with salt.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
While we usually think of glands like the thyroid or pituitary when we hear the word 'hormones,' many other organs in your body have a secret double-life! They act as part-time hormone factories to keep your body balanced.

Let us match them up one by one:

A. Heart -> III. Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF)
Imagine your blood pressure gets too high. The upper chambers of your heart (the atria) physically stretch out like an overfilled water balloon. In response, the heart wall releases ANF. 'Natriuretic' means 'peeing out sodium.' This hormone travels to the kidneys and tells them to flush salt and water out of your body, which lowers your blood volume and brings your blood pressure back down to a safe level.

B. Kidney -> I. Erythropoietin (EPO)
Your kidneys filter blood, meaning they constantly monitor how much oxygen is floating around. If oxygen levels drop (like if you travel to a high mountain), the kidney releases EPO. EPO travels straight to your bone marrow and commands it to manufacture millions of new Red Blood Cells (erythrocytes) to carry more oxygen.

C. Gastro-intestinal tract -> IV. Secretin
When acidic food leaves your stomach and enters your intestines, your gut panics—it does not want an acid burn! So, the intestinal walls release a hormone called Secretin. Secretin runs over to the pancreas and tells it to release bicarbonate (which is like baking soda) to neutralize the dangerous acid instantly.

D. Adrenal Cortex -> II. Aldosterone
The adrenal cortex (the outer shell of the adrenal gland) makes Aldosterone. This is the body's ultimate 'salt-saver.' If your blood pressure drops or you are losing sodium, aldosterone tells your kidneys, 'Stop peeing out salt! Absorb it back into the blood!' Water naturally follows salt, so this boosts your blood volume.

Matching these gives us the perfect combination: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

questions.Question: Which of the following hormones released from the pituitary is actually synthesized in the hypothalamus?
questions.Hint: Look for the hormone that is stored in the POSTERIOR pituitary gland. The posterior pituitary is just a storage warehouse, not a manufacturing plant.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this, we need to look at the brain's ultimate management structure. The Pituitary Gland is famous—it is often called the 'Master Gland' because it controls almost all the other glands in your body. But the Pituitary actually has a boss sitting right above it: the Hypothalamus!

The Pituitary gland is divided into two main parts: the Anterior (front) lobe and the Posterior (back) lobe. 

The Anterior pituitary is an actual factory. It makes its own hormones from scratch. Hormones like Prolactin (for milk production), Growth Hormone (for making you taller and stronger), and Luteinizing Hormone (for regulating reproduction) are all genuinely manufactured right there in the anterior pituitary cells.

But the Posterior pituitary is basically a cheater! It does not manufacture any hormones at all. Instead, it acts as a storage warehouse. The boss, the Hypothalamus, actually manufactures two very important hormones: Oxytocin and Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH/Vasopressin). 

Once the Hypothalamus synthesizes these hormones, it sends them traveling down incredibly long nerve fibers (axons) directly into the posterior pituitary gland. The posterior pituitary simply holds onto them in little storage vesicles. When the body needs them—for example, when oxytocin is needed to cause uterine contractions during childbirth or to help a mother release breast milk—the posterior pituitary finally releases them into the blood. 

So, even though Oxytocin is 'released' by the pituitary, it was 'synthesized' (born and created) in the Hypothalamus!

questions.Question:
Consider the following statements regarding function of adrenal medullary hormones: 
(A) It causes pupilary constriction. 
(B) It is a hyperglycemic hormone. 
(C) It causes piloerection. 
(D) It increases strength of heart contraction.
MCQ_Options: Statements B, C, and D are correct
Statements A, B, and C are correct
Only statements A and D are correct
Statements A, B, C, and D are correct
questions.Hint: Adrenal medullary hormones are adrenaline and noradrenaline. Think about what your body physically does when a scary dog chases you. Do your pupils get smaller or bigger to let in light?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
The hormones of the adrenal medulla are Epinephrine (adrenaline) and Norepinephrine (noradrenaline). We call these the 'Fight or Flight' hormones. They are dumped into your blood during extreme stress, fear, or emergencies. 

To figure out what they do, just imagine you are walking through a dark forest and suddenly, a massive bear steps onto the path. What does your body need to survive?

First, you need energy to sprint away or fight. Your body instantly breaks down glycogen (stored sugar) in your liver and dumps glucose into your blood. This massive sugar spike fuels your muscles. Because it raises blood sugar, it is a 'hyperglycemic' hormone. (Statement B is Correct).

Second, you might notice your hair standing on end, giving you goosebumps. This is called 'piloerection.' In animals with fur, this makes them look much larger and more intimidating to predators. In humans, we just get goosebumps, but the mechanism is exactly the same! (Statement C is Correct).

Third, to deliver that sugar and oxygen to your running muscles, your heart needs to pump furiously. Adrenaline severely increases both the speed (heart rate) and the sheer squeezing strength of your heart contractions. (Statement D is Correct).

Now, what about your eyes? If you are facing a threat, especially in the dark, you need to see as much of your surroundings as possible. To let more light in, the black part of your eyes (the pupils) gets much BIGGER. This is called pupillary 'dilation.' Statement A says it causes 'constriction' (getting smaller), which is exactly the opposite of what you want in an emergency! When you are relaxed and reading a book, your pupils constrict; when you are terrified, they dilate.

Therefore, Statement A is totally wrong, making B, C, and D the only correct statements.
questions.Answer: Statements B, C, and D are correct

questions.Concept: Endocrine Glands and their Specific Hormones
questions.Question:
Match List-I with List-II 
List-I 
A. Progesterone 
B. Relaxin 
C. Melanocyte stimulating hormone 
D. Catecholamines 
List-II 
I. Pars intermedia 
II. Ovary 
III. Adrenal Medulla 
IV. Corpus luteum
questions.Hint: Progesterone supports pregnancy (made by the yellow body left after ovulation). Relaxin helps birth (made by female gonads). Melanin relates to skin. Catecholamines are stress hormones.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let us take a grand tour of the body's chemical factories and match the hormone to its source!

A. Progesterone -> IV. Corpus luteum
Every month during a female's menstrual cycle, an egg is released from a tiny sac in the ovary called a follicle. Once the egg pops out, the leftover broken sac doesn't just die; it transforms into a temporary yellow gland called the 'Corpus luteum' (which literally means 'yellow body' in Latin). This gland's entire job is to pump out Progesterone, a hormone that builds up the thick, cozy lining of the uterus, preparing it just in case a baby needs to grow there.

B. Relaxin -> II. Ovary
If a woman does get pregnant and it is time to deliver the baby, the baby has to pass through the pelvic bones. The Ovary (and later the placenta) releases a hormone brilliantly named 'Relaxin.' True to its name, it relaxes the tough ligaments holding the pelvic bones together, allowing the hips to widen slightly so the baby can be born safely.

C. Melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH) -> I. Pars intermedia
Your pituitary gland has a tiny middle section called the Pars intermedia. It releases MSH, which travels to your skin and tells special cells called melanocytes to produce more melanin (dark pigment). This plays a role in skin darkening and protecting against UV radiation.

D. Catecholamines -> III. Adrenal Medulla
'Catecholamines' is just the fancy scientific family name for Adrenaline and Noradrenaline. As we learned earlier, these are the ultimate emergency alarms. They are synthesized in the core, or 'medulla', of the adrenal glands, which sit right on top of your kidneys like little party hats.

Putting it all together, the perfect match is A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III.

questions.Question:
Match List-I with List-II. 
List-I 
A. Epinephrine 
B. Thyroxine 
C. Oxytocin 
D. Glucagon 
List-II 
I. Hyperglycemia 
II. Smooth muscle contraction 
III. Basal metabolic rate 
IV. Emergency hormone
questions.Hint: Epinephrine is for panic. Thyroxine is your body's temperature and energy thermostat. Oxytocin squeezes muscles during birth. Glucagon stops you from passing out when you haven't eaten.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's match these fascinating biological messengers to their ultimate jobs in the body.

A. Epinephrine -> IV. Emergency hormone
Epinephrine is the exact same thing as Adrenaline. If a fire alarm goes off in your school, adrenaline is the chemical fire alarm going off in your blood! It prepares your body to fight for your life or run like the wind. Hence, it is correctly crowned the 'Emergency hormone.'

B. Thyroxine -> III. Basal metabolic rate (BMR)
Your thyroid gland (in your neck) produces Thyroxine. Think of Thyroxine as the master thermostat of your body. It dictates your Basal Metabolic Rate—which basically means how fast your cells burn fuel to create energy and heat while you are resting. If you have too much thyroxine, you feel hot, jittery, and lose weight. If you have too little, you feel freezing, sluggish, and gain weight.

C. Oxytocin -> II. Smooth muscle contraction
There are two types of muscles: skeletal (the ones you control, like your biceps) and smooth (the ones that move automatically, like your stomach or uterus). Oxytocin is a master at making smooth muscles squeeze. Its most famous job is causing the smooth muscles of the uterus to powerfully contract during childbirth to push the baby out, and squeezing the smooth muscles in the breasts to eject milk for the baby to drink.

D. Glucagon -> I. Hyperglycemia
Glucagon is the arch-nemesis of Insulin. Insulin lowers blood sugar, but what happens if you skip breakfast and lunch? Your blood sugar drops dangerously low. Your pancreas releases Glucagon, which acts like a key opening an emergency pantry in your liver. It forces the liver to dump stored sugar (glycogen) back into the blood, causing your blood sugar to rise back up. High blood sugar is scientifically called 'Hyperglycemia' (Hyper = high, glyc = sugar, emia = in blood).

Therefore, the proper linkage is A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

questions.Concept: Hormones of Heart, Kidney and Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.Question:
Identify the wrong statements : 
A. Erythropoietin is produced by juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney 
B. Leydig cells produce Androgens 
C. Atrial Natriuretic factor, a peptide hormone is secreted by the seminiferous tubules of the testes 
D. Cholecystokinin is produced by gastrointestinal tract 
E. Gastrin acts on intestinal wall and helps in the production of pepsinogen
questions.Hint: Look closely at the names! Does 'Atrial' sound like it belongs in the testes? And does 'Gastrin' act on the intestines or somewhere else?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's imagine your body as a massive, high-tech factory. Hormones are the urgent text messages sent between different departments to keep everything running smoothly. Most of these messages come from dedicated 'post offices' called endocrine glands, but some come from other organs that just happen to have a side hustle in messaging! Let's decode the statements one by one to see which ones are lying to us.

Statement A: Erythropoietin (EPO) is produced by the kidney. This is TRUE! When your kidneys sense low oxygen, they send out EPO, a hormone that yells at your bone marrow to 'Make more red blood cells!' 

Statement B: Leydig cells produce Androgens. TRUE! In the testes, Leydig cells are the VIP workers responsible for making testosterone (an androgen), which causes male characteristics.

Statement C: Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF) is secreted by the testes. FALSE! The biggest clue is in the name. 'Atrial' refers to the atria, the top chambers of your HEART! When your blood pressure gets dangerously high, the walls of your heart stretch and release ANF. ANF travels to the kidneys and tells them to release sodium into your urine (Natriuretic means sodium in urine). Water follows the sodium, which lowers your blood volume and drops your blood pressure back to normal.

Statement D: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is produced by the gastrointestinal tract. TRUE! CCK is released by your small intestine when you eat fatty food, telling your pancreas and gallbladder to release digestive juices.

Statement E: Gastrin acts on the intestinal wall to produce pepsinogen. FALSE! The prefix 'Gastro-' always means STOMACH, not intestine! Gastrin is released by your stomach and acts ON your stomach to make it pump out highly acidic gastric juices, including hydrochloric acid and pepsinogen (which helps digest proteins).

Since C and E are completely biologically incorrect, they are our wrong statements!

questions.Question: Which of the following is not a steroid hormone?
questions.Hint: Steroid hormones are made from fats (cholesterol), allowing them to pass easily through cell membranes. The incorrect option is a hormone made of proteins, regulating your blood sugar.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this, you need to know what hormones are actually made of. Think of hormones like different types of delivery packages. Some packages are made of waterproof plastic, and some are made of cardboard. In the body, we have two main chemical types of hormones: Steroid hormones (made of lipids/fats) and Peptide hormones (made of amino acids/proteins).

Steroid hormones are literally created out of cholesterol. Because your cell membranes are also made of fats, steroid hormones are like ghosts—they can walk straight through the cell membrane walls without knocking! The major steroid hormones in your body usually come from the adrenal cortex (like Cortisol, your stress hormone, and Aldosterone) and your gonads (like Testosterone in males and Estrogen/Progesterone in females). So, Testosterone, Cortisol, and Estrogen are all classic, fat-based steroid hormones.

But what about Insulin? Insulin is a protein hormone, specifically a 'peptide'. It is made of 51 amino acids strung together like beads on a necklace. Because it is a protein and water-soluble, it cannot phase through the fat-based walls of your cells. Instead, Insulin has to 'ring the doorbell' by binding to a receptor on the outside of the cell surface to tell the cell to absorb sugar from the blood. 

So, if you remember that sex hormones and stress hormones are steroids, it becomes super easy to spot the odd one out: Insulin is a peptide, not a steroid!

questions.Concept: Hormonal Control of the Reproductive System
questions.Question:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R :
Assertion A : FSH acts upon ovarian follicles in female and Leydig cells in male.
Reason R : Growing ovarian follicles secrete estrogen in female while interstitial cells secrete androgen in male human being.
MCQ_Options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.Hint: Think about the acronyms. LH controls Leydig cells (L matches L). FSH acts on Sertoli cells in males, not Leydig cells!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's look at how the brain controls the reproductive system! The master gland in the brain (the pituitary) releases two major text-message hormones to control reproduction: LH (Luteinizing Hormone) and FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone).

Let's test Assertion A: Does FSH act on ovarian follicles in females and Leydig cells in males? In females, FSH absolutely acts on the ovarian follicles (the hint is in the name: Follicle Stimulating Hormone!). It tells the baby eggs to grow. But in males, this is a trap! In males, we have two main types of cells in the testes: Leydig cells and Sertoli cells. Here is an awesome memory trick: LH stimulates Leydig cells (L goes with L!). FSH stimulates Sertoli cells (Sertoli has an 'S', FSH has an 'S'). Sertoli cells are 'nurse' cells that help sperm grow. Because Assertion A says FSH acts on Leydig cells, Assertion A is completely FALSE.

Now let's check Reason R: Do growing ovarian follicles secrete estrogen, and do interstitial (Leydig) cells secrete androgen? Yes! As the female ovarian follicle grows like a balloon, its walls produce estrogen, the hormone that makes female traits. In males, the interstitial cells (which is just the scientific name for Leydig cells, because they sit in the 'interstitial' spaces between sperm tubes) produce androgens, mainly testosterone. So, Reason R is an absolute biological FACT.

Therefore, our final verdict is that the Assertion is a lie, but the Reason is the truth!
questions.Answer: A is false but R is true

questions.Question:
Match List I with List II :
List-I 
A. Exophthalmic goiter 
B. Acromegaly 
C. Cushing’s syndrome 
D. Cretinism 

List-II 
I. Excess secretion of cortisol, moon face & hypergylcemia. 
II. Hypo-secretion of thyroid hormone and stunted growth. 
III. Hyper secretion of thyroid hormone & protruding eye balls. 
IV. Excessive secretion of growth hormone.
questions.Hint: Look at 'Exophthalmic'—'Exo' means out, and 'ophthalmic' means eye. Which option mentions protruding eyeballs?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hormones are powerful chemicals; having too much or too little can cause extreme changes in the human body. Let's act like doctors diagnosing four different patients!

Patient A has 'Exophthalmic goiter' (also known as Graves' disease). Let's break down the word: 'Exo' means outside, and 'ophthalmic' refers to the eyes. This happens when the thyroid gland goes into hyper-drive (Hyperthyroidism). The body's metabolism engine revs way too fast, and fat builds up behind the eyes, making them bulge out. So, A matches with III (Hyper secretion of thyroid hormone & protruding eyeballs).

Patient B has 'Acromegaly'. If a grown adult suddenly starts producing way too much Growth Hormone (GH) from their pituitary gland, they don't get taller because their long bones are sealed. Instead, their face, hands, and feet grow super thick and large. This is Acromegaly. So, B matches with IV (Excessive secretion of growth hormone).

Patient C has 'Cushing’s syndrome'. Imagine someone under extreme, constant stress. Their body pumps out massive amounts of the stress hormone 'Cortisol'. Too much cortisol redistributes body fat to the face (causing a round 'moon face') and back of the neck, and causes high blood sugar (hyperglycemia). So, C matches with I.

Patient D has 'Cretinism'. If a baby is born and doesn't get enough thyroid hormone (Hypothyroidism), their physical growth and mental development become severely stunted. The thyroid is crucial for brain and bone growth in infants! So, D matches with II.

Putting it all together, the perfect match is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

questions.Concept: Hormones of Heart, Kidney and Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.Question:
Match List I with List II.
List-I 
A. CCK 
B. GIP 
C. ANF 
D. ADH 

List-II 
I. Kidney 
II. Heart 
III. Gastric gland 
IV. Pancreas
questions.Hint: ANF stands for Atrial Natriuretic Factor (Atria = upper chambers of the Heart). ADH is Anti-Diuretic Hormone, which prevents you from losing too much water in your urine.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's connect these hormonal text messages (List I) to the body parts they talk to or come from (List II)!

A. CCK (Cholecystokinin): Imagine you just ate a massive, greasy slice of pizza. When that fat hits your small intestine, your intestine screams, 'I need help digesting this!' It releases CCK. CCK travels to your Pancreas and Gallbladder, telling them to pump out digestive enzymes and bile. So, CCK acts on the Pancreas (A matches IV).

B. GIP (Gastric Inhibitory Peptide): The name gives it away! 'Gastric' means stomach, and 'Inhibitory' means to slow down. When food leaves the stomach and enters the intestine, GIP is released to tell the Gastric glands in the stomach, 'Hey, the food has moved on, you can stop making stomach acid now!' (B matches III).

C. ANF (Atrial Natriuretic Factor): If your blood pressure gets dangerously high, the upper chambers of your heart (the Atria) get stretched out. They panic and release ANF. ANF is the Heart's way of lowering blood pressure by telling the kidneys to pee out more salt and water. So, ANF comes from the Heart! (C matches II).

D. ADH (Anti-Diuretic Hormone): A 'diuretic' makes you pee. So an 'Anti-diuretic' STOPS you from peeing! When you are dehydrated on a hot summer day, your brain releases ADH. It travels down to your Kidneys and says, 'Save water! Don't let it escape into the urine!' Your kidneys obey, making your urine super concentrated and yellow. (D matches I).

The final perfect match is A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

questions.Question:
Which of the following are NOT under the control of thyroid hormone?
A. Maintenance of water and electrolyte balance 
B. Regulation of basal metabolic rate 
C. Normal rhythm of sleep-wake cycle 
D. Development of immune system 
E. Support the process of RBCs formation
questions.Hint: The sleep-wake cycle is controlled by the pineal gland (melatonin), and the immune system development is heavily controlled by the thymus (thymosin).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
The thyroid gland is a butterfly-shaped organ sitting right at the base of your neck. Think of it as the ultimate thermostat and engine controller for your entire body. Let's see what it does and doesn't do from our list!

Does it control Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)? Yes! (Statement B). BMR is how fast your body burns fuel (calories) just to stay alive. The thyroid hormone (Thyroxine) acts like the gas pedal for your cells. 
Does it support RBC formation? Yes! (Statement E). Making red blood cells requires energy and metabolism, which the thyroid stimulates.
Does it maintain water and electrolyte balance? Yes! (Statement A). Since the thyroid regulates cell activity everywhere, it subtly influences how much water and salt your cells and kidneys process.

Now, what about C and D? 
Statement C mentions the 'sleep-wake cycle' (your circadian rhythm). Your thyroid has nothing to do with your bedtime! That is the job of the Pineal Gland, a tiny pea-sized structure deep in your brain that releases Melatonin when it gets dark to make you sleepy.
Statement D mentions the 'development of the immune system'. While general metabolism helps, the specific training of your immune system (like T-cells) is done by a completely different gland called the Thymus, which sits near your heart and releases Thymosin.

Because C and D are controlled by the Pineal and Thymus glands respectively, they are NOT under the control of the thyroid gland!

questions.Question: Select incorrect statement, regarding chemical structure of insulin.
MCQ_Options: Mature insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains: chain A and chain B.
Chain A and chain B are linked together by disulfide bridges.
Proinsulin contains an extra stretch of amino acids called the C-peptide.
The C-peptide is retained in the mature, fully active insulin molecule.
questions.Hint: Think of insulin like a brand new pair of sneakers with a bulky security tag attached. The tag (C-peptide) must be removed before you can actually use them!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Insulin is an incredibly important hormone made by the pancreas that lowers your blood sugar. But the pancreas doesn't make insulin in its final, active form right away. It makes a larger, inactive precursor called 'Pro-insulin'.

Let's imagine Pro-insulin is a long string of beads (amino acids) that has three sections: Chain A, Chain B, and Chain C (the C-peptide). Because the body is very careful, it keeps this hormone inactive while it's being stored. 

When your blood sugar spikes and it's time for Insulin to go to work and be a superhero, it needs to get ready. The 'C-peptide' acts like an annoying extra piece of packaging or a safety pin. Enzymes in the pancreas come along and snip off the C-peptide! 

Once the C-peptide is thrown away, we are left with only Chain A and Chain B. But how do these two separate chains stay together? They are locked in place by special chemical handshakes called 'disulfide bridges' (strong bonds between sulfur atoms). This A+B combo is the final, fully mature, and active Insulin molecule that goes into your blood.

Looking at our options, the statement claiming that 'The C-peptide is retained in the mature, fully active insulin molecule' is totally incorrect! The whole point of becoming mature insulin is to cut the C-peptide off and throw it away.
questions.Answer: The C-peptide is retained in the mature, fully active insulin molecule.

questions.Question:
15. Which of the following statements are correct with respect to the hormone and its function?
(A) Thyrocalcitonin (TCT) regulates the blood calcium level.
(B) In males, FSH and androgens regulate spermatogenesis.
(C) Hyperthyroidism can lead to goitre.
(D) Glucocorticoids are secreted in Adrenal Medulla.
(E) Parathyroid hormone is regulated by circulating levels of sodium ions.
questions.Hint: Think about where Glucocorticoids actually come from (cortex vs medulla) and remember that Parathyroid hormone monitors calcium, not sodium!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's become medical detectives and break down each of these statements one by one to see which ones are telling the truth!

Statement (A) talks about Thyrocalcitonin (TCT). Your thyroid gland makes this hormone when you have too much calcium in your blood. It acts like a strict traffic cop, telling the calcium to get out of the blood and go into the bones. So, it definitely regulates blood calcium levels! This statement is TRUE.

Statement (B) mentions FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone) and androgens (like testosterone) in males. Imagine building a complex machine (a sperm cell). You need a project manager (FSH) to oversee the process and the raw energy/materials (testosterone) to get it built. Together, they regulate 'spermatogenesis' (the creation of sperm). This statement is TRUE.

Statement (C) says Hyperthyroidism can lead to goitre. A 'goitre' is an enlarged thyroid gland. While we usually associate simple goitres with a lack of iodine (Hypothyroidism), an overactive thyroid (Hyperthyroidism) can also cause the gland to swell up massively (known as Exophthalmic goitre or Graves' disease). So, this statement can be considered TRUE in biology, although in many standard exams, the most indisputable truths are A and B.

Statement (D) claims Glucocorticoids are secreted in the Adrenal Medulla. Think of your adrenal gland like a peanut M&M. The chocolate shell is the 'Cortex' and the peanut inside is the 'Medulla'. The Medulla makes your fight-or-flight hormones (adrenaline). The Cortex makes hormones for stress, salt, and sugar (glucocorticoids). So, D is FALSE because glucocorticoids come from the cortex, not the medulla!

Statement (E) says Parathyroid hormone is regulated by sodium ions. Nope! Parathyroid hormone is obsessed with Calcium, not Sodium. It is the arch-nemesis of TCT. When calcium is low, Parathyroid hormone brings it back up. So, E is FALSE.

Looking at our options, (A) and (B) are the most definitively correct textbook statements without any caveats, making '(A) and (B) only' the safest and most accurate choice in competitive exams.

questions.Question:
16. Match the following:
List-I
A. Palm bones
B. Wrist bones
C. Ankle bones
D. Digit bones

List-II
I. Phalanges
II. Metacarpals
III. Carpals
IV. Tarsals
questions.Hint: Remember this cool trick: You drive a 'CAR' with your 'CARpals' (wrists), and you step on 'TAR' with your 'TARsals' (ankles)!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Learning the bones of the hands and feet can sound like trying to learn an alien language, but it's actually super logical once you know the secret codes! Let's decode them together.

First, let's look at the Wrist bones (B). A great way to remember this is to think about driving a car. You steer a car using your wrists! The medical word for wrist bones is 'Carpals' (List II - III). So, B matches with III.

Next, the Ankle bones (C). When you walk on a road, your feet and ankles step on the black 'tar'. So, your ankle bones are called 'Tarsals' (List II - IV). So, C matches with IV.

Now, what about the bones that make up the flat part of your hand (the Palm bones - A) and the sole of your foot? In science, the prefix 'Meta-' often means 'beyond' or 'after'. The bones just beyond your wrist (carpals) that make up your palm are called the 'Metacarpals' (List II - II). So, A matches with II.

Finally, we have the Digit bones (D). Digits are just a fancy science word for your fingers and toes. The bones inside your fingers and toes are called 'Phalanges' (List II - I). Think of a 'phalanx', which was an ancient military formation of soldiers standing tightly together in lines, just like the bones in your fingers! So, D matches with I.

Putting it all perfectly together: A-II (Palm = Metacarpals), B-III (Wrist = Carpals), C-IV (Ankle = Tarsals), D-I (Digits = Phalanges).

questions.Question:
17. Given below are two statements:
Statement I:
Parathyroid hormone acts on bones and stimulates the process of bone resorption.
Statement II:
Parathyroid hormone along with Thyrocalcitonin plays a significant role in carbohydrate metabolism.
MCQ_Options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.Hint: Ask yourself: Does the Parathyroid gland care about the sugar (carbohydrates) you eat, or is it exclusively obsessed with keeping calcium levels balanced in your blood?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's imagine your body has a 'Calcium Bank' and a 'Blood Highway'. Your bones are the Calcium Bank, storing almost all the calcium in your body. 

Statement I talks about the Parathyroid Hormone (PTH). PTH is like a bank robber or a withdrawal slip. Whenever your blood highway is running low on calcium, the parathyroid glands release PTH. PTH goes straight to the bone bank and stimulates a process called 'bone resorption'. 'Resorption' is just a fancy medical word for breaking down bone tissue to release its stored calcium into the blood. So, Statement I is absolutely CORRECT!

Statement II claims that PTH and Thyrocalcitonin play a role in 'carbohydrate metabolism'. Carbohydrates are sugars and starches (like bread, pasta, and candy). The hormones that manage carbohydrates are Insulin and Glucagon (from the pancreas), not PTH! 

PTH and Thyrocalcitonin are completely, 100% focused on Calcium. They don't care about carbohydrates at all. Thyrocalcitonin acts as the opposite of PTH; it takes calcium from the blood and deposits it back into the bone bank (lowering blood calcium). Because they only manage calcium, Statement II is completely INCORRECT.

Therefore, Statement I is true, and Statement II is false. It's beautiful how the body delegates specific jobs to specific hormones so they don't get confused!
questions.Answer: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

questions.Question:
18. Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A):
FSH which interacts with membrane bound receptors does not enter the target cell.
Reason (R):
Binding of FSH to its receptors generates second messenger (cyclic AMP) for its biochemical and physiological responses.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer.
MCQ_Options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.Hint: Think of FSH as a pizza delivery driver. Since he can't go inside the house (Assertion), what must he do? He rings the doorbell, which causes someone inside the house (the second messenger) to go fetch the pizza money (Reason)!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this, let's picture your cells as heavily guarded castles. The wall of the castle is the cell membrane, which is made mostly of fats (lipids). 

Now, hormones come in two main types: fat-soluble (like steroid hormones) and water-soluble (like protein hormones). Fat-soluble hormones are like VIP guests; they can melt right through the fatty castle walls and walk straight inside the cell. But FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone) is a water-soluble protein hormone. Since oil and water do not mix, FSH absolutely cannot cross the fatty cell membrane. This makes Assertion (A) completely CORRECT—FSH does not enter the target cell!

So, if FSH can't go inside, how does it tell the cell what to do? 

It acts like a delivery driver! FSH stays outside the cell and binds to a 'membrane-bound receptor' on the surface—this is like ringing the castle's doorbell. When the doorbell rings, it triggers a chain reaction inside the castle without the delivery driver ever stepping foot inside. This chain reaction creates a 'second messenger' inside the cell, such as cyclic AMP (cAMP). This second messenger is like a butler inside the castle who hears the bell and runs around doing all the actual chores (the biochemical and physiological responses). This makes Reason (R) completely CORRECT as well.

Finally, does Reason (R) explain Assertion (A)? Yes! The whole reason the cell evolved to use a 'second messenger' system is precisely BECAUSE the hormone cannot enter the cell. Since FSH is blocked from entering, it is forced to rely on generating a second messenger to get the job done. Therefore, both statements are true, and R is the perfect, logical explanation for A.
questions.Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.Question:
19. Which of the following are not the effects of Parathyroid hormone?
(a) Stimulates the process of bone resorption
(b) Decreases Ca2+ level in blood
(c) Reabsorption of Ca2+ by renal tubules
(d) Decreases the absorption of Ca2+ from digested food
(e) Increases metabolism of carbohydrates
questions.Hint: Remember the golden rule of Parathyroid Hormone (PTH): It will do absolutely EVERYTHING in its power to INCREASE calcium levels in the blood. Which options describe the exact opposite or something totally unrelated?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's recall the sole purpose of the Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) in your body. PTH is the ultimate 'Calcium Raiser'. Whenever the calcium levels in your blood drop dangerously low, PTH is released to save the day and push those levels back UP.

Let's evaluate the given effects based on this golden rule:

(a) Stimulates the process of bone resorption: 'Resorption' means breaking down bone to release its stored calcium into the blood. This INCREASES blood calcium. So, this IS an effect of PTH.

(b) Decreases Ca2+ level in blood: Wait a minute! PTH wants to increase calcium, not decrease it. Lowering calcium is the job of its rival hormone, Calcitonin. So, this is NOT an effect of PTH.

(c) Reabsorption of Ca2+ by renal tubules: Your kidneys constantly filter blood to make urine. PTH yells at the kidneys, 'Don't pee out that calcium! We need it!' so the kidneys reabsorb calcium back into the blood. This IS an effect of PTH.

(d) Decreases the absorption of Ca2+ from digested food: When you drink milk, PTH actually works with Vitamin D to INCREASE the amount of calcium your intestines absorb from that milk. It would never decrease it! So, this is NOT an effect of PTH.

(e) Increases metabolism of carbohydrates: As we learned earlier, PTH only cares about calcium. It has absolutely zero interest in carbohydrates, sugars, or fats. So, this is NOT an effect of PTH.

To summarize, the statements that are NOT the effects of PTH are (b), (d), and (e). The body's hormone systems are incredibly specific, and knowing a hormone's 'main goal' (like PTH wanting more blood calcium) makes solving these puzzles super easy!

questions.Concept: Hormones of Heart, Kidney and Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.Question: 20. Erythropoietin hormone which stimulates R.B.C. formation is produced by:
questions.Hint: Think about the organ that filters your blood all day long to make urine. Because it constantly filters blood, it's the perfect 'sensor' to detect if your blood lacks oxygen!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered how your body knows when it needs to create more blood? It's a fascinating process! 

Your Red Blood Cells (R.B.C.s) are like little delivery trucks that carry Oxygen to every single cell in your body. If you suddenly move to a high-altitude mountain where the air is thin, or if you lose blood, your body needs to manufacture more R.B.C.s quickly to keep up with the oxygen demand.

But which organ acts as the 'oxygen sensor'? You might guess the heart or the lungs, but it's actually the Kidneys! Your kidneys filter about 20% of all the blood pumped by your heart every single minute to create urine. Because they see so much blood passing through them constantly, they are perfectly positioned to monitor oxygen levels.

Inside the kidneys, there is a special group of cells called the Juxtaglomerular cells (or JG cells). When these JG cells detect that oxygen levels in the blood are dropping, they panic a little bit and secrete a chemical messenger (a hormone) called Erythropoietin (EPO).

Let's break down the word: 'Erythro' means Red, and 'poiesis' means to make or create. So, Erythropoietin literally means 'Red Blood Cell Maker'! This hormone travels through the blood to your bone marrow (the spongy tissue inside your bones where blood is manufactured) and shouts, 'Work faster! We need more Red Blood Cells!'

(Fun fact: Some athletes cheat by illegally injecting synthetic Erythropoietin into their bodies to get more red blood cells, which gives their muscles more oxygen and unnatural endurance. This is a form of sports doping!)

Looking at the other options: The Alpha cells of the pancreas make glucagon for blood sugar. The Adrenal medulla makes adrenaline for 'fight or flight'. The Thyroid makes hormones for metabolism. Only the JG cells of the kidney produce this amazing blood-building hormone.

questions.Question: 22. Artificial light, extended work-time and reduced sleep-time disrupt the activity of –
questions.Hint: Think about the body's 'internal clock' and the hormone that makes you sleepy when it gets dark outside.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Have you ever wondered how your body just *knows* when it's time to go to sleep and when it's time to wake up? It's not magic; it's a tiny, pinecone-shaped structure deep inside your brain called the **Pineal Gland**. 

Think of the pineal gland as your body's personal night watchman. When the sun goes down and it gets dark, your eyes send a signal to your brain saying, 'Hey, the lights are out!' The pineal gland responds by producing a hormone called **Melatonin**. Melatonin is basically a chemical lullaby. It flows through your blood, telling all your organs to cool down, relax, and get ready for sleep. It regulates what we call our 'circadian rhythm' (our 24-hour internal biological clock).

But here is where modern life causes a glitch! In today's world, even after the sun sets, we turn on bright room lights, stare at our glowing computer screens, and scroll on our bright smartphones. This artificial light tricks the brain into thinking the sun is still up! Because the eyes are detecting light, the pineal gland gets confused and says, 'Wait, it's still daytime? I better hold off on releasing the melatonin.' 

Because the melatonin is suppressed, your body doesn't get the signal to feel sleepy. This is exactly why late-night texting, extended work hours, and bright room lights make it incredibly hard to fall asleep and mess up your entire sleep cycle. So, artificial light directly disrupts the activity of your pineal gland!

questions.Question: 23. Match the following hormones with the respective disease: Select the correct option.
questions.Hint: Which hormone acts like a 'traffic cop' for blood sugar, and which hormone needs iodine to prevent your neck from swelling?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine your body's endocrine system is a highly complex factory. The hormones are the factory workers, and each has a very specific, crucial job to do. If a worker decides to go on strike (under-secretion) or decides to work in hyper-drive and produce too much (over-secretion), the factory breaks down and causes a 'disease.' Let's look at a couple of the most famous hormone-disease pairings to understand how this works.

First, let's look at **Insulin**. Every time you eat a slice of pizza or an apple, your digestive system breaks the food down into glucose (sugar), which enters your bloodstream. But glucose can't just wander into your cells on its own; the cell doors are locked! Insulin, produced by the pancreas, is the 'key' that unlocks your cells so glucose can enter and be used for energy. If your pancreas doesn't make enough insulin, the glucose is trapped in the bloodstream. This dangerous buildup of sugar in the blood is called **Diabetes mellitus**.

Next, let's look at **Thyroxine**. This hormone is produced by your butterfly-shaped thyroid gland in your neck. Thyroxine is the 'engine pedal' of your body; it controls your metabolism. To make thyroxine, your thyroid gland absolutely needs Iodine (a mineral found in salt and seafood). If you don't eat enough iodine, the thyroid gland panics. It desperately tries to catch whatever tiny bits of iodine might be passing by in the blood, and in its struggle to work harder, the gland physically grows massive! This swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck is called a **Goiter**.

So, when matching hormones to their respective diseases, Insulin is paired with Diabetes mellitus, and Thyroxine is paired with Goiter. The entire system is about a delicate balance, and when that balance tips, our body gives us clear physical signs!

questions.Question: 24. How does steroid hormone influence the cellular activities?
MCQ_Options: By entering the cell, binding to an intracellular receptor, and altering gene expression (DNA)
By binding to the cell membrane and activating a secondary messenger like cyclic AMP
By physically destroying the cell membrane to let nutrients inside
By binding directly to ribosomes to stop protein synthesis
questions.Hint: Steroid hormones are made of lipids (fats). Because cell membranes are also made of lipids, steroids have 'VIP Access' to walk right through the door and head straight to the boss's office (the nucleus)!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand how hormones work, you need to understand that cells are like exclusive nightclubs. They have a strict 'bouncer' at the door—the cell membrane. This membrane is made of a lipid (fat) bilayer. It doesn't let just anything inside.

Most hormones are made of proteins, which are water-soluble. Since oil/fat and water don't mix, protein hormones get stopped by the bouncer. But **Steroid Hormones** (like testosterone, estrogen, and cortisol) are special. They are made of cholesterol, which is a lipid. Because the cell membrane is lipid, and the steroid hormone is lipid, they mix perfectly! The bouncer looks at the steroid hormone and says, 'Oh, you're one of us. VIP access! Go right on in.'

Once the steroid hormone strolls effortlessly through the cell membrane into the cytoplasm, it looks for its specific partner, called an **Intracellular Receptor**. They hug and form a 'Hormone-Receptor Complex.' Now, this powerful duo marches straight into the 'boss's office'—the Nucleus.

Inside the nucleus is your DNA, the master instruction manual for everything your cell does. The hormone-receptor complex binds directly to a specific section of the DNA. It acts like a highlighter pen, telling the cell, 'Hey, read this instruction right now!' This triggers the DNA to be copied into mRNA (transcription), which is then used to build brand new proteins (translation). These new proteins then change the physical and chemical activities of the cell. 

So, steroid hormones influence cellular activities by crossing the membrane, binding to an internal receptor, and directly changing gene expression (how your DNA is used) to build new proteins. It's a deep, fundamental change from the inside out!
questions.Answer: By entering the cell, binding to an intracellular receptor, and altering gene expression (DNA)

questions.Question: 25. Identify A, B and C in the diagrammatic representation of the mechanism of hormone action.
MCQ_Options: A - Cell Membrane Receptor, B - Secondary Messenger (like cAMP), C - Biochemical Response
A - Nucleus, B - DNA, C - Protein Synthesis
A - Intracellular Receptor, B - ATP, C - Gene Expression
A - Ribosome, B - Messenger RNA, C - Cellular Growth
questions.Hint: If a hormone is not a steroid, it cannot enter the cell. It must ring a 'doorbell' (A) on the outside, which triggers a signal (B) on the inside, leading to a result (C).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Even though we can't see the specific diagram this question refers to, in biology tests, diagrammatic representations of hormone action almost always test the difference between the two main types of hormones: Steroid (lipid) hormones and Protein/Peptide (water-soluble) hormones. Since we just talked about steroids, let's explore the classic Protein Hormone diagram!

Imagine you are a delivery driver (the Protein Hormone) trying to deliver a crucial message to a family, but you are not allowed inside their house. The house is the cell, and the walls of the house are the cell membrane. Because you are water-soluble, you cannot pass through the fatty lipid membrane walls. You are stuck outside.

So, what do you do? You walk up to the front door and press the doorbell! In this biological diagram, **'A' is the Cell Membrane Receptor**. It acts exactly like a doorbell located on the outer surface of the cell.

When you press the doorbell (when the hormone binds to the receptor), you don't enter the house, but you cause a reaction *inside* the house. The ringing sound alerts a person inside the house to run and deliver your message to the rest of the family. In biology, this 'inside messenger' is called a Secondary Messenger. The most famous one is Cyclic AMP (cAMP) or Calcium ions. So, **'B' is the Secondary Messenger (like cAMP)**.

Once the secondary messenger spreads the word inside the cell, the cell's machinery activates and carries out the necessary action. Maybe it starts breaking down glycogen into sugar, or maybe it releases an enzyme. This final action is the response. Therefore, **'C' is the Biochemical Response**.

This system is brilliant! It allows a hormone to cause massive changes inside a cell without ever actually stepping foot inside it. It's the ultimate biological relay race: Hormone -> Receptor (A) -> Secondary Messenger (B) -> Biochemical Response (C).
questions.Answer: A - Cell Membrane Receptor, B - Secondary Messenger (like cAMP), C - Biochemical Response

questions.Question: 26. Which of the following is an amino acid derived hormone?
questions.Hint: Look for the hormone that controls your 'fight or flight' response. It is made by slightly modifying a single amino acid called Tyrosine.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To get this right, let's think about building with LEGOs. Hormones come in different shapes and sizes based on what materials the body used to build them. 

Some hormones are built out of fats (cholesterol). We call these Steroid hormones. From your options, Estradiol and Estriol are forms of estrogen, which are classic steroid hormones. Ecdysone is also a steroid hormone found in insects that helps them molt. Because these are built from fats, they are not our answer.

Other hormones are built out of Amino Acids. Amino acids are the single, tiny LEGO blocks that usually snap together to build large proteins. But sometimes, the body decides not to build a giant protein. Instead, it takes just *one single* amino acid LEGO block, makes a few tiny chemical tweaks to it, and turns it into a hormone!
