questions.Answer: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

questions.Question:
10. Given below are two statements: 
Statement I: In eukaryotes there are three RNA polymerases in the nucleus in addition to the RNA polymerase found in the organelles. 
Statement II: All the three RNA polymerases in eukaryotic nucleus have different roles.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.Hint: Eukaryotic cells are like highly complex factories. They don't just use one universal machine; they have specialized machines for different tasks. Think about RNA Pol I, II, and III.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are running a simple lemonade stand (a prokaryotic cell like bacteria). Because your business is small, you only need one single, multi-purpose machine that does everything: it juices the lemons, adds the sugar, and pours the water. This is why bacteria only have one single type of RNA Polymerase that makes all types of RNA.

Now imagine you are running a giant, high-tech, multi-billion-dollar car factory—this is your Eukaryotic cell (like human, plant, or animal cells). A factory this complex cannot rely on just one machine. Inside the main control center (the Nucleus), you have three completely different, highly specialized 3D-printing machines. 

1. RNA Polymerase I (The Scaffold Builder): This machine exclusively prints 'rRNA' (Ribosomal RNA). rRNA is the heavy-duty building material used to construct the cell's protein factories (ribosomes).
2. RNA Polymerase II (The Blueprint Copier): This machine prints 'mRNA' (Messenger RNA). It copies the actual instructions from the DNA recipe book that tell the cell how to make specific proteins.
3. RNA Polymerase III (The Delivery Truck Maker): This machine prints 'tRNA' (Transfer RNA) and a few other small RNAs. tRNA molecules act like little delivery trucks that carry individual amino acids to the protein factory.

So, as you can see, all three polymerases in the nucleus have very distinct, different jobs. That means Statement II is absolutely correct.

What about Statement I? Well, apart from these three master machines in the nucleus, Eukaryotic cells also have mini-factories like Mitochondria (and Chloroplasts in plants) that generate energy. Since these organelles actually evolved from ancient bacteria billions of years ago, they still carry around their own unique, separate, single RNA polymerase! Thus, Statement I is also a perfectly true biological fact.
questions.Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

questions.Question:
11. Given below are two statements : 
Statement I : RNA interference takes place in all Eukaryotic organisms as method of cellular defense. 
Statement II : RNAi involves the silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary single-stranded RNA molecule that binds and prevents translation of mRNA 
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.Hint: Look very closely at Statement II. Does the trigger for RNA interference start as a SINGLE-stranded RNA, or is the presence of a DOUBLE-stranded RNA the ultimate red flag for the cell's defense system?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about microscopic ninjas and cellular security systems! 

Statement I says that RNA interference (RNAi) takes place in all Eukaryotes as a cellular defense. This is True! Your cells are constantly being attacked by sneaky viruses. Many of these viruses try to hijack your cell's factories by injecting their own genetic instructions. To fight back, all eukaryotic cells (plants, animals, fungi) evolved a brilliant security system called RNAi to hunt down and destroy these foreign instructions.

Now, how does this security system know what to destroy? Here is the secret: Normal, healthy human/plant cells almost exclusively use Single-Stranded RNA (like mRNA) to send messages. Viruses, however, often use Double-Stranded RNA (dsRNA) to replicate. 

When your cell's security cameras detect a weird, foreign DOUBLE-stranded RNA floating around, alarms go off! The cell recognizes this dsRNA as a virus fingerprint. Special ninja proteins (called Dicer) rush in and chop that double-stranded RNA into tiny little pieces. Then, another protein squad (called RISC) takes one of those tiny pieces and uses it as a "Wanted Poster" to hunt down and silence any matching viral mRNA, stopping the virus from translating its proteins.

Now read Statement II carefully: It claims RNAi involves the silencing of mRNA due to a complementary SINGLE-STRANDED RNA molecule. This statement is considered incorrect in the context of standard biology textbooks because the core definition and initiating trigger of RNAi is the binding of a complementary DOUBLE-STRANDED RNA (dsRNA) molecule that initiates the silencing of the target mRNA. Because Statement II incorrectly identifies the trigger as single-stranded instead of double-stranded, it is false.
questions.Answer: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

questions.Question: 12. The lactose present in the growth medium of bacteria is transported to the cell by the action of
questions.Hint: Look at the name of the options! Which word sounds like it is giving 'permission' for something to pass through a barrier?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine a tiny bacterium floating in a puddle of milk. Milk contains a sugar called 'lactose', which the bacterium would love to eat for energy. However, the bacterium has a thick cell membrane acting like the walls of an exclusive nightclub, and the lactose molecules are outside, waiting in line to get in. 

To get the lactose inside, the bacterium needs a 'bouncer' or a specialized door on its membrane that allows the lactose to enter. 

In bacteria like E. coli, the system that handles lactose is called the 'Lac Operon'. This system produces three specific worker proteins to deal with lactose:
1. Beta-galactosidase: This is the 'chef'. Once lactose is inside, this enzyme chops the lactose in half so the bacterium can actually digest it and get energy.
2. Transacetylase: We still don't fully understand everything this protein does, but it acts like an assistant, helping with the overall metabolic process by adding chemical tags to certain molecules.
3. Permease: This is the 'door-opener'! Permease is a transport protein that embeds itself in the cell membrane and creates a channel. It literally gives 'permission' for the lactose in the outside growth medium to be transported inside the cell.

Without Permease, the lactose would just bounce off the outside of the bacterial cell. Therefore, the lactose is transported into the cell by the action of Permease.

questions.Question: 13. A transcription unit in DNA is defined primarily by the three regions in DNA and these are with respect to upstream and down stream end;
questions.Hint: Think of a transcription unit like a movie script. You need an 'Intro' (to tell you where to start), the actual 'Body' of the script (the main story), and the 'Credits' (to tell you it's over).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand a 'Transcription Unit', you have to understand how a cell reads a gene to make an RNA copy. Imagine you are reading a massively long scroll of text with no spaces or punctuation. How would you know where a specific story starts and where it ends? 

Nature solved this problem by defining a specific "Transcription Unit" on the DNA. It consists of three perfectly organized regions:

1. The Promoter: This is the "Start Reading Here" sign. It is located at the beginning of the gene (which biologists call the 'upstream' end). It acts like a landing pad for the enzyme RNA Polymerase. Without the promoter, the enzyme wouldn't know where to attach to the DNA.

2. The Structural Gene: This is the actual story! It is the core sequence of DNA that contains the valuable instructions for building a protein. As the RNA Polymerase moves across this section, it reads the DNA letters and builds the RNA strand.

3. The Terminator: This is the "The End" sign. It is located at the very end of the gene (called the 'downstream' end). When RNA Polymerase hits this sequence, it realizes the story is over. It stops copying and falls off the DNA, releasing the newly made RNA.

So, from upstream to downstream, the three primary regions that define a transcription unit are the Promoter, the Structural Gene, and the Terminator.

questions.Question: 14. Which of the following statement is correct regarding the process of replication in E.coli?
MCQ_Options: DNA dependent DNA polymerase catalyses polymerization only in the 3' to 5' direction.
Replication is highly energy-expensive and requires Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs).
The lagging strand is synthesized continuously without any breaks.
Replication can initiate randomly anywhere on the DNA sequence.
questions.Hint: Building a massive molecule like DNA is like building a giant Lego tower. Does snapping all those pieces together happen for free, or does it take a lot of effort and energy?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore how a bacterium like E. coli copies its DNA. It is a monumental task! E. coli has a DNA molecule with millions of base pairs. Copying this requires incredible speed and massive amounts of cellular energy.

Let's evaluate the options to see how the cell actually pulls this off:

Option 1 says the enzyme (DNA Polymerase) works in the 3' to 5' direction. This is FALSE. DNA Polymerase is an incredibly stubborn molecular builder. It absolutely refuses to build backward. It can ONLY build new DNA in one specific direction: the 5' (five-prime) to 3' (three-prime) direction. 

Option 3 says the 'lagging strand' is synthesized continuously. This is FALSE. Because DNA Polymerase is so stubborn and only moves 5' to 3', one strand of DNA (the leading strand) gets built smoothly and continuously. But the other opposite strand (the lagging strand) has to be built awkwardly in short, choppy, backward pieces called Okazaki fragments.

Option 4 says replication can initiate anywhere. FALSE! As we learned earlier, replication MUST start at a very specific sequence called the Origin of Replication (ori).

Option 2 says Replication is highly energy-expensive and requires 'Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates' (dNTPs). This is TRUE! dNTPs are essentially floating DNA letters (A, T, C, G) that have three energy-packed phosphates attached to them, exactly like ATP (the cell's energy currency). They serve a brilliant dual purpose: first, they are the actual physical building blocks (the Lego pieces) that make up the new DNA. Second, when the enzyme breaks off two of those phosphates, it releases a huge burst of energy. This explosive energy is used to permanently weld the letter into the growing DNA chain. So, DNA replication is an incredibly energy-expensive process powered by dNTPs!
questions.Answer: Replication is highly energy-expensive and requires Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs).

questions.Question:
Match List I with List II:
List-I
A. Frederick Griffith
B. Francois Jacob & Jacque Monod
C. Har Gobind Khorana
D. Meselson & Stahl
List-II
I. Genetic code
II. Semi-conservative mode of DNA replication
III. Transformation
IV. Lac operon
questions.Hint: Think about the scientist who worked with mice and pneumonia bacteria, and the duo who figured out how bacteria digest milk sugar.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! To solve this, let's take a quick trip back in time to meet some legendary biological detectives and look at the mind-blowing discoveries they made!

First up, Frederick Griffith (A). Back in 1928, he was playing around with bacteria that cause pneumonia in mice. He discovered something spooky: harmless bacteria could suddenly 'transform' into deadly bacteria if they were mixed with dead deadly ones! It was like they inherited a ghost's superpower. This phenomenon was called 'Transformation' (III).

Next, let's meet Francois Jacob & Jacque Monod (B). Imagine you have a smart house that only turns on the lights when you walk into a room to save energy. Bacteria do this too! These scientists figured out that bacteria only turn on the genes to digest milk sugar (lactose) when milk is actually around. This gene-switching system is called the 'Lac operon' (IV).

Then we have Har Gobind Khorana (C). Imagine DNA is a super-secret alien language. Khorana was one of the master codebreakers who helped create the dictionary for this language. He synthesized RNA molecules in a lab to figure out exactly which three-letter 'words' (codons) code for which amino acids. He helped crack the 'Genetic code' (I)!

Finally, Meselson & Stahl (D). When DNA copies itself, how does it do it? Does it print a whole new copy, or split in half? They used special 'heavy' nitrogen to prove that a DNA double helix unzips, and each old half builds a brand new partner half. Since half is old and half is new, it's called the 'Semi-conservative mode of DNA replication' (II).

So, putting it all together: Griffith goes with Transformation, Jacob/Monod with Lac operon, Khorana with Genetic code, and Meselson/Stahl with Semi-conservative replication!

A. Down’s syndrome
B. α-Thalassemia
C. β-Thalassemia

List-II
I. 11th chromosome
II. ‘X’ chromosome
III. 21st chromosome
IV. 16th chromosome
questions.Hint: Remember that Down's is also known as Trisomy 21, and Klinefelter's affects male sex chromosomes.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Alright, let's dive into the fascinating world of human chromosomes! Imagine your DNA is an instruction manual for building 'You', and it is divided into 23 chapters (chromosome pairs). Sometimes, Mother Nature makes a tiny typo or binds the book a little differently. Let's look at what happens when these specific chapters are affected.

First, Down's syndrome (A). Normally, you get exactly two copies of every chromosome chapter—one from mom, one from dad. But sometimes, a person gets three copies of Chapter 21! Because of this extra 21st chromosome, they develop Down's syndrome. So, A matches with III (21st chromosome).

Next, let's talk about Thalassemia, which is a blood disorder where the body struggles to make hemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells). Hemoglobin is built using two main parts: an alpha part and a beta part. 
Think of alpha-Thalassemia (B) as a glitch in the 'alpha' factory. The instructions for this factory are located on the 16th chromosome. So, B matches with IV (16th chromosome).
Think of beta-Thalassemia (C) as a glitch in the 'beta' factory. The instructions for this factory are stored on the 11th chromosome. So, C matches with I (11th chromosome).

Finally, Klinefelter’s syndrome (D). We usually determine biological sex using the 23rd pair of chromosomes. Females have XX, and males have XY. In Klinefelter’s syndrome, a boy is born with an extra 'X' chromosome, making his blueprint XXY. This extra 'X' chromosome alters how his body develops. So, D matches with II ('X' chromosome).

Matching them all up perfectly gives us A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II. By understanding which 'chapter' of the DNA book has a typo, doctors can understand exactly how to help people with these conditions!

questions.Question: Which one is the correct product of DNA dependent RNA polymerase to the given template? 3’TACATGGCAAATATCCATTCA5’
questions.Hint: DNA uses T (Thymine), but RNA uses U (Uracil). Also, RNA polymerase reads the template from 3' to 5', but builds the new RNA strand in the 5' to 3' direction!

Let's crack this genetic code! Imagine you are a biological copy machine known as an enzyme called 'DNA-dependent RNA polymerase'. Your job is to read a master blueprint (DNA) and create a temporary working copy (RNA) that can be sent out into the cell to build proteins. This process is called transcription.

Here are the absolute, unbreakable rules of being this copy machine:
Rule 1: Directionality. You always read the DNA template from the 3' end to the 5' end. But, as you read it, you build the new RNA strand in the opposite direction, from 5' to 3'. It's like reading a book right-to-left while writing your notes left-to-right!
Rule 2: Base Pairing. You have to match the puzzle pieces perfectly. 
- If DNA has a T (Thymine), you put an A (Adenine) in the RNA.
- If DNA has an A (Adenine), you put a U (Uracil) in the RNA. (Remember, RNA hates Thymine, so it uses Uracil instead!)
- If DNA has a C (Cytosine), you put a G (Guanine).
- If DNA has a G (Guanine), you put a C (Cytosine).

Let's do this step-by-step using our given template: 3' T A C A T G G C A A A T A T C C A T T C A 5'

1. Since the template starts with 3', our new RNA will start with 5'.
2. Match the letters:
DNA: T -> RNA: A
DNA: A -> RNA: U
DNA: C -> RNA: G
DNA: A -> RNA: U
DNA: T -> RNA: A
DNA: G -> RNA: C
DNA: G -> RNA: C
DNA: C -> RNA: G
DNA: A -> RNA: U
DNA: A -> RNA: U
DNA: A -> RNA: U
DNA: T -> RNA: A
DNA: A -> RNA: U
DNA: T -> RNA: A
DNA: C -> RNA: G

questions.Question:
Match List I with List II:
List-I
A. RNA polymerase III
B. Termination of transcription
C. Splicing of Exons
D. TATA box
List-II
I. snRNPs
II. Promotor
III. Rho factor
IV. SnRNAs, tRNA
questions.Hint: Think of what cuts up RNA during splicing, and which 'factor' tells the transcription process to stop.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a fantastic question about the behind-the-scenes movie production crew that makes transcription happen! Let's match up these molecular actors with their roles.

A. RNA polymerase III: In eukaryotes (like us), there are three main 'directors' (RNA polymerases) that make different types of RNA. RNA Pol I makes the big ribosomes, RNA Pol II makes the messenger RNA (the actual instructions for proteins), and RNA Pol III is in charge of making the transfer RNAs (tRNAs) and small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs). So, RNA polymerase III matches with IV (SnRNAs, tRNA).

B. Termination of transcription: When the RNA polymerase reaches the end of the gene, how does it know when to stop copying? In bacteria, a special protein called the 'Rho factor' acts like a giant stop sign or a bouncer, physically pulling the RNA polymerase off the DNA track so transcription terminates. So, Termination of transcription matches with III (Rho factor).

C. Splicing of Exons: When our cells first make RNA, it's full of junk sequences called 'introns' that interrupt the good stuff ('exons'). Imagine a movie full of boring bloopers. The cell uses molecular scissors to cut out the introns and glue the good exons together. These scissors are actually complex machines called snRNPs (pronounced 'snurps', which stands for small nuclear ribonucleoproteins!). So, Splicing matches with I (snRNPs).

D. TATA box: Before the RNA polymerase can start copying a gene, it needs to know exactly where the gene begins. It looks for a sequence of DNA that acts like a bright neon 'START HERE' sign. This sequence is often T-A-T-A-A-A, so we lovingly call it the TATA box. The TATA box is the core part of the 'Promoter' region of a gene. So, TATA box matches with II (Promotor).

Matching them all up, we get A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II. Biology is just like a highly organized movie set!

questions.Question: The last chromosome sequenced in Human Genome Project was :
questions.Hint: Chromosomes are numbered roughly based on their size. The biggest one took the longest amount of time to map completely!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about one of the coolest scientific projects in human history: The Human Genome Project (HGP)! Started in 1990, the goal of this project was to read and map every single letter (A, T, C, G) of human DNA. It was like trying to map an entire undiscovered galaxy, but inside our cells.

Now, human DNA is divided into 23 pairs of chromosomes. When scientists decided to number these chromosomes, they did something very logical: they numbered them mostly by size! Chromosome 1 is the absolute largest, carrying the most DNA and the most genes (around 2,968 genes!). Chromosome 22 is one of the smallest.

Because Chromosome 1 is such a massive, giant library of genetic information, it naturally took the longest amount of time to decode. Even though the Human Genome Project was declared 'essentially complete' in April 2003, the final, completely finished sequence of Chromosome 1 wasn't published until May 2006! It was the final boss, the very last piece of the human genetic puzzle to be fully mapped. 

So, if you ever feel like you have a huge project taking forever to finish, just remember that even the world's greatest scientists took over 15 years to finish reading Chromosome 1!

questions.Question: Name the component that binds to the operator region of an operon and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon.
questions.Hint: Think of a word that means 'to hold back' or 'suppress' an action.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you have a toy train (which represents our enzyme, RNA polymerase) that wants to drive down a train track (the DNA) to deliver a payload (transcribing the gene). 

In bacteria, genes are organized into clusters called 'operons'. Before the train can get to the actual genes, it has to pass through a specific patch of track called the 'operator region'. 

Now, bacteria are incredibly smart about conserving energy. If they don't need the proteins that a specific operon makes, they won't let the train drive down the track. How do they stop it? They plop a giant boulder right on top of the operator region. Because the boulder is sitting exactly on the track, the toy train (RNA polymerase) physically crashes into it and cannot move forward to read the genes.

In biological terms, this 'boulder' is a special protein called a 'Repressor protein'. When a repressor protein binds to the operator, it completely blocks the path of RNA polymerase, thereby shutting off (or repressing) the transcription of those genes. When the bacteria suddenly needs the genes again, a molecule will come and remove the repressor boulder, allowing the train to zoom down the track once more. It's a beautifully simple and effective switch!

questions.Question:
Given below are two statements :
Statement I :
The process of copying genetic information from one strand of the DNA into RNA is termed as transcription.
Statement II :
A transcription unit in DNA is defined primarily by the three regions in the DNA i.e., a promotor, the structural gene and a terminator.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
questions.Hint: Think of transcription like a recipe. Does it need a start point (promoter), the actual ingredients (structural gene), and an end point (terminator)?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's investigate these two statements like biological detectives to see if they hold up to the facts!

Let's look at Statement I: 'The process of copying genetic information from one strand of the DNA into RNA is termed as transcription.'
Think of the nucleus of a cell like a highly secure library, and the DNA is an ancient, priceless recipe book that is never allowed to leave the library. If the cell's kitchen (the ribosome) needs a recipe to bake a protein cake, it has to send a scribe to make a cheap, disposable copy of the recipe on a scrap piece of paper. This scrap paper is RNA. The act of 'transcribing' or copying the DNA letters into RNA letters is indeed called Transcription! So, Statement I is 100% correct.

Now let's look at Statement II: 'A transcription unit in DNA is defined primarily by the three regions in the DNA i.e., a promotor, the structural gene and a terminator.'
If you are copying a recipe, how do you know where the recipe begins and where it ends? The DNA strand is massive, so the enzyme (RNA polymerase) needs landmarks. 
1. It looks for the 'Promotor'—this is like the Title of the recipe that screams 'Start copying right here!'.
2. Then it copies the 'Structural gene'—this is the actual meat of the recipe, the instructions for the protein.
3. Finally, it hits the 'Terminator'—this is the period at the end of the sentence that says 'Stop copying, you're done!'.
A full transcription unit absolutely contains these three specific regions. Therefore, Statement II is also 100% correct.

Since both statements are perfectly accurate descriptions of how biology works, the correct option is that both are correct!
questions.Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.

questions.Concept: Search for Genetic Material (The Hershey-Chase Experiment)
questions.Question: 22. Which scientist conducted an experiment with 32P and 35S labelled phages for demonstrating that DNA is the genetic material?
MCQ_Options: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty
questions.Hint: Think of the famous 'blender experiment' from 1952 that finally proved what material viruses inject into bacteria.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are a detective trying to solve a massive mystery: What is the secret code of life made of? Is it Protein, or is it DNA? For a long time, scientists weren't sure. To solve this, in 1952, two brilliant scientists named Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase designed an incredibly clever experiment using 'bacteriophages'. 

A bacteriophage (or phage for short) is a tiny virus that looks a bit like a lunar lander. It attacks bacteria. These viruses are very simple; they are essentially just a shell made of protein, with a coil of DNA stuffed inside. When a virus attacks a bacteria, it acts like a microscopic syringe. It attaches to the outside and injects its 'genetic material' inside to hijack the bacteria's factory. But does it inject DNA or Protein? 

Hershey and Chase used radioactivity to 'tag' and track these molecules, like putting a GPS tracker on a suspect. 
DNA contains a lot of Phosphorus (P) but no Sulfur. Protein contains Sulfur (S) but no Phosphorus. 
So, they grew one batch of viruses in radioactive Phosphorus (32P) to make their DNA glow. They grew another batch in radioactive Sulfur (35S) to make their protein coats glow. 

After letting these radioactive viruses attack the bacteria, they threw everything into an ordinary kitchen blender to shake the empty virus shells off the outside of the bacteria. What did they find? Only the radioactive Phosphorus (32P) had gone *inside* the bacteria! The radioactive Sulfur (35S) stayed outside. This was the ultimate, irrefutable proof: DNA is the genetic material that gets passed on and holds the instructions for life. It was a mic-drop moment in biology!

questions.Concept: Properties of Genetic Material (DNA vs. RNA)
questions.Question:
23. Given below are two statements :
Statement I :
RNA being unstable, mutate at a faster rate.
Statement II :
RNA can directly code for synthesis of proteins hence can easily express the characters.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.Hint: Compare DNA to a heavy, protected master blueprint in a vault, and RNA to a disposable sticky-note copy. Which one is easier to mess up (mutate), and which one is handed directly to the factory workers (ribosomes)?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's break down how our cells handle information. Imagine your DNA as an ancient, highly valuable master recipe book kept safe in a heavily guarded library (the nucleus of the cell). It is double-stranded, super stable, and carefully protected. 

Now, let's look at Statement I: 'RNA being unstable, mutate at a faster rate.' RNA is like a quick photocopy of one recipe from that master book, written on a flimsy sticky note. Chemically, RNA is single-stranded and has an extra oxygen atom (an -OH group at the 2' position of its sugar), making it highly reactive and easily breakable. Because it is so fragile and lacks the 'backup copy' a double strand provides, errors (mutations) happen much more frequently. This is why RNA viruses (like the flu or COVID-19) evolve and mutate so rapidly! So, Statement I is completely correct.

Now for Statement II: 'RNA can directly code for synthesis of proteins hence can easily express the characters.' Think of the cellular machinery that builds proteins (ribosomes) as factory workers. These workers cannot read the heavy master DNA book; they only understand the language of the RNA sticky notes. RNA is the direct messenger (mRNA). As soon as the RNA is made, the ribosomes read it and immediately start building the protein, which creates your traits (characters). DNA, on the other hand, cannot build proteins directly; it must be copied into RNA first. Therefore, RNA directly codes for protein synthesis. Statement II is also perfectly correct.

Since both statements are biologically accurate descriptions of RNA's behavior, the answer is that both are correct.
questions.Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

questions.Question:
24. Select the correct statements about sickle cell anaemia.
(A) There is a change in gene for beta globin.
(B) In the beta globin, there is valine in the place of Lysine.
(C) It is an example of point mutation.
(D) In the normal gene U is replaced by A.
questions.Hint: Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a tiny single-letter typo in the DNA. Remember the specific amino acid swap: Glutamic acid is replaced by Valine.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Sickle cell anaemia is a fascinating but serious genetic condition. To understand it, think of your red blood cells as soft, bouncy, doughnut-shaped taxis that carry oxygen through the narrow highways of your blood vessels. 

Inside these taxis is a protein called Hemoglobin. Hemoglobin is made of different parts, including something called 'beta-globin'. 
Let's evaluate the statements one by one:

(A) 'There is a change in gene for beta globin.' - Yes! The genetic instructions (the gene) for making the beta-globin protein get mutated. This is true.

(B) 'In the beta globin, there is valine in the place of Lysine.' - This is a trap! In a normal person, the 6th amino acid in the beta-globin chain is Glutamic Acid. In sickle cell anaemia, Glutamic Acid is replaced by Valine. (It has nothing to do with Lysine). Valine hates water, so the hemoglobin molecules clump together to hide from the water in the cell. This clumping stretches the soft red blood cell into a rigid, sharp 'sickle' or crescent moon shape. These pointy cells cause traffic jams in the blood vessels. Statement B is false.

(C) 'It is an example of point mutation.' - A point mutation is when exactly ONE single letter (base pair) in the DNA code is changed. Sickle cell is the classic example of this! The DNA changes from CTC to CAC. One tiny typo ruins the whole protein. Statement C is true.

(D) 'In the normal gene U is replaced by A.' - Genes are made of DNA. DNA does NOT contain the letter U (Uracil); it only has A, T, C, and G. Uracil is only found in RNA. So, talking about 'U' in a gene is fundamentally incorrect. The actual mutation in the mRNA is GAG changing to GUG (A is replaced by U, not the other way around). Statement D is false.

Therefore, only statements (A) and (C) are correct!

questions.Concept: Regulation of Gene Expression (The Lac Operon)
questions.Question: 25. Which one of the following acts as an inducer for lac operon?
questions.Hint: Bacteria are smart. They won't turn on the factory to digest milk sugar unless milk sugar is actually present in their environment.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are a bacterium living in a human's stomach. Your job is to eat whatever comes your way. Making enzymes (digestive juices) takes a lot of energy, so you don't want to waste energy making enzymes for a food that isn't even there. You only want the factory turned 'ON' when the specific food arrives. 

This smart energy-saving system is called an 'Operon'. The 'Lac Operon' specifically handles Lactose, which is the sugar found in milk. 

Normally, when there is no milk around, a molecular padlock called a 'repressor' clamps down on the DNA. It blocks the factory machinery from reading the genes. The factory is OFF.

But what happens when you drink a glass of milk? Lactose enters the bacterium. This Lactose (specifically a slightly modified form called allolactose) acts like a key. It binds to the padlock (repressor), changing its shape so it falls off the DNA. Suddenly, the block is gone! The factory machinery rushes in, reads the genes, and starts producing the enzymes needed to digest the lactose.

Because Lactose triggers or 'induces' the factory to turn on, we call it the 'Inducer'. Without lactose, the system stays asleep. So, the molecule that acts as the inducer for the lac operon is Lactose!

questions.Concept: Search for Genetic Material (Hershey-Chase Experiment Details)
questions.Question:
26. With reference to Hershey and Chase experiments. Select the correct statements.
(A) Viruses grown in the presence of radioactive phosphorus contained radioactive DNA.
(B) Viruses grown on radioactive sulphur contained radioactive proteins.
(C) Viruses grown on radioactive phosphorus contained radioactive protein.
(D) Viruses grown on radioactive sulphur contained radioactive DNA.
(E) Viruses grown on radioactive protein contained radioactive DNA.
questions.Hint: Remember the chemical makeup: DNA has a phosphate-sugar backbone (Phosphorus), and proteins are made of amino acids, some of which contain Sulfur.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's revisit our favorite genetic detectives, Hershey and Chase! They were working with viruses (bacteriophages) that have only two parts: a DNA core on the inside, and a protein coat on the outside. They needed a way to color-code these two parts to see which one gets injected into a bacteria.

To color-code them, they used radioactivity. But how do you ensure the radioactive tag *only* sticks to the DNA, and a different tag *only* sticks to the protein? You have to look at their chemical ingredients!

1. DNA is built like a twisted ladder. The side-rails of this ladder are made of sugar and Phosphates. Therefore, DNA is packed with Phosphorus. But DNA has absolutely NO Sulfur. So, if you grow viruses in a soup of Radioactive Phosphorus (32P), the viruses will incorporate it into their DNA. Their DNA becomes radioactive. This makes Statement (A) completely correct, and Statement (C) incorrect.

2. Proteins are made of long chains of amino acids. Two specific amino acids (cysteine and methionine) contain Sulfur atoms. Proteins have NO Phosphorus. So, if you grow viruses in a soup of Radioactive Sulfur (35S), they will use that sulfur to build their outer protein coats. Their protein shell becomes radioactive. This makes Statement (B) completely correct, and Statement (D) incorrect.

Statement (E) is just biologically nonsensical (you don't grow viruses 'on' radioactive protein to get radioactive DNA).

By matching the chemical elements to the molecules they belong to (Phosphorus = DNA, Sulfur = Protein), Hershey and Chase successfully color-coded the virus! So, the only true statements are (A) and (B).

questions.Question:
27. The salient features of genetic code are :
(A) The code is palindromic
(B) UGA act as initiator codon
(C) The code is unambiguous and specific
(D) The code is nearly universal
questions.Hint: Think of the genetic code as an English dictionary used by the cell. Does one word have confusing multiple meanings (ambiguous)? Do humans use a different cellular dictionary than a banana tree?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
The genetic code is the ultimate secret language of life. It translates the 4-letter alphabet of RNA (A, U, C, G) into the 20-letter alphabet of Proteins (amino acids). It reads the letters in groups of three, called 'codons' (like 3-letter words). Let's see what makes this language so special by checking the statements:

(A) 'The code is palindromic' - A palindrome is a word that reads the same forwards and backwards, like RACECAR. The genetic code is NOT read forwards and backwards. It is read strictly in one direction (5' to 3'). Certain DNA sequences (like restriction enzyme sites) are palindromic, but the genetic code itself is not. So, A is false.

(B) 'UGA act as initiator codon' - False! When the cellular machinery is reading the RNA, it needs to know when to start and stop. The Start (initiator) codon is AUG (You can remember it like 'Are U Going?'). UGA is actually a STOP codon. When the machine reads UGA, it says 'U Go Away!' and stops building the protein. So, B is false.

(C) 'The code is unambiguous and specific' - This means there is no confusion in the dictionary. The codon 'UUU' will ALWAYS mean the amino acid Phenylalanine. It will never suddenly mean something else. One word = one exact meaning. This is true! 

(D) 'The code is nearly universal' - This is the most mind-blowing fact in biology. The exact same dictionary is used by almost every living thing on Earth. The codon 'UUU' codes for Phenylalanine in a human, in a dog, in a banana tree, and in a tiny bacteria. Because of this, we can actually put human DNA into a bacteria, and the bacteria will read it perfectly to make human proteins (like insulin for diabetics!). This is true.

Therefore, only statements (C) and (D) correctly describe the magnificent genetic code.

questions.Question: 28. The phenomenon of pleiotropism refers to
MCQ_Options: A single gene controlling multiple phenotypic traits
Multiple genes controlling a single phenotypic trait
A gene that suppresses the expression of another gene
A trait that is influenced by environmental factors
questions.Hint: Look at the root of the word: 'Pleio' means 'many', and 'tropy' means 'ways' or 'changes'. It's like one master switch turning on the lights, the music, and the AC all at once.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Genetics can sometimes feel like a simple math equation: One gene = One trait. For example, a gene for eye color gives you your eye color. But biology loves to be complicated and efficient!

Enter the phenomenon of 'Pleiotropy' (pronounced ply-oh-tro-pee). The word comes from Greek: 'Pleio' means many, and 'tropos' means ways or effects. 

Pleiotropy occurs when ONE single gene controls MULTIPLE, seemingly unrelated traits in your body. 
Imagine you have a smart home. Usually, one light switch turns on one light bulb. That's a normal gene. But a Pleiotropic gene is like a 'Master Switch'. You flip that ONE switch, and suddenly the lights turn on, the air conditioning blasts cold air, the blinds roll up, and the stereo starts playing music. One cause, multiple different effects.

A classic biological example of pleiotropy is the disease Phenylketonuria (PKU). It is caused by a mutation in just ONE single gene. That gene is supposed to make an enzyme that breaks down an amino acid. But because that one gene is broken, a cascade of events happens causing multiple traits: mental retardation, a reduction in hair, and a change in skin pigmentation. How crazy is that? One broken genetic switch affects the brain, the hair, and the skin!

So, if you ever see the word Pleiotropism, just think: 'One gene, many effects.' 
(Note: The opposite of this is Polygenic inheritance, where *many* genes work together to control *one* trait, like human height.)
questions.Answer: A single gene controlling multiple phenotypic traits

questions.Question: 29. Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs) refers to
MCQ_Options: All genes that are expressed as RNA
All genes whether they are expressed or unexpressed
Only the DNA sequences that code for structural proteins
Certain repeating sequence patterns in the genome
questions.Hint: Focus carefully on the word 'Expressed'. What molecule in the cell represents the 'expression' of a DNA gene?
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Imagine your body's entire DNA genome is an insanely massive, gigantic cookbook containing over 3 billion letters of information. Inside this colossal book, some pages have real, delicious recipes for making proteins (these are the genes), while millions of other pages just contain gibberish, spacer text, or evolutionary leftovers that don't code for anything. When scientists embarked on the monumental Human Genome Project, they faced a tough choice: do we painstakingly read every single letter of the entire book (including the gibberish), or do we try to find a shortcut and only read the actual recipes that get cooked? The 'recipes that get cooked' are the genes that actually produce RNA. By capturing only the RNA that a cell actively makes and turning it back into tiny DNA tags, scientists created what we call 'Expressed Sequence Tags' (ESTs). It's a brilliant, massive shortcut! You are literally 'tagging' the DNA sequences that are actively 'expressed' (turned into RNA). This method saved an incredible amount of time and money, allowing researchers to quickly identify the most important, active parts of human DNA without getting bogged down by the silent, non-coding regions. So, ESTs refer specifically to all the genes that are expressed as RNA.
questions.Answer: All genes that are expressed as RNA

questions.Question: 30. Unequivocal proof that DNA is the genetic material was first proposed by
MCQ_Options: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty
questions.Hint: Think of the famous 'blender experiment' from 1952 involving tiny viruses and radioactive glowing elements.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Back in the mid-1900s, biologists were having a massive debate: 'Is DNA the boss of the cell, or are proteins the boss?' Proteins are incredibly complex and have many different building blocks (20 amino acids), so many scientists strongly believed proteins had to be the ones carrying the secret genetic codes. DNA, with only 4 building blocks, seemed too simple. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase wanted to settle this debate once and for all. In 1952, they performed an absolute masterpiece of an experiment using tiny viruses called bacteriophages. Picture these bacteriophages as microscopic, alien-like moon landers. These viruses only have two main parts: a tough protein coat on the outside, and a core of DNA stuffed inside. Hershey and Chase smartly made one batch of viruses with radioactive proteins (using radioactive sulfur, because sulfur is in proteins, not DNA) and another batch with radioactive DNA (using radioactive phosphorus, because phosphorus is in DNA, not proteins). They let these glowing viruses attach to and infect bacteria. After the viruses injected their genetic material, the scientists put the bacteria in a kitchen blender to shake off the empty virus shells! When they checked the infected bacteria, they only found the radioactive DNA inside! The radioactive proteins were just empty shells left outside. This unequivocally (without any doubt) proved that DNA is the master instruction manual that enters the cell.

questions.Question: 31. What is the role of RNA polymerase III in the process of transcription in Eukaryotes?
questions.Hint: Remember the simple factory trick: '1, 2, 3 = r, m, t'! Polymerase I makes rRNA, Polymerase II makes mRNA. What does III make?
questions.Detailed_Explanation: If you look inside a simple bacterial cell (a prokaryote), there is just one single, hard-working enzyme that does all the work of making RNA from DNA. But in more complex, advanced cells like human cells (eukaryotes), there is a brilliant division of labor to handle the massive workload. We have three different, highly specialized 'RNA making machines' called RNA polymerases: I, II, and III. Think of them as three specialized manufacturing factories in a busy city. Factory I (RNA polymerase I) specializes in making the heavy machinery of the cell—the ribosomal RNA (rRNA) that forms the core of ribosomes. Factory II (RNA polymerase II) is the most famous; it makes the messenger RNA (mRNA), which acts as the crucial instruction manuals carrying recipes from DNA to make proteins. But what about Factory III? RNA polymerase III is like the factory that makes the delivery trucks! It manufactures transfer RNA (tRNA). These tRNAs are tiny, folded molecules that act like delivery trucks, physically bringing the correct amino acids to the ribosome to build proteins. It also produces a few other small helper RNAs, like 5S rRNA and snRNAs. A classic trick to remember this division is '1, 2, 3 = r, m, t'! So, RNA polymerase III specifically transcribes tRNA.

questions.Concept: Properties of Genetic Material (DNA vs RNA)
questions.Question: 32. Given below are two statements: Statement I: RNA mutates at a faster rate. Statement II: Viruses having RNA genome and shorter life span mutate and evolve faster.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.Hint: Think about why RNA is considered a very unstable, flimsy molecule chemically, and how this instability drives the rapid changes seen in viruses like the flu or COVID-19.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: To truly understand this, imagine DNA as a sturdy, hard-cover encyclopedia that is kept safely in a library, and RNA as a quick, flimsy, single-use sticky note. At a chemical level, RNA is far more unstable than DNA. Why? Because the sugar in RNA has an extra oxygen atom (an -OH group at the 2' position). This extra oxygen acts like a reactive hook, making the RNA molecule highly prone to breaking down or reacting with other chemicals. Also, RNA is usually single-stranded, lacking the protective double-helix embrace that DNA enjoys. Because of this inherent chemical instability, when RNA is copied, mistakes—known as mutations—happen very easily and quickly. This makes Statement I completely and entirely true! Now, let's take this logic and apply it to the real world, like with viruses. Think of the flu, the common cold, or the SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) virus. These tiny invaders don't use DNA; they use RNA as their genetic material. Because their RNA mutates so incredibly quickly, and because viruses reproduce by the millions in a matter of hours (giving them a very short life span), their entire population evolves at super speed. This rapid evolution is exactly why you need to get a brand new flu vaccine every single year—the virus literally changes its 'disguise' by mutating its RNA! So, Statement II is also absolutely correct. Fast mutations lead to fast evolution.
questions.Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

questions.Question: 33. Given below are two statements: Statement I: In prokaryotes, the positively charged DNA is held with some negatively charged proteins in a region called nucleoid. Statement II: In eukaryotes, the negatively charged DNA is wrapped around the positively charged histone octamer to form nucleosome.
MCQ_Options: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
questions.Hint: Wait a minute... is DNA naturally positively charged or negatively charged? Think about the phosphate groups in the DNA backbone!
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Let's be scientific detectives and investigate the very first statement. DNA is a massive, long molecule made of billions of smaller building blocks called nucleotides. Every single nucleotide has a phosphate group attached to its backbone. These phosphate groups are completely packed with negatively charged oxygen atoms. Because of all these phosphate groups, DNA acts like a long, highly charged negative electrical wire. It is ALWAYS negatively charged! So, when Statement I claims that DNA is 'positively charged', it is telling a massive, completely backwards lie. Because DNA is so negative, if you try to pack two strands close together, they will repel each other (like two negative ends of a magnet). To solve this packing problem, the cell uses positively charged proteins as biological 'spools' to wrap the negative DNA around. Remember, opposites attract! In complex cells like our own eukaryotic cells, these positively charged protein spools are called histones. Specifically, eight of these histone proteins clump together to form a 'histone octamer'. The negative DNA loops beautifully around this positive octamer like a thread around a spool, forming a neat little package called a nucleosome. This means Statement II is perfectly accurate and scientifically sound! So, the first statement fundamentally fails basic chemistry, while the second statement perfectly describes how your cells pack 2 meters of DNA into a microscopic nucleus.
questions.Answer: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

questions.Question: 34. Choose the correct answer from the options given below: Match List I with List II.
questions.Hint: Whenever a question is missing data, think about standard patterns. How do genes map to proteins in a classic system like the Lac Operon?
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Alright, you'll notice right away that the actual text of this question is missing 'List I' and 'List II'. In real exams, a scanning error or a misprint might drop the lists entirely! But as your legendary biology mentor, I cannot let you leave empty-handed. Let's use this mysterious missing question as an epic opportunity to teach you how matching questions work by looking at the famous 'Lac Operon' system in bacteria. Imagine bacteria have a set of switches to digest lactose (milk sugar). List I would have the genes: the 'i' gene, 'z' gene, 'y' gene, and 'a' gene. List II would have their jobs. The 'i' gene is the bossy inhibitor—it codes for the Repressor protein that keeps the system turned off. The 'z' gene codes for Beta-galactosidase, the chemical scissors that actually cut lactose in half. The 'y' gene codes for Permease, which acts like a bouncer opening the cell membrane door to let lactose inside. Finally, the 'a' gene codes for Transacetylase, a helper enzyme. When you face a complete matching question, the golden rule is to find the one pair you are 100% confident about. If you know 'z' makes Beta-galactosidase, you look at the options and eliminate any choice that doesn't have that pair. It's like solving a puzzle! Even though the lists vanished here, understanding how to match genes to their protein functions will guarantee you dominate the real test when it arrives!

questions.Question: 35. Which one of the following is the sequence on corresponding coding strand, if the sequence on mRNA formed is as follows 5'AUCGAUCGAUCGAUCGAUCGAUCG AUCG 3'?
questions.Hint: The 'coding' strand of DNA is the boss strand that the mRNA perfectly mimics, except for one crucial letter swap! RNA uses Uracil (U), but what letter does DNA use?
questions.Detailed_Explanation: To solve this puzzle, we have to visualize the magical process of transcription, which is how a cell reads its DNA to make a temporary RNA copy. DNA is a double helix, meaning it has two strands zipped together. When it's time to make RNA, the two strands temporarily unzip. One DNA strand acts as the 'template'—the physical mold that the new RNA gets built upon. But the OTHER DNA strand is called the 'coding strand'. Here is the most amazing, secret shortcut in molecular biology: the resulting mRNA sequence is an ALMOST EXACT COPY of the coding strand! Why? Because they are both complementary to the exact same template mold. The only difference is that DNA and RNA speak slightly different chemical dialects. DNA uses the letter 'T' (Thymine), whereas RNA is a bit quirky and uses the letter 'U' (Uracil) instead. The question gives us the freshly made mRNA sequence: 5'-AUCGAUCGAUCGAUCGAUCGAUCG AUCG-3'. Since we know the coding strand is practically identical to this mRNA, all we have to do to find the coding strand is take that mRNA sequence and systematically swap every single 'U' back into a 'T'! Everything else, including the direction reading from 5' to 3', stays exactly identical. So, the sequence 'AUCG' simply becomes 'ATCG'. The correct coding strand sequence is 5'-ATCGATCG...-3'. It's just like translating a document from American English to British English—almost everything is identical except for swapping a few specific letters!

questions.Question: 36. In lac operon, z gene codes for:
questions.Hint: Think of the enzyme that acts like molecular scissors to break down lactose (a complex sugar) into simpler sugars (glucose and galactose). The 'z' gene is the primary star of this process!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine a bacterial cell, like the E. coli living in your gut, as a tiny, highly efficient factory. This factory loves to use glucose for energy because it is easy to burn. But sometimes, there is no glucose available, and the only food around is lactose (the sugar found in milk). To digest lactose, the bacteria need to build new special machines (enzymes). 

However, building machines takes a lot of energy, so the factory keeps the blueprints locked up when there is no lactose. This locked blueprint system is called an 'operon.' The 'lac operon' specifically controls lactose digestion. When lactose enters the cell, it acts like a key that unlocks the blueprint. 

This blueprint contains three main instructions, or structural genes, lined up in a row: z, y, and a. 

The 'z' gene is the very first and most important instruction on this assembly line. It codes for an amazing machine called beta-galactosidase. What does beta-galactosidase do? It acts exactly like a pair of molecular scissors. Lactose is a disaccharide, meaning it is made of two smaller sugars stuck together. Beta-galactosidase chops the lactose molecule right down the middle, separating it into glucose and galactose. Now, the bacteria can easily eat the glucose for energy! 

To give you the full picture, the 'y' gene makes permease, which is like a specialized door built into the cell wall to let more lactose inside, and the 'a' gene makes transacetylase, which helps get rid of toxic byproducts. But the 'z' gene is always responsible for the main event: making beta-galactosidase to cut the sugar. By turning these genes on only when lactose is around, the bacteria saves a ton of energy!

questions.Question: 37. Given below are two statements. Statement I: DNA polymerases catalyses polymerisation only in one direction, that is 5′ → 3′ Statement II : During replication of DNA, on one strand the replication is continuous while on the other strand it is discontinuous.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.Hint: Think about the 'builder' enzyme, DNA polymerase. It strictly obeys a one-way street rule! Because the two sides of a DNA helix run in opposite directions, how does this one-way rule affect the building process when the DNA unzips?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's imagine DNA as a massive, twisted double-sided zipper. When a cell gets ready to divide, it needs to make an exact copy of its DNA. To do this, it uses an enzyme called helicase to unzip the two strands, creating a 'Y' shape known as the replication fork. 

Now, the cell brings in a builder machine called DNA polymerase to construct the new matching halves of the zipper. But this builder has an incredibly strict rule: it can ONLY build a new DNA strand in one specific direction, from the 5-prime end to the 3-prime end (written as 5′ → 3′). It literally cannot operate in reverse. This strict one-way rule is exactly what Statement I says, so Statement I is 100% correct! 

Now, let's look at what happens because of this rule. The two original strands of DNA are 'antiparallel,' meaning they run in opposite directions, like cars driving on opposite sides of a highway. When the zipper opens, the builder on one side has it easy. It just follows the unzipping fork perfectly smoothly, building continuously in the 5′ → 3′ direction. We call this the 'leading strand.' 

But on the other side of the highway, the builder faces a huge problem. It has to build away from the unzipping fork to obey its 5′ → 3′ rule. As the zipper opens up more and more, the builder has to keep jumping backward toward the fork to fill in the newly exposed gaps. Because of this jumping back, it builds the new DNA in short, choppy little chunks called Okazaki fragments. We call this the 'lagging' or 'discontinuous' strand. Later, another enzyme called DNA ligase comes in to glue all these choppy chunks together. 

This is exactly what Statement II describes. The discontinuous building on one strand is a direct, unavoidable consequence of the one-way building rule stated in Statement I. Therefore, both statements are perfectly scientifically accurate!
questions.Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

questions.Concept: Experimental Proof of DNA as Genetic Material
questions.Question: 38. If DNA contained sulfur instead of phosphorus and proteins contained phosphorus instead of sulfur, what would have been the outcome of Hershey and Chase experiment?
MCQ_Options: Radioactive sulfur would be found inside the bacterial cell, proving DNA is the genetic material.
Radioactive phosphorus would be found inside the bacterial cell, proving protein is the genetic material.
Both sulfur and phosphorus would enter the cell.
Neither sulfur nor phosphorus would enter the cell.
questions.Hint: Hershey and Chase used radioactive tags to see what a virus injects into a bacterium to pass on its traits. Normally, DNA has Phosphorus and enters the cell. If we completely flip the chemistry so DNA has Sulfur instead, which radioactive tag ends up inside the bacteria?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
The Hershey-Chase experiment of 1952 is one of the coolest, most brilliant detective stories in the history of biology. At the time, scientists were arguing: what molecule actually carries our genetic secrets? Is it DNA, or is it protein? 

To solve the mystery, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase used bacteriophages. These are tiny viruses that infect bacteria. Structurally, these viruses are incredibly simple: they are basically just a squiggly piece of DNA stuffed inside a hard protein shell. It's like a piece of chocolate (DNA) inside a plastic wrapper (protein). When a virus attacks a bacterium, it latches onto the outside and injects its genetic material inside, while the empty protein 'wrapper' stays outside. 

To figure out what went inside, they used radioactive glowing tags. In the real world, DNA is rich in Phosphorus (P) but has absolutely zero Sulfur (S). On the other hand, proteins are rich in Sulfur (S) but have practically no Phosphorus. They made two batches of viruses: one with radioactive Phosphorus (to track DNA) and one with radioactive Sulfur (to track protein). After letting the viruses attack, they put them in a blender to knock the empty wrappers off. They found that only the radioactive Phosphorus made it inside the bacteria. Case closed: DNA is the genetic material! 

But your question asks us to imagine an alternate universe! 'What if' the chemistry was flipped? What if DNA was made of Sulfur, and protein was made of Phosphorus? 

If that were true, the molecule that actually gets injected into the bacteria (the DNA) would be carrying the radioactive Sulfur tag. The empty protein wrapper left floating outside would be carrying the radioactive Phosphorus tag. When the scientists checked inside the bacterial cells after the blender step, their detectors would light up with radioactive Sulfur! Thus, they would find radioactive Sulfur inside the cell, and they would still correctly conclude that whatever went inside (the Sulfur-carrying DNA) is the true genetic material.
questions.Answer: Radioactive sulfur would be found inside the bacterial cell, proving DNA is the genetic material.

questions.Question: 39. Against the codon 5′ UAC 3′, what would be the sequence of anticodon on tRNA?
questions.Hint: Use the RNA base pairing rules (A pairs with U, C pairs with G). Most importantly, remember that when two strands of nucleic acids stick together, they must be 'antiparallel' (one points 5' to 3', so the other must point 3' to 5').
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine a highly advanced factory assembly line inside your cells. The factory is building proteins, and the instruction tape running along the conveyor belt is called mRNA. The instructions are written in three-letter words called 'codons.' 

To build the protein, delivery trucks called tRNA (transfer RNA) zoom around bringing specific building blocks (amino acids) to the assembly line. But how does the tRNA truck know exactly where to drop its cargo? Each tRNA truck has a scanning barcode on its bottom called an 'anticodon.' This anticodon must perfectly match and stick to the 'codon' on the mRNA instruction tape. 

This sticking together happens through the beautiful rules of complementary base pairing. In the RNA world, there is no Thymine (T), only Uracil (U). So, the rule is: Adenine (A) always pairs with Uracil (U), and Cytosine (C) always pairs with Guanine (G). 

The question gives us the mRNA codon: 5′ UAC 3′. 

First, let's find the matching letters. 
- U matches with A. 
- A matches with U. 
- C matches with G. 
So, the sequence of letters must be AUG. 

But wait, there is an absolute rule in biology that we can never break: two strands of nucleic acids can only bind together if they are 'antiparallel.' This means they must face in opposite directions! Since the mRNA codon is written left-to-right from the 5′ end to the 3′ end (5′ → 3′), the matching tRNA anticodon must plug into it starting from the 3′ end going to the 5′ end. 

Therefore, reading exactly left to right matching the letters, the anticodon sequence is 3′ AUG 5′. If you look at the options, 3′ AUG 5′ perfectly displays both the correct base pairs and the vital antiparallel orientation. If it said 5′ AUG 3′, the strands would clash and fail to bind. Always check the prime (′) numbers!

questions.Question: 40. If A and C make 30% and 20% of DNA, respectively, what will be the percentage composition of T . and G ?
questions.Hint: Remember Erwin Chargaff's strict rule for double-stranded DNA! Adenine (A) exclusively pairs with Thymine (T), and Cytosine (C) exclusively pairs with Guanine (G). This means their amounts must be identical.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's imagine a magnificent molecular dance party happening right inside the nucleus of your cells! At this DNA dance party, the rules are incredibly strict but beautiful: Adenine (A) will ONLY ever dance with Thymine (T), and Cytosine (C) will ONLY ever dance with Guanine (G). 

This brilliant discovery was made by a scientist named Erwin Chargaff, and it is known globally as Chargaff's Rule. To understand why this rule exists, we have to look at the physical shapes of these molecules. Adenine and Guanine are large, double-ringed molecules called 'purines'. Cytosine and Thymine are smaller, single-ringed molecules called 'pyrimidines'. To keep the twisting DNA staircase perfectly even in width, a large purine must always be paired with a small pyrimidine! Furthermore, they connect using chemical magnets called hydrogen bonds: A and T share two hydrogen bonds, while C and G share three. 

Because they only exist in these exclusive pairs, the mathematics of DNA becomes beautifully simple. If we know how many 'A' dancers there are, we automatically know how many 'T' dancers there are, because no one dances alone. 

The question tells us that Adenine (A) makes up 30% of the DNA. Because every single A is locked in a pair with a T, Thymine (T) must also make up exactly 30% of the DNA. 

Next, the question tells us Cytosine (C) makes up 20% of the DNA. Since every C dances exclusively with a G, Guanine (G) must also make up exactly 20%. 

Let's check our total math to be sure we've accounted for the whole DNA molecule: 30% (A) + 30% (T) + 20% (C) + 20% (G) = 100%. Everything adds up perfectly! So, T is 30% and G is 20%. It really is that simple once you understand the dance rules of the nucleus!

questions.Question: 41. The process of translation of mRNA to proteins begins as soon as :
MCQ_Options: The small subunit of the ribosome encounters the mRNA
The large subunit of the ribosome joins the complex
The first tRNA binds to the start codon
questions.Hint: Think about the very first physical contact required in the cytoplasm to initiate the reading of the mRNA recipe. The protein-building machine comes in two pieces; which piece grabs the mRNA first?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you have just written a highly secret recipe for a cake (the mRNA) inside your home office (the nucleus). You print it out and carry it to your kitchen counter (the cytoplasm). To actually bake the cake (the protein), you need a master chef. In a cell, the 'chef' is an amazing molecular machine called the ribosome. 

But here is the cool part: the ribosome doesn't roam around as one giant piece. When it isn't working, it is split into two separate halves: a small subunit and a large subunit. They float around the cytoplasm completely independently. 

So, when does the process of 'translation' officially begin? The exact moment of initiation triggers the second the small subunit of the ribosome bumps into and attaches to the mRNA strand. 

The small subunit is like the chef's eyes locking onto the paper of the recipe. Once this small subunit binds to the mRNA, it starts sliding down the strand looking for the special 'Start' signal (the AUG codon). When it finds the start codon, a delivery truck (initiator tRNA) carrying the very first ingredient (an amino acid called Methionine) parks onto it. Only after all of this happens does the heavy large subunit crash down on top, locking everything together to form the complete functioning factory. 

However, the grand sequence of events is set into motion much earlier. Biologically, the true trigger—the recognized beginning of the translation phase—is that initial encounter when the small subunit of the ribosome physically latches onto the mRNA. Before that moment, the mRNA is just floating instructions. The small subunit's attachment changes everything!
questions.Answer: The small subunit of the ribosome encounters the mRNA

questions.Question: 42. DNA polymorphism forms the basis of :
questions.Hint: 'Poly' means many, and 'morph' means forms. Because human DNA naturally has small variations (many forms) across different people, what amazing forensic and medical tools can scientists create?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's break down the fascinating scientific word 'Polymorphism.' In Greek, 'Poly' means many, and 'morph' means form. So, DNA polymorphism simply means that our DNA exists in many slightly different forms across different people in the population. 

You and I share about 99.9% of the exact same DNA sequence. That is what makes us humans! It gives us one head, two arms, and a beating heart. But what about that tiny, leftover 0.1% difference? That is where polymorphisms live. These are little variations, mutations, or 'typos' mostly hidden in the non-coding 'junk' parts of our DNA. Because they are in non-coding regions, they don't hurt us or cause diseases, but they are inherited from our parents. They act like a completely unique genetic barcode! 

Because scientists know these unique variations exist, they can exploit them for two massive breakthroughs. 

First, Genetic Mapping. Scientists can use these known variations like mile-markers on a highway. By tracing how these markers are passed down in families, they can map out our chromosomes and locate exactly where hidden disease-causing genes are located. 

Second, DNA Fingerprinting! This was developed by a genius named Alec Jeffreys. Since everyone's 'barcode' of variations (called VNTRs) is totally unique, forensic scientists can take a tiny drop of blood or a single hair left at a crime scene, extract the DNA, and look at the polymorphisms. If the barcode of the blood matches the suspect's barcode perfectly, they have caught their criminal! 

If human DNA was 100% identical and had no polymorphisms, everyone's DNA test would look exactly the same. Therefore, the very existence of DNA polymorphism forms the foundational basis for both genetic mapping and DNA fingerprinting!

questions.Question:
Read the following statements and choose the set of correct statements :
(a) Euchromatin is loosely packed chromatin
(b) Heterochromatin is transcriptionally active
(c) Histone octomer is wrapped by negatively charged DNA in nucleosome
(d) Histones are rich in lysine and arginine
(e) A typical nucleosome contains 400 bp of DNA helix
questions.Hint: Think of DNA as a really long thread. How do you pack it so it doesn't tangle? Remember, DNA is an acid, so think about what kind of charge it carries, and how the 'spools' must be charged to hold onto it tight!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's solve this by thinking about how your cells pack away DNA. Imagine you have a 2-meter-long charging cable and you need to stuff it into your tiny pocket. If you just shove it in, it becomes a tangled, unusable nightmare. Your microscopic cells have the exact same problem: they have 2 meters of DNA that strictly needs to fit inside a microscopic nucleus. How do they do it? They use specialized biological 'spools' called histones to wrap the DNA up neatly!

Let's look at the statements one by one like a detective:
(a) Euchromatin is the loosely packed DNA. Think of it as an open book that the cell machinery can easily read to make proteins. Because it is loose and readable, this statement is absolutely TRUE.
(b) Heterochromatin is tightly, densely packed DNA. Because it's packed so tight, the cell's reading machinery can't squeeze inside to read it. It is transcriptionally inactive (silent). So, this statement is FALSE.
(c) DNA is called Deoxyribonucleic ACID. Because of its phosphate groups, DNA carries a strong *negative* electrical charge. Histones are *positively* charged. As we know from magnets, opposites attract! The negative DNA wraps perfectly and tightly around the positive histone octamer (a group of 8 histones). This is TRUE.
(d) To make the histones positively charged, they are loaded with special building blocks (amino acids) called lysine and arginine. These specific amino acids naturally carry positive charges, acting like the positive end of a battery. This is TRUE.
(e) A single 'spool' wrapped with DNA is called a nucleosome. If you count the steps (base pairs) on the DNA wrapped around one nucleosome, a typical one has about 200 base pairs, not 400. So this is FALSE.

Looking at our detective work, the correct statements are (a), (c), and (d)!

questions.Question: If a geneticist uses the blind approach for sequencing the whole genome of an organism, followed by assignment of function to different segments, the methodology adopted by him is called as :
questions.Hint: If you are reading an entire massive book blindly (even the blank pages and gibberish) and only later figuring out what each chapter means, you are 'annotating' the full sequence!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are an adventurous explorer who just uncovered a massive ancient scroll written in an alien language. You are tasked with understanding what it says, and you essentially have two main ways to study it.

Approach 1: You could quickly skim through the scroll and only look at the parts that look like actual recipes or useful instructions, ignoring all the blank spaces and gibberish. In biology, when scientists only look at the genes that actually make proteins (the useful recipes), it is called using Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs).

Approach 2: You decide to be incredibly thorough. You sit down and blindly copy down *every single letter* on the entire scroll, from start to finish. You write down the important recipes, the blank spaces, the repeated nonsense, everything! Only after copying the whole massive scroll do you sit down with a dictionary and figure out what each part does.

This second method is exactly what scientists did during the famous Human Genome Project! They called this bold strategy **Sequence Annotation**. They sequenced the whole human genome blindly—the important genes, the 'junk' DNA, all 3 billion letters of it. Then, they used powerful supercomputers to 'annotate' or assign functions to the different segments. It is exactly like copying an entire giant textbook first, and then going back later with a colorful highlighter to mark up the chapters, headings, and index. It's a huge task, but it gives you the complete picture of an organism's genetic code!

questions.Question: If the length of a DNA molecule is 1.1 metres, what will be the approximate number of base pairs?
questions.Hint: The distance between two steps (base pairs) on the DNA spiral staircase is 0.34 nanometers (0.34 x 10^-9 meters). If you know the total length is 1.1 meters, just divide the total length by the step size!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's solve this biological math puzzle together! Don't worry, it is actually a lot of fun to visualize. Imagine your DNA is a super-long, twisted spiral staircase. Every single step on this spiral staircase is called a 'base pair' (bp), because it is made of two chemical bases holding hands across the middle.

Biologists have used advanced x-rays to measure the exact distance between two steps on this microscopic staircase. It turns out the distance is incredibly tiny—about $0.34 \times 10^{-9}$ meters. (That is 0.34 nanometers!).

Now, the question gives us a really cool piece of information: the total length of the DNA staircase is 1.1 meters long.

Think about it like this: If you have a real staircase that is 10 meters tall, and each step is 1 meter tall, how many steps are there? You just divide 10 by 1, which equals 10 steps! We use the exact same logic here.

Number of steps (base pairs) = Total length of DNA / distance between each step.
Number of base pairs = 1.1 meters / ($0.34 \times 10^{-9}$ meters).

When you divide 1.1 by 0.34, you get roughly 3.23. Then you bring the $10^{-9}$ up to the top from the denominator, making it a positive $10^9$. Rounding it to a simpler number gives us exactly $3.3 \times 10^9$ base pairs!

That is 3.3 billion base pairs packed into a single cell! Fun fact: 3.3 billion base pairs is the exact size of a human haploid cell (like a sperm or egg cell). A regular human skin cell has double that—6.6 billion base pairs stretching over 2.2 meters! You are literally carrying miles of biological code inside you.

questions.Question: In an E. Coli strain i gene gets mutated and its product can not bind the inducer molecule. If growth medium is provided with lactose, what will be the outcome?
MCQ_Options: The lac operon will remain permanently turned off.
The lac operon will be expressed continuously (constitutively).
RNA polymerase will easily bind to the promoter.
Z, Y, and A genes will be transcribed at a very high rate.
questions.Hint: The repressor protein is like a stubborn security guard. If the 'inducer' (lactose) cannot grab him to pull him away from his post, he will never step away from the DNA!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is one of my absolute favorite biological puzzles! We are looking at a system in bacteria called the *lac operon*. Think of the lac operon as a special factory that digests milk sugar (lactose). The bacteria only wants to turn this factory ON when milk is actually around. Otherwise, it wastes precious energy.

To keep the factory OFF when there is no milk, a stubborn 'security guard' protein (called the repressor, which is made by the *i* gene) sits right on top of the factory's power switch (the operator region of the DNA). When the guard is sitting there, the factory cannot run at all.

Normally, when lactose arrives, it acts like a bribe. Lactose (the inducer) binds to the security guard, changes his shape, and makes him fall off the power switch. Boom! The switch is flipped, and the factory turns ON to digest the sugar.

BUT, in this specific question, the *i* gene is mutated! The security guard's 'hands' are broken, and he CANNOT grab the lactose bribe anymore.

If he can't bind to the lactose inducer, he never gets distracted. He doesn't even know the lactose is there! He will just sit on the power switch forever, stubbornly doing his job. So, even if you feed the bacteria a massive ton of lactose, the factory will never turn on. The lac operon remains permanently switched off, and transcription of the digestion genes cannot happen!
questions.Answer: The lac operon will remain permanently turned off.

questions.Question: Ten E.coli cells with 15N - dsDNA are incubated in medium containing 14N nucleotide. After 60 minutes, how many E.coli cells will have DNA totally free from 15N ?
questions.Hint: Bacteria divide every 20 minutes. Keep tracking the 'heavy' strands—they never disappear, but they get spread thinner among the new 'light' cells. Sketch out 3 generations (which is 60 minutes)!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Get ready to track some heavy DNA! This question is based on the famous Meselson-Stahl experiment, which proved how DNA perfectly copies itself.

Imagine DNA as a zipper with two sides. When it copies itself, the zipper unzips down the middle. Each old half gets a brand new half built right next to it. This is called semi-conservative replication.

We start with 10 E.coli cells. Their DNA is made entirely of heavy Nitrogen (15N). So both sides of their DNA zippers are HEAVY. Let's call them (Heavy-Heavy).
Now, we put them in a bath of light Nitrogen (14N). Every new half-zipper built from now on will be LIGHT.

Bacteria divide every 20 minutes. We are given 60 minutes, which means 3 generations of division (60 / 20 = 3).

Generation 0 (Start): 10 cells. All 10 have (Heavy-Heavy) DNA. That means we have 20 Heavy strands in total. *Golden Rule: These 20 Heavy strands will NEVER disappear, but no new Heavy strands will ever be made.*

Generation 1 (20 mins): The 10 cells divide into 20 cells. The 20 Heavy strands split up. So all 20 cells get one old Heavy strand and build one new Light strand. All 20 cells are (Heavy-Light) hybrids!

Generation 2 (40 mins): The 20 cells divide into 40 cells. The 20 Heavy strands still only go into 20 cells (making them Heavy-Light hybrids). The remaining 20 cells get entirely new Light-Light DNA!

Generation 3 (60 mins): The 40 cells divide into 80 cells total. The 20 Heavy strands STILL only go into 20 cells (making 20 Heavy-Light hybrids). This means out of 80 total cells, exactly 20 have some Heavy 15N DNA.

The question asks: How many cells are TOTALLY FREE from 15N (Heavy)?
We take the Total cells (80) and subtract the Hybrid cells that have 15N (20).
80 - 20 = 60 cells.
Exactly 60 cells will have purely Light-Light DNA!

questions.Question: Complete the flow chart on central dogma: DNA -> (A) -> mRNA -> (B) -> Protein. What are processes A and B?
